Thus $T$ is an ideal of the Noetherian ring $B$, hence finitely generated as $B$- and as $A$-module, and $\pi^nT=0$. As an $A$-module it is annihilated by $a$ (it is a $B$-module) and by $\pi^n$, so $\operatorname{Supp}_A(T)\subseteq V(a,\pi)\subseteq\{\mathfrak m\}$; by the auxiliary claim $\operatorname{length} T<\infty$.

STEP 6. $\operatorname{length} T/\pi T=\operatorname{length}(0:_B\pi)$.
Let $F$ be any finite-length $A$-module with $\pi^mF=0$. The map $F\to \pi F$, $f\mapsto\pi f$, is surjective with kernel $0:_F\pi$, so $0\to 0:_F\pi\to F\to\pi F\to0$ is exact; and $0\to\pi F\to F\to F/\pi F\to0$ is exact. All terms have finite length (subquotients of $F$), so additivity gives $\operatorname{length}F=\operatorname{length}(0:_F\pi)+\operatorname{length}\pi F=\operatorname{length}\pi F+\operatorname{length}F/\pi F$, whence
$$\operatorname{length} F/\pi F=\operatorname{length}(0:_F\pi).\tag{6.1}$$
Apply this to $F=T$ (with $m=n$ from Step 5). Since every element of $B$ killed by $\pi$ is killed by $\pi^1$, it lies in $T$; hence $0:_T\pi=0:_B\pi$. Therefore
$$\operatorname{length} T/\pi T=\operatorname{length}(0:_T\pi)=\operatorname{length}(0:_B\pi).\tag{6.2}$$

STEP 7. $0:_B\pi\ \simeq\ 0:_M t$ as $A$-modules (here $0:_Aa=0$ is used).
Define $\varphi:0:_B\pi\to M$ as follows. Given $\bar b\in 0:_B\pi$, choose a lift $x\in A$ with $\bar b=x+aA$. Then $0=\pi\bar b=\pi x+aA$, so $\pi x\in aA$, say $\pi x=ac$ with $c\in A$. Since $a$ is a non-zero-divisor, this $c$ is **unique**. Set $\varphi(\bar b)=c+\pi A\in M=A/\pi A$.
Well-definedness in the choice of lift: if $x'=x+ay$ is another lift, then $\pi x'=\pi x+a\pi y=a(c+\pi y)$, and uniqueness of the element $c'$ with $\pi x'=ac'$ gives $c'=c+\pi y$, so $c'+\pi A=c+\pi A$. (Without $0:_Aa=0$ neither uniqueness nor well-definedness holds.)
$A$-linearity: for lifts $x_1,x_2$ of $\bar b_1,\bar b_2$ with $\pi x_i=a c_i$, we have $\pi(x_1+x_2)=a(c_1+c_2)$, so $\varphi(\bar b_1+\bar b_2)=c_1+c_2+\pi A$; and $\pi(rx)=a(rc)$ gives $\varphi(r\bar b)=r\varphi(\bar b)$.
Image: $t\,\varphi(\bar b)=ac+\pi A=\pi x+\pi A=0$ in $M$, so $\operatorname{im}\varphi\subseteq 0:_M t$.
Injectivity: if $\varphi(\bar b)=0$ then $c=\pi c'$ for some $c'\in A$, so $\pi x=a\pi c'=\pi(ac')$; since $\pi$ is $A$-regular (a), $x=ac'$, hence $\bar b=x+aA=0$.
Surjectivity onto $0:_M t$: let $\bar c=c+\pi A\in M$ with $t\bar c=0$, i.e. $ac\in\pi A$; write $ac=\pi x$. Put $\bar b=x+aA\in B$. Then $\pi\bar b=\pi x+aA=ac+aA=0$, so $\bar b\in 0:_B\pi$, and by definition of $\varphi$ applied to the lift $x$ (with $\pi x=ac$) we get $\varphi(\bar b)=c+\pi A=\bar c$.
Thus $\varphi$ is an isomorphism $0:_B\pi\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ 0:_M t$; in particular
$$\operatorname{length}(0:_B\pi)=\operatorname{length}(0:_M t)<\infty.\tag{7.1}$$
(Equivalently: this is the connecting homomorphism of the snake lemma applied to the commutative diagram with exact rows $0\to A\xrightarrow{a}A\to B\to0$ and vertical maps $\times\pi$; the left two vertical maps are injective by (a), giving exactness $0\to 0:_B\pi\xrightarrow{\ \delta\ }A/\pi A\xrightarrow{\ t\ }A/\pi A$, with $\delta(x+aA)=c+\pi A$ when $\pi x=ac$.)

STEP 8. Conclusion.
Combining (4.2), (6.2) and (7.1),
$$\operatorname{length}_A A/(\pi,I)=\operatorname{length}_A M/tM-\operatorname{length}_A T/\pi T=\operatorname{length}_A M/tM-\operatorname{length}_A(0:_B\pi)=\operatorname{length}_A M/tM-\operatorname{length}_A(0:_M t),$$
which is the required identity. Every module whose length was subtracted was shown to have finite length in Steps 2 and 5, so no step involves an undefined quantity. This completes the proof. $\blacksquare$

statement: Let k be a field finitely generated over its prime field, let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let L/k be a finitely generated field extension of transcendence degree at least one, and let α ∈ CH^d(X × X) have zero image in CH^d(X_L × X_L). Then there exists a field E, finitely generated over k and of transcendence degree one over k, such that the image of α in CH^d(X_E × X_E) is zero.
proof:
Proof. Put Y=X×_k X. Since dim Y=2d, CH^d(Y) is the group of d-cycles modulo rational equivalence. Let A be a d-cycle on Y representing α. Since α_L=0, A_L is rationally equivalent to zero. By the graph description of rational equivalence, there exists a (d+1)-cycle C on Y_L×P^1_L, with no irreducible component contained in any fiber of the projection to P^1_L, such that ∂C=A_L, where ∂D=D_0-D_∞ denotes the difference of the fiber cycles over 0 and ∞ (identified with cycles on Y_L via the first projection). Indeed, divisors of rational functions are exactly boundaries of closures of graphs of rational functions.

Because L/k is finitely generated, choose a finitely generated k-domain A_0⊂L with Frac(A_0)=L and such that C is defined over A_0. Let S_0=Spec A_0, T=Y_{S_0}×P^1_{S_0}, H_0=Y_{S_0}×{0}, H_∞=Y_{S_0}×{∞}. Choose a (d+1)-cycle C_0 on T whose generic fiber is C, by taking closures of the generic integral components of C.

Claim: after replacing S_0 by a non-empty open subset U, there is a (d+1)-cycle C_U on T_U such that (1) C_U→U is flat and every fiber has dimension d+1; (2) no irreducible component of any fiber C_{U,u} is contained in H_{0,u} or H_{∞,u}; (3) ∂C_U=A_U in Z_d(Y_U).

Proof of claim. Write C=Σ n_i[Z_{i,η}] with Z_{i,η} integral, and let Z_i⊂T be the closure of Z_{i,η}; put C_0=Σ n_i[Z_i]. Each Z_i is integral and dominant over S_0. Since Z_{i,η} is not contained in H_{0,η} or H_{∞,η}, no component of Z_i is contained in H_0 or H_∞. By generic flatness (standard generic flatness for finite type algebras over a Noetherian domain), after shrinking S_0 to a non-empty open subset, each Z_i→U is flat. By upper semicontinuity of fiber dimension, shrink further so every fiber of Z_i→U has dimension d+1.

For ε∈{0,∞}, set W_{i,ε}=Z_i∩H_ε. Its generic fiber is Z_{i,η}∩H_{ε,η}; since Z_{i,η} is an integral variety of dimension d+1 not contained in the Cartier divisor H_{ε,η}, this generic fiber has pure dimension d. Remove from the base the images of those irreducible components of W_{i,ε} that do not dominate S_0. Then every component of W_{i,ε} dominates the base. Apply generic flatness to each such component and shrink further so all components of W_{i,ε} are flat over U; shrink also so their fibers have dimension d. This also gives (2): if a component of (Z_i)_u were contained in H_{ε,u}, it would be a vertical component of W_{i,ε}, which has been removed.

On this open set define C_U=Σ n_i[Z_i|_U] and C_{U,ε}=Σ n_i[W_{i,ε}|_U]. Then C_{U,ε} is the cycle obtained by intersecting C_U with H_ε, and ∂C_U=C_{U,0}-C_{U,∞}. The generic fiber of ∂C_U is ∂C=A_η. Therefore D=A_U-∂C_U has generic fiber zero. Hence every irreducible component of D is vertical over U. Removing the images of these finitely many vertical components gives a non-empty open subset, still called U, on which D=0. This proves the claim.

Now choose a closed point u∈U. Such a point exists because A_0 is a finitely generated k-algebra, hence Jacobson, and U is non-empty open. Let F=κ(u). By Zariski's lemma, F/k is finite. Base change the relative rational equivalence from U to u. Since C_U, C_{U,0}, C_{U,∞} are flat over U and no component is contained in H_0 or H_∞, taking the fiber over u commutes with taking the boundary: ∂C_u=(C_{U,0})_u-(C_{U,∞})_u=(∂C_U)_u=A_u. Thus C_u is a (d+1)-cycle on Y_F×P^1_F with no components in the two horizontal divisors and with ∂C_u=A_F. Hence A_F is rationally equivalent to zero, so α_F=0 in CH^d(Y_F)=CH^d(X_F×X_F).

Finally set E=F(t), the rational function field in one variable over F. Then E is finitely generated over k and has transcendence degree one over k. By lemma_46 (with base field F and extension E/F), the base-change map CH^d(X_F×X_F)→CH^d(X_E×X_E) is a ring homomorphism, hence sends 0 to 0. Therefore α_E=0. This proves the lemma.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let L/k be a field extension, and let alpha \in CH^d(X\times X) have zero image in CH^d(X_L\times X_L). Then there exists a positive integer n such that n\cdot alpha = 0.
proof:
{
  "lemma_id": "kernel_classes_are_torsion",
  "cited_lemmas": [],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "Proof. Put V = X ×_k X. We first use the elementary fact that for any field extension F'/F and any m, pullback of m-cycles Z_m(Y_F) → Z_m(Y_{F'}) is injective. Indeed, write a cycle as ∑ n_i [Y_i] with distinct integral Y_i. If its pullback is zero, then for each i the scheme Y_i ×_F F' is nonempty because F' ⊗_F κ(Y_i) ≠ 0; every component of it has closure Y_i, and components lying over different Y_i are disjoint. The coefficient of a component over Y_i is n_i times a positive integer, so n_i = 0.

If α = 0, take n = 1. If d = 0, then X is finite étale over k, rational equivalence on V is trivial, and α_L = 0 means that a representative Z of α satisfies Z_L = 0 as a cycle. The injectivity just proved gives Z = 0, hence α = 0. Thus assume d ≥ 1.

Choose a d-cycle Z = ∑_i n_i Z_i on V representing α. Since α_L = 0, by the P^1 description of rational equivalence there are finitely many integral closed subschemes Γ_j ⊂ V_L × P^1_L of dimension d+1, dominant over P^1_L, and integers c_j such that Z_L = ∑_j c_j (p_j)_*([Γ_{j,0}] - [Γ_{j,∞}]) in Z_d(V_L), where p_j: Γ_j → V_L is the projection and Γ_{j,0}, Γ_{j,∞} are the inverse images of the sections 0,∞: Spec L → P^1_L. This description is equivalent to the usual one: the graph of a rational function gives such a family, and the divisor of the coordinate function on P^1 gives the corresponding principal divisor.

Choose a finitely generated subfield K/k of L over which all Γ_j are defined. Let Γ_{j,K} ⊂ V_K × P^1_K be the corresponding closed subschemes. Since Γ_{j,K,L} = Γ_j is integral, Γ_{j,K} is integral. Define B_K = ∑_j c_j (p_{j,K})_*([Γ_{j,K,0}] - [Γ_{j,K,∞}]). Base changing this equality over K to L gives Z_L, because Cartier pullback and proper pushforward commute with flat base change. By injectivity of cycle pullback K → L, B_K = Z_K.

Choose a finitely generated k-domain A with Frac(A) = K. By spreading out, after replacing A by a localization A_f, there exist closed subschemes ScriptGamma_j ⊂ V_A ×_A P

^1_A whose generic fibre over K is Γ_{j,K}. Let Z_A be the base change of Z to V_A. For each j let p_j:ScriptGamma_j→V_A and h_j:ScriptGamma_j→P^1_A be the projections, and put ScriptGamma_{j,0}=h_j^{-1}(0) and ScriptGamma_{j,∞}=h_j^{-1}(∞). By generic flatness, and by deleting the closed subsets over which the two divisors acquire vertical components, we may shrink A so that each ScriptGamma_j is integral and flat over A of relative dimension d+1, and each ScriptGamma_{j,0} and ScriptGamma_{j,∞} is flat over A of relative dimension d; after this shrink they are effective Cartier divisors on the fibres over a non-empty open U⊂Spec A. Define B_A=∑_j c_j(p_j)_*([ScriptGamma_{j,0}]-[ScriptGamma_{j,∞}]). Since Cartier pullback and proper pushforward commute with flat base change, the generic fibre of B_A is B_K=Z_K. Hence Δ_A=Z_A-B_A has zero generic fibre, so Supp(Δ_A) is a finite union of closed subsets of Spec A not containing the generic point. Choose a closed point s∈U not in Supp(Δ_A); this is possible because A is a finitely generated k-domain, hence Jacobson, and closed points are dense in U. Put E=κ(s). By Zariski's lemma E/k is finite. Specialising at s gives Z_E=(B_A)_s. By compatibility of proper pushforward of cycles flat over A with flat base change, and by Cartier base change for the two effective Cartier divisors, (B_A)_s=∑_j c_j(p_{j,s})_*([ScriptGamma_{j,0,s}]-[ScriptGamma_{j,∞,s}]). Fix j, write Y=ScriptGamma_{j,s}, Y_0=ScriptGamma_{j,0,s}, and Y_∞=ScriptGamma_{j,∞,s}. Then Y⊂V_E×P^1_E has pure dimension d+1. Write [Y]=∑_a m_a[E_a] as a sum over integral components with multiplicities. The coordinate t on P^1_E is a rational function on Y which is invertible at the generic point of every E_a, since no E_a is contained in Y_0 or Y_∞. For an effective Cartier divisor D on a pure-dimensional noetherian scheme Y, if [Y]=∑_a m_a[E_a] and D contains no E_a, then [D]=∑_a m_a[D∩E_a]. Indeed, at a codimension-one point C, let O=O_{Y,C}; if f is a local equation for D, the coefficient of C in [D] is length_O(O/(f)), and the additivity of length in one-dimensional noetherian local rings gives length_O(O/(f))=∑_a length_{O_{p_a}}(O_{p_a}) length_{O/p_a}(O/p_a(f)), where p_a runs over the primes of O of dimension one corresponding to the components E_a containing C. Applying this to D=Y_0 and D=Y_∞ gives [Y_0]-[Y_∞]=∑_a m_a(div(t|_{E_a})). Therefore (p_{j,s})_*([Y_0]-[Y_∞])=∑_a m_a(p_{j,s})_*div(t|_{E_a}). Each term (p_{j,s})_*div(t|_{E_a}) is rationally trivial on V_E, because p_{j,s}|_{E_a}:E_a→V_E is proper and E_a is integral of dimension d+1. Hence Z_E is rationally trivial, i.e. α_E=0. Finally, let π:V_E→V be the finite locally free base-change map. Since α_E=0, π^*α=0. The projection formula for finite locally free maps of rank [E:k] gives π_*π^*α=[E:k]α. Thus [E:k]α=0. Taking n=[E:k] completes the proof."}

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let L/k be a field extension, and let K = ker(CH^d(X \times_k X) \to CH^d(X_L \times_L X_L)). Let \Delta \subset X \times_k X be the diagonal and let Y \subsetneq X be a proper closed subset such that dim((Y \times_k Y) \setminus \Delta) \le d-1. If \alpha \in K is such that \alpha \circ \alpha has a cycle representative supported on Y \times_k Y, then \alpha is nilpotent for composition of correspondences.
proof:
NOTATION AND CONVENTIONS. Write R = CH^d(X \times_k X) for the ring of degree-0 correspondences on X, with product \beta \circ \delta = p_{13*}(p_{12}^*\beta \cdot p_{23}^*\delta) on X^3 and unit [\Delta]; this is an associative ring, and R = CH_d(X\times_k X) identifies with codimension-d classes since \dim(X\times X)=2d. For \beta\in R let e(\beta) denote the invariant used in eoinm lemma_19 / eoinm lemma_24 / Spark lemma_53, namely the minimum of \dim(\operatorname{Supp}(Z)\setminus\Delta) over codimension-d (equivalently d-dimensional) cycles Z on X\times_k X with [Z]=\beta, with \dim\emptyset := -1. Two elementary facts about this invariant are used below, both immediate from the definition:
(a) the minimum exists, since the set of attained values is a non-empty subset of \{-1,0,1,\dots,2d\} (every class has a representative, supports are closed in the noetherian space X\times X so dimensions are \le 2d, and the empty support contributes -1);
(b) for any single chosen representative Z of \beta one has e(\beta) \le \dim(\operatorname{Supp}(Z)\setminus\Delta).
We also use monotonicity of dimension for locally closed subsets of a noetherian topological space: if S'\subset S then \dim S' := \sup\{\dim T : T\subset S' \text{ closed irreducible}\} \le \dim S, because every irreducible closed subset of S' is also one of S (its closure in S has the same dimension). Finally, Y\times_k Y \to X\times_k X is a closed immersion (base change of the closed immersion Y\hookrightarrow X), so we identify |Y\times_k Y| with a closed subset of |X\times_k X|.

STEP 1 (the square lies in the kernel). By eoinm lemma_16, K = \ker(R\to \mathrm{CH}^d(X_L\times_L X_L)) is a two-sided ideal of R. Since \alpha\in K and \alpha\in R, the product \alpha\circ\alpha lies in K (left-ideal property suffices). Put \gamma := \alpha\circ\alpha \in K. Note that \gamma is indeed an element of CH^d(X\times X): p_{12}^*\alpha\cdot p_{23}^*\alpha is a codimension-2d class on X^3 and p_{13} is proper of relative dimension d, so the pushforward is a codimension-d class on X\times X.

STEP 2 (the support bound forces e(\gamma) \le d-1). By hypothesis there exists a codimension-d cycle Z on X\times_k X with [Z]=\gamma and \operatorname{Supp}(Z)\subseteq |Y\times_k Y|. Then
\operatorname{Supp}(Z)\setminus\Delta \;\subseteq\; (Y\times_k Y)\setminus\Delta .
If Z\neq 0, monotonicity gives \dim(\operatorname{Supp}(Z)\setminus\Delta) \le \dim((Y\times_k Y)\setminus\Delta) \le d-1 by the hypothesis of the lemma. If Z=0, then \operatorname{Supp}(Z)=\emptyset and \dim(\operatorname{Supp}(Z)\setminus\Delta)=\dim\emptyset=-1\le d-1, since d\ge 0. Thus in all cases
\dim(\operatorname{Supp}(Z)\setminus\Delta)\le d-1,
and by fact (b) applied to this representative Z,
e(\gamma)\ \le\ d-1.
(Incidentally, if 2\dim Y<d then Y\times_k Y contains no d-dimensional subvariety at all, so Z=0 and \gamma=0 holds directly; the bound above covers this case uniformly.)

STEP 3 (the e-filtration kills \gamma). Apply eoinm lemma_24 to X/k, the extension L/k, the kernel K, the diagonal \Delta and the invariant e. It states that for each m\in\{-1,0,\dots,d\}, F^m := \{\beta\in K : e(\beta)\le m\} satisfies F^m=0 whenever m<d (and F^d=K). Take m=d-1. Then m<d, and m=-1 is permitted when d=0, so eoinm lemma_24 gives F^{d-1}=\{0\}. By Step 1, \gamma\in K, and by Step 2, e(\gamma)\le d-1; hence \gamma\in F^{d-1}=\{0\}, i.e.
\alpha\circ\alpha = \gamma = 0 \quad\text{in } \mathrm{CH}^d(X\times_k X).

STEP 4 (nilpotence). The equality \alpha^{\circ 2}=0 in the ring R means exactly that \alpha is nilpotent for composition of correspondences, with N=2\ge 1 (and then \alpha^{\circ M}=0 for every M\ge 2). This is the desired conclusion.

ALTERNATIVE (INDEPENDENT) DERIVATION OF THE SAME CONCLUSION, using weaker input. Steps 1 and 2 give \gamma\in K with e(\gamma)\le d-1. Spark lemma_53 then yields \gamma^{\circ(d+1)}=0, i.e. \alpha^{\circ 2(d+1)}=0 in R, which already states that \alpha is nilpotent (take N=2d+2). This derivation does not use eoinm lemma_24 and shows the conclusion is robust; the route through eoinm lemma_24 gives the strictly stronger statement \alpha^{\circ 2}=0.

REMARKS ON THE LOGIC OF THE ARGUMENT. (i) The hypothesis Y\subsetneq X is never used; only the numerical hypothesis \dim((Y\times_k Y)\setminus\Delta)\le d-1 enters, and it enters only in Step 2. (ii) The hypothesis \alpha\in K is used exactly once, in Step 1, and it is essential: the conclusion is obtained by feeding the class \gamma, which is both in K and has e-value < d, into the vanishing F^{d-1}=0 of eoinm lemma_24. Support information alone gives no nilpotence (e.g. when 2\dim Y = d the class [Y\times_k Y] is a nonzero idempotent of CH^d(X\times X) supported on Y\times Y), so no argument that merely tracks supports can prove this lemma. (iii) No claim of the form e(\gamma)\le 2\dim Y-1 is made: deleting the diagonal need not lower the dimension of Y\times Y; the honest bound \dim((Y\times_k Y)\setminus\Delta)\le d-1 is assumed, and it is precisely the hypothesis that pushes e(\gamma) strictly below d, the threshold at which eoinm lemma_24 stops giving information (its F^d=K). (iv) No base-change/descent input (Spark lemma_41, 57, 58, 66) and no intermediate smooth projective variety is needed: the whole argument takes place inside the e-framework on X\times_k X.

Thus every \alpha\in K whose square is representable with support in Y\times_k Y, with \dim((Y\times_k Y)\setminus\Delta)\le d-1, satisfies \alpha^{\circ 2}=0 and is therefore nilpotent for composition of correspondences. \hfill\blacksquare

statement: Let Y/k be a quasi-projective variety of dimension n, let K = k(t) be the function field of P^1_k, and let pi: Y \times_k P^1_k -> P^1_k be the projection. For each integer m \ge 1, define \partial_m : Z_m(Y \times_k P^1_k) -> Z_{m-1}(Y_K) by Z-linear extension from the rule that, for T integral closed of dimension m, \partial_m[T] is the fundamental cycle of the scheme-theoretic generic fibre T_\eta = T \times_{P^1_k} Spec K, namely the sum over the generic points xi of T_\eta of length_{O_{T_\eta,xi}}(O_{T_\eta,xi}) times the closure of xi in Y_K, when T dominates P^1_k, and \partial_m[T] = 0 when T is contained in a fibre of pi. Then the image under \partial_m of a cycle in Z_m(Y \times_k P^1_k) that is rationally equivalent to zero is rationally equivalent to zero in Z_{m-1}(Y_K).
proof:
PROOF.

Notation. Write \bar Y := Y \times_k \mathbf P^1_k, let \eta \in \mathbf P^1_k be the generic point and K = k(\mathbf P^1_k) = k(t). Let U_0 = \operatorname{Spec} k[t], U_1 = \operatorname{Spec} k[t^{-1}] be the two standard affines of \mathbf P^1_k. For an integral scheme V, k(V) denotes its function field. Since Y is a variety, Y is integral, separated and of finite type over k, and it has an affine open cover.

We use the following standard theorems of commutative algebra and scheme theory, stated explicitly so every appeal is visible:
(F1) Zariski's lemma: a field which is a finitely generated algebra over a subfield k is algebraic (indeed finite) over k.
(F2) Noether normalisation: if A is a finitely generated domain over a field F, then A admits a finite injective F[x_1,...,x_r] -> A with r = trdeg_F Frac(A); in particular dim A = trdeg_F Frac(A), and finite (integral) extensions preserve dimension.
(F3) Krull's principal ideal theorem: a minimal prime over a principal ideal in a Noetherian ring has height <= 1.
(F4) Chevalley: the image of a constructible subset under a morphism of finite type of Noetherian schemes is constructible.
(F5) Length is additive on short exact sequences of finite-length modules.
(F6) For a multiplicative set S in a ring A, Spec(S^{-1}A) -> Spec A is a homeomorphism onto the subspace {p in Spec A : p \cap S = \emptyset}.
(F7) Tower formula for transcendence degree: k \subset F \subset L fields implies trdeg_k L = trdeg_k F + trdeg_F L.

STEP 0. Dimensions and conventions.
For an affine open Y' = Spec B \subset Y (B a finitely generated k-domain of dimension n), Noether normalisation gives a finite injective k[x_1,...,x_n] -> B, hence a finite injective k[x_1,...,x_n][u] -> B[u]; thus dim(B[u]) = n+1. As B[u] is also a domain, each Y' \times_k \mathbf A^1 is integral of dimension n+1. Covering Y by such Y' shows \bar Y_\varepsilon := Y \times_k U_\varepsilon \cong \mathbf A^1_Y is integral of dimension n+1 (\varepsilon = 0,1), and \bar Y = \bar Y_0 \cup \bar Y_1 with \bar Y_0 \cap \bar Y_1 = \mathbf G_{m,Y} \neq \emptyset; hence \bar Y is integral of dimension n+1. Similarly Y_K = Y \times_k Spec K is quasi-projective of finite type over K of dimension n: for Y' = Spec B as above, B \otimes_k K is finite over K[x_1,...,x_n], hence of dimension n. We set Z_j(-) = 0 for j < 0. Only \partial_m with m >= 1 is ever used, and \partial_0 is never defined nor invoked.

STEP 1. Dichotomy for integral closed subschemes of dimension >= 1, and the two cases.
Let T \subset \bar Y be integral closed of dimension m >= 1. The map \pi|_T is of finite type with T Noetherian, so by (F4) E := \pi(|T|) is constructible; it is non-empty and irreducible (continuous image of an irreducible space). Its closure is an irreducible closed subset of \mathbf P^1_k, hence is either a single closed point, or {\eta}, or all of \mathbf P^1_k.

We shall use the following affine cover of T throughout. Fix an affine open cover {Y' = Spec B} of Y. For each Y' and each \varepsilon, T \cap (Y' \times_k U_\varepsilon) is a closed subscheme of the affine scheme Y' \times_k U_\varepsilon = Spec(B \otimes_k k[t]) (resp. Spec(B \otimes_k k[t^{-1}])), because T is closed in \bar Y and Y' \times_k U_\varepsilon is open in \bar Y; hence it is affine. Discarding empty members, these opens V cover T; write V = Spec A. Then A is a finitely generated k-algebra, and since V is a non-empty open of the integral scheme T, A is a finitely generated k-domain of dimension m.

Case (i): closure of E is a closed point s. Then E = {s}. Fix a standard affine U = Spec R containing s (R = k[t] or k[t^{-1}]; every closed point lies in at least one of U_0, U_1) and let p \subset R be the maximal ideal of s. Since |T| \subset \pi^{-1}(s) \subset \pi^{-1}(U), every member of the cover above with \varepsilon chosen so that U_\varepsilon = U covers T: V = T \cap (Y' \times_k U) = Spec A, and A is a finitely generated R-algebra. For every prime q \subset A the corresponding point of T maps to s, so q \cap R = p. Hence pA is contained in every prime of A, i.e. in the nilradical of A, which is (0) because A is a domain. Thus pA = 0, so A is an R/p = \kappa(s)-algebra and V -> U factors through Spec \kappa(s). The condition that \pi|_T factor through the closed subscheme {s} \hookrightarrow \mathbf P^1_k is the vanishing of the ideal sheaf \pi_T^{-1}(\mathcal I_{\{s\}})\cdot\mathcal O_T = p\cdot\mathcal O_T; this vanishes on the open cover {V}, hence globally. So \pi|_T factors through Spec \kappa(s) (the factorisation through a closed subscheme is unique). As T -> \bar Y is a closed immersion, T is a closed subscheme of \bar Y \times_{\mathbf P^1_k} Spec \kappa(s) = Y \times_k Spec \kappa(s) = \pi^{-1}(s): T is contained in the fibre over s.

Case (ii): E = {\eta}. We show this cannot occur. Take any non-empty member V = Spec A of the cover of Step 1, lying over U = Spec R (R = k[t] or k[t^{-1}]). V is a non-empty open of the irreducible space T, so \pi(V) is a non-empty constructible irreducible subset of E = {\eta}, hence \pi(V) = {\eta}. Thus every prime q \subset A satisfies q \cap R = (0). The kernel of R -> A is contained in every prime of A, hence in the nilradical (0); so R \hookrightarrow A is injective. Since A \neq 0 it has a maximal ideal n. Then A/n is a field which is a finitely generated k-algebra, so by (F1) A/n is algebraic over k. But n \cap R = (0), so R embeds into A/n, and the image of t (resp. t^{-1}) is transcendental over k, contradiction. Hence Case (ii) does not occur.

Case (iii): closure of E is \mathbf P^1_k. A dense constructible subset of \mathbf P^1_k contains a non-empty open subset, and every non-empty open of \mathbf P^1_k contains \eta; hence \eta \in E and \pi|_T is dominant; we say T dominates \mathbf P^1_k.

Conclusion of Step 1: every integral closed T \subset \bar Y of dimension m >= 1 either dominates \mathbf P^1_k or is contained in the scheme-theoretic fibre over a closed point. The two alternatives are mutually exclusive since T \neq \emptyset. In particular, for such T the generic fibre T_\eta := T \times_{\mathbf P^1_k} Spec K is empty in Case (i) (as Spec \kappa(s) \times_{\mathbf P^1_k} Spec K = \emptyset for s \neq \eta), and non-empty in Case (iii).

STEP 2. Well-definedness and shape of \partial_m on integral closed subschemes of dimension m >= 1.

Claim 2.1. Let T \subset \bar Y be integral closed of dimension m >= 1 dominating \mathbf P^1_k, with generic point \zeta_T. Then:
(a) |T_\eta| is the subspace {x \in |T| : \pi(x) = \eta} of |T|; T_\eta is integral of dimension m-1 with generic point \zeta_T; and T_\eta -> Y_K is a closed immersion.
(b) k(T_\eta) = k(T).
(c) For every x \in |T_\eta|, the closure of x in T_\eta equals \overline{\{x\}}^{\,T} \times_{\mathbf P^1_k} Spec K (equality of subsets of |T_\eta|).
(d) The fundamental cycle of T_\eta defined in the statement is the single cycle [\overline{\{\zeta_T\}}^{\,Y_K}] with coefficient 1; in particular it is an (m-1)-cycle on Y_K.

Proof of the claim. Cover T by the non-empty affine opens V = Spec A of Step 1 lying over a fixed chart U = Spec R (R = k[t] or k[t^{-1}]); this is legitimate since the \bar Y_\varepsilon cover \bar Y. Fix such a V.

Injectivity of R -> A: since \pi|_T is dominant with T and \mathbf P^1_k integral, there is an induced extension of function fields k(\mathbf P^1_k) = k(t) -> k(T), which is injective as a map of fields. If 0 \neq h \in R mapped to 0 in A, its image in k(T) would be 0, so h = 0 in k(t), contradiction. Thus R \hookrightarrow A, and S := R \setminus \{0\} maps into A \setminus \{0\}.

Base change is localisation: V_\eta := V \times_{\mathbf P^1_k} Spec K = V \times_U Spec K = Spec(A \otimes_R K) = Spec(S^{-1}A), the last identity being the definition of the localisation as a base change (A \otimes_R S^{-1}R = S^{-1}A). No flatness statement is used or needed. By (F6), |V_\eta| -> |V| is a homeomorphism onto {q \in Spec A : q \cap S = \emptyset} = {x \in |V| : \pi(x) = \eta}. Gluing over the cover, |T_\eta| is the subspace {x \in |T| : \pi(x) = \eta} of |T|, proving the first assertion of (a).

S^{-1}A is a non-zero domain (a localisation of the domain A at a set avoiding 0), so V_\eta is integral; its generic point is (0) \subset S^{-1}A, corresponding to (0) \subset A, i.e. to \zeta_T. Note \pi(\zeta_T) = \eta, since \zeta_T is the generic point of T and a dominant map of integral schemes sends generic point to generic point; hence \zeta_T \in |T_\eta|.

Irreducibility of T_\eta: let W \subset |T_\eta| be a non-empty open. Write W = W' \cap |T_\eta| with W' open in |T|. Then W' \neq \emptyset, so W' \cap V \neq \emptyset for some member V of the cover; W' \cap V is a non-empty open of the irreducible space V, hence contains \zeta_T; and \zeta_T \in |T_\eta|; so \zeta_T \in W. Thus every non-empty open of |T_\eta| contains \zeta_T. Any two non-empty opens then meet, so |T_\eta| is irreducible with generic point \zeta_T; combined with the fact that the V_\eta are integral open subsets covering T_\eta, T_\eta is integral.

Dimension: S^{-1}A is a finitely generated K-algebra (generated by the k-algebra generators of A) and a domain. By (F2), dim S^{-1}A = trdeg_K Frac(S^{-1}A). Since S \cap (0) = \emptyset, Frac(S^{-1}A) = Frac(A). By (F2) applied to the finitely generated k-domain A, trdeg_k Frac(A) = dim A = m; and trdeg_k K = 1. By (F7), trdeg_K Frac(A) = m - 1. Hence dim V_\eta = m-1 for every member of the cover, so dim T_\eta = m-1. This proves (a) (the closed immersion T_\eta -> Y_K is the base change of the closed immersion T -> \bar Y along Spec K -> \mathbf P^1_k).

(b) k(T_\eta) = Frac(S^{-1}A) = Frac(A) = k(T).

(c) Let x \in |T_\eta| and let V = Spec A be a member of the cover containing x; let q \subset A be the prime of x (so q \cap S = \emptyset). Using the homeomorphism of (F6), inside the open V_\eta of |T_\eta| we have
  \overline{\{x\}}^{T_\eta} \cap V_\eta = V(S^{-1}q) = {q' \in Spec A : q' \supset q,\ q' \cap S = \emptyset},
since primes of S^{-1}A correspond to primes of A disjoint from S; and, using |T_\eta| = {\pi = \eta} as a subspace of |T|,
  (\overline{\{x\}}^{\,T} \times_{\mathbf P^1_k} Spec K) \cap V_\eta = \{q' \in \mathrm{Spec}\,A : q' \supset q\} \cap \{q' : q' \cap S = \emptyset\},
the same subset of |V_\eta|. Both \overline{\{x\}}^{T_\eta} and \overline{\{x\}}^{\,T} \cap |T_\eta| are closed in |T_\eta| (the first by definition, the second because \overline{\{x\}}^{\,T} is closed in |T|), and they agree on the open cover {V_\eta} of |T_\eta|; hence they are equal.

(d) By the definition in the statement, the fundamental cycle of T_\eta is \sum_\xi length_{\mathcal O_{T_\eta,\xi}}(\mathcal O_{T_\eta,\xi})\,[\overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,Y_K}], summed over the generic points \xi of T_\eta. By (a) there is exactly one, \xi = \zeta_T. Since T_\eta is integral, \mathcal O_{T_\eta,\zeta_T} is the local ring at the generic point, i.e. the field k(T_\eta); a field has length 1 as a module over itself. So the fundamental cycle is [\overline{\{\zeta_T\}}^{\,Y_K}]. Since T_\eta \hookrightarrow Y_K is a closed immersion and T_\eta is integral with generic point \zeta_T, \overline{\{\zeta_T\}}^{\,Y_K} = T_\eta set-theoretically, of dimension m-1; hence this is an (m-1)-cycle on Y_K. \qed(claim)

By Step 1 and the claim, the assignment on the basis of Z_m(\bar Y) given by
  [T] \mapsto [\overline{\{\zeta_T\}}^{\,Y_K}] if T dominates \mathbf P^1_k, and [T] \mapsto 0 if T is contained in a fibre,
is well defined, and \partial_m is its Z-linear extension; this is exactly the map of the statement.

STEP 3. Divisors on integral finite type schemes over a field.
Let W be an integral scheme of finite type over a field (k or K) of dimension r >= 1. For f \in k(W)^* set div_W(f) := \sum_{\xi \in W^{(1)}} ord_\xi(f)\,[\overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,W}], where for \xi of codimension 1, \mathcal O_{W,\xi} is a 1-dimensional Noetherian local domain and, writing f = a/b with a,b \in \mathcal O_{W,\xi}\setminus\{0\},
  ord_\xi(f) := length_{\mathcal O_{W,\xi}}(\mathcal O_{W,\xi}/(a)) - length_{\mathcal O_{W,\xi}}(\mathcal O_{W,\xi}/(b)).
We check this is well defined and has finite support.
(i) Finiteness of the lengths: by (F3) every minimal prime of (a) has height <= 1; as \mathcal O_{W,\xi} is a 1-dimensional local domain and (a) \neq 0, such a minimal prime is the maximal ideal; hence Spec(\mathcal O/(a)) = {\mathfrak m}, so \mathcal O/(a) is a Noetherian ring with a single prime, i.e. Artinian, of finite length.
(ii) Independence of f = a/b: if also f = c/d with c,d \neq 0, then ad = bc. Multiplication by d gives an exact sequence 0 -> \mathcal O/(c) -> \mathcal O/(cd) -> \mathcal O/(d) -> 0 (injective since \mathcal O is a domain and d \neq 0: dx \in (cd) implies x \in (c)). By (F5), length \mathcal O/(cd) = length \mathcal O/(c) + length \mathcal O/(d). Applying this to ad = bc gives length \mathcal O/(a) + length \mathcal O/(d) = length \mathcal O/(b) + length \mathcal O/(c), i.e. the difference is unchanged.
(iii) Finite support: cover W by finitely many non-empty affine opens U_1,...,U_s (W is Noetherian, hence quasi-compact). Each U_i contains the generic point \zeta_W and \mathcal O_{W,\zeta_W} = Frac\,\Gamma(U_i) = k(W), so write f = a_i/b_i with a_i,b_i \in \Gamma(U_i)\setminus\{0\}. Put Z_i := V(a_i) \cup V(b_i) \subset U_i (closed in U_i) and
  E := \bigcup_{i=1}^{s}\big(\overline{Z_i}^{\,W} \cup (W \setminus U_i)\big).
This is a finite union of closed subsets of W, hence closed in W. The generic point \zeta_W does not lie in E: \zeta_W \in U_i and a_i,b_i are non-zero elements of the domain \Gamma(U_i), so \zeta_W \notin Z_i; and since Z_i is closed in U_i we have \overline{Z_i}^{\,W} \cap U_i = Z_i, while \zeta_W \in U_i, so \zeta_W \notin \overline{Z_i}^{\,W}. Thus E is a proper closed subset of the r-dimensional irreducible space W, and dim E <= r-1. If \xi \in W^{(1)} \setminus E then \xi \in U_i for all i and a_i,b_i \notin p_\xi, so both are units of \mathcal O_{W,\xi} and ord_\xi(f) = 0 - 0 = 0. Finally W^{(1)} \cap E is finite: its points are exactly the generic points of the irreducible components of E of dimension r-1 (a codimension-one point of W lying in E is the generic point of such a component, and conversely), and a Noetherian space has finitely many irreducible components. Hence div_W(f) \in Z_{r-1}(W) is well defined.

STEP 4. The key identity (correctly indexed).
Let m >= 1, let T \subset \bar Y be integral closed of dimension m+1, and let f \in k(T)^*. Then
  \partial_m(div_T(f)) = div_{T_\eta}(f) in Z_{m-1}(Y_K) if T dominates \mathbf P^1_k, and \partial_m(div_T(f)) = 0 if T is contained in a fibre.

Write div_T(f) = \sum_{\xi \in T^{(1)}} n_\xi\,[\overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,T}] with n_\xi = ord_\xi^T(f); the sum is finite by Step 3, and each \overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,T} is an integral closed subscheme of \bar Y of dimension m (since dim T = m+1 and \xi has codimension 1).

Vertical case. If T \subset \pi^{-1}(s), then every \overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,T} \subset \pi^{-1}(s) is an integral closed subscheme of \bar Y of dimension m contained in a fibre, so \partial_m[\overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,T}] = 0 by definition of \partial_m; by Z-linearity \partial_m(div_T f) = 0.

Horizontal case. Assume T dominates; then dim T_\eta = m by Claim 2.1. Split T^{(1)} into H := {\xi : \pi(\xi) = \eta} and V := {\xi : \pi(\xi) \neq \eta}.
For \xi \in V: \pi(\xi) is a closed point s of \mathbf P^1_k (the only non-closed point is \eta), and \pi(\overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,T}) is constructible with closure \overline{\{\pi(\xi)\}} = \{s\}; hence \pi(\overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,T}) = \{s\}. Applying Step 1 Case (i) to the integral closed subscheme \overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,T} of dimension m >= 1 gives that \overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,T} is contained in the fibre \pi^{-1}(s), so \partial_m[\overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,T}] = 0.
For \xi \in H: put W := \overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,T}, of dimension m. Since \pi(\xi) = \eta, W dominates \mathbf P^1_k. Claim 2.1 applied to W (dimension m >= 1) says W_\eta is integral of dimension m-1 with generic point \xi (the generic point of W), and by (d) \partial_m[W] = [\overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,Y_K}]. Therefore
  \partial_m(div_T f) = \sum_{\xi \in H} n_\xi\,[\overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,Y_K}].

By Step 3 applied to the integral K-scheme T_\eta of dimension m, div_{T_\eta}(f) = \sum_{\zeta \in (T_\eta)^{(1)}} ord_\zeta^{T_\eta}(f)\,[\overline{\{\zeta\}}^{\,Y_K}]. We identify the two sums.

Bijection H <-> (T_\eta)^{(1)}. Use the identification |T_\eta| = {x \in |T| : \pi(x) = \eta} of Claim 2.1(a), and send \xi \in H to the same point viewed in |T_\eta|.
- If \xi \in H, then W = \overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,T} has dimension m >= 1 and dominates, so by Claim 2.1(a),(c), \overline{\{\xi\}}^{T_\eta} = W_\eta is integral of dimension m-1 with generic point \xi. Since dim T_\eta = m, this says precisely \xi \in (T_\eta)^{(1)}.
- If \zeta \in (T_\eta)^{(1)}, let \xi \in |T| be the corresponding point and W := \overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,T}, of dimension d. First d >= 1: if d = 0 then W = \{\xi\} is a single point, closed in T, hence closed in \bar Y; since \bar Y is of finite type over k, (F1) gives that \kappa(\xi) is algebraic over k; but \pi is a k-morphism with \pi(\xi) = \eta, so the induced map \kappa(\eta) = k(t) -> \kappa(\xi) is an injective k-algebra homomorphism, forcing k(t) to be algebraic over k, impossible because t is transcendental over k. Hence d >= 1. Then W dominates \mathbf P^1_k (its image contains the dense point \eta), so Claim 2.1 gives dim W_\eta = d-1, and by (c), W_\eta = \overline{\{\xi\}}^{T_\eta} = \overline{\{\zeta\}}^{T_\eta}, which has dimension m-1 because \zeta has codimension 1 in the m-dimensional T_\eta. Thus d-1 = m-1, i.e. d = m, so \xi has codimension 1 in T, i.e. \xi \in T^{(1)} \cap H. Both constructions are the identity on underlying points, so they are mutually inverse bijections.

Equality of coefficients. Let \xi \in H and let V = Spec A be a member of the affine cover of Step 1 containing \xi, over U = Spec R (R = k[t] or k[t^{-1}]), and let q \subset A be the prime of \xi (so q \cap S = \emptyset, S = R\setminus\{0\}). Then \mathcal O_{T,\xi} = A_q and \mathcal O_{T_\eta,\xi} = (S^{-1}A)_{S^{-1}q}. Both are subrings of Frac(A) = k(T) = k(T_\eta) (Claim 2.1(b)), and they are literally equal:
  (S^{-1}A)_{S^{-1}q} = \{a/(s t') : a \in A,\ s \in S,\ t' \in A\setminus q\} = \{a/t' : a \in A,\ t' \in A\setminus q\} = A_q,
because 1 \in S and every s \in S is a unit of A_q (as S \cap q = \emptyset). Hence for f \in k(T)^* = k(T_\eta)^*, writing f = a/b in this common local ring, the two integers ord_\xi^T(f) and ord_\xi^{T_\eta}(f) of Step 3 are computed by the same lengths in the same local ring, so they are equal.

Combining, \partial_m(div_T f) = \sum_{\zeta \in (T_\eta)^{(1)}} ord_\zeta^{T_\eta}(f)\,[\overline{\{\zeta\}}^{\,Y_K}] = div_{T_\eta}(f). This proves Step 4.

STEP 5. Conclusion.
Let z \in Z_m(\bar Y) be rationally equivalent to zero. By the definition of rational equivalence, z = \sum_{j=1}^{s} div_{W_j}(g_j) with W_j \subset \bar Y integral closed of dimension m+1 and g_j \in k(W_j)^*. (If m+1 > dim \bar Y = n+1 there are no such W_j, the subgroup of rationally trivial m-cycles is {0}, so z = 0 and \partial_m(z) = 0 is rationally trivial; this covers m >= n+1.) By Step 4, for each j either \partial_m(div_{W_j}(g_j)) = 0 (when W_j is contained in a fibre), or (W_j)_\eta is an integral closed subscheme of Y_K of dimension m (Claim 2.1 with m+1 in place of m) and
  \partial_m(div_{W_j}(g_j)) = div_{(W_j)_\eta}(g_j),
which is rationally equivalent to zero in Z_{m-1}(Y_K) by the very definition of rational equivalence on Y_K. By Z-linearity of \partial_m,
  \partial_m(z) = \sum_j \partial_m(div_{W_j}(g_j))
is a finite sum of cycles rationally equivalent to zero in Z_{m-1}(Y_K); the cycles rationally equivalent to zero form a subgroup of Z_{m-1}(Y_K) (it is by definition the subgroup generated by divisors of rational functions on integral closed subschemes), hence \partial_m(z) is rationally equivalent to zero.

This establishes the lemma for every m >= 1. \qed

statement: Let k be a field, let X/k be an integral projective variety of dimension d ≥ 2, and let C be an integral closed subscheme of X×_k X of dimension 1. Then for each of the two projections p: X×_k X → X, the image p(C) is a closed subset of X of dimension at most 1.
proof:
Let p_1,p_2:X x_k X -> X be the two projections. It suffices to prove the assertion for p_1; the argument for p_2 is identical (or follows by swapping the two factors).

Since X/k is projective, the structure morphism X -> Spec(k) is proper. The projection p_1 is obtained from X -> Spec(k) by base change along X -> Spec(k); hence p_1 is proper. The inclusion i:C -> X x_k X is a closed immersion, hence proper. Therefore f:=p_1|_C=p_1 o i:C -> X is proper. Proper morphisms are closed; consequently p_1(C)=f(C) is a closed subset of X. The same argument applies to p_2.

It remains to bound the dimension of p_1(C). Endow the closed subset Z:=p_1(C) with its reduced induced scheme structure. Since C is integral, its underlying topological space is irreducible. The continuous image of an irreducible space is irreducible: if Z were the union of two proper closed subsets, their preimages under the surjection f_Z:C -> Z would give a decomposition of C into two proper closed subsets, impossible. Hence Z is irreducible. Because X is integral and Z is an irreducible reduced closed subscheme of X, Z is integral. The morphism f:C -> X factors through Z: the set-theoretic image is contained in Z, and since C is reduced, any function vanishing on Z pulls back to a section of O_C vanishing at every point, hence to zero. The induced morphism f_Z:C -> Z is surjective.

Let eta_C be the generic point of C and eta_Z the generic point of Z. For every nonempty open subset V of Z, f_Z^{-1}(V) is nonempty and open in C. Since C is irreducible, every nonempty open subset of C contains eta_C. Thus f_Z(eta_C) lies in every nonempty open subset of Z. In an irreducible scheme the unique point contained in all nonempty open subsets is the generic point; hence f_Z(eta_C)=eta_Z.

The morphism f_Z induces a local homomorphism of stalks O_{Z,eta_Z} -> O_{C,eta_C}. These stalks are the function fields k(Z) and k(C). A unital ring homomorphism between fields is injective, so k(Z) embeds as a subfield of k(C). For an integral variety over a field, the Krull dimension equals the transcendence degree of its function field over the base field. Therefore dim Z = trdeg_k k(Z) <= trdeg_k k(C) = dim C = 1.
Since Z has the same underlying topological space as the closed subset p_1(C), dim p_1(C)=dim Z <= 1. This proves the statement for p_1, and hence for both projections.

statement: Let k be a field, let X/k be an integral projective variety of dimension d ≥ 2, and let S ⊂ X ×_k X ×_k P^1_k be an integral closed subscheme of dimension 2 mapping dominantly to P^1_k. Then for every closed point s ∈ P^1_k, every irreducible component of the scheme-theoretic fibre S_s = S ×_{P^1_k} Spec κ(s) has dimension 1, and there exist closed subsets Y_1, Y_2 ⊂ X, each of dimension at most 1, such that the image of the topological space |S_s| in X ×_k X is contained in |Y_1 ×_k Y_2|.
proof:
PROOF. Write $\pi_3:X\times_k X\times_k \mathbf P^1_k\to \mathbf P^1_k$ for the third projection and $f:=\pi_3|_S:S\to \mathbf P^1_k$; by hypothesis $f$ is dominant. Let $s\in \mathbf P^1_k$ be a CLOSED point throughout.

STEP 0 (Preliminaries; $f$ is surjective). Since $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is projective, so is $X\times_k X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, hence $\pi_3$ is projective (base change of a projective morphism), in particular proper and closed. The inclusion $i:S\hookrightarrow X\times_k X\times_k\mathbf P^1_k$ is a closed immersion, hence proper and closed. Thus $f=\pi_3\circ i$ is a composition of closed maps, hence closed; its image is therefore both closed and dense (dominance), so $f$ is surjective and every fibre $S_s$ is non-empty. The scheme $S$ is a closed subscheme of a $k$-scheme of finite type, hence noetherian; since $S$ is integral, all its local rings are domains.

We use the standard dimension formula for varieties over a field: if $V$ is integral of finite type over $k$ and $\xi\in V$, then
(\ast)\qquad \dim\overline{\{\xi\}}+\dim\mathcal O_{V,\xi}=\dim V.
For completeness we recall the reduction and the two standard ingredients. Take a non-empty affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}R\subset V$ with $\xi\in U$; then $R$ is a finitely generated $k$-domain with $\operatorname{Frac}R=k(V)$, and the two standard facts (a) $\dim R=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\operatorname{Frac}R$ and (b) every maximal chain of primes of a finitely generated $k$-domain has length $\dim R$ (Noether normalization plus lying-over; equivalently, finitely generated algebras over a field are universally catenary and equidimensional) give, for $\mathfrak p\subset R$ the prime of $\xi$, $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p+\dim R/\mathfrak p=\dim R$. Since $\dim\mathcal O_{V,\xi}=\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p$, $\dim\overline{\{\xi\}}=\dim\overline{\{\xi\}}^{\,U}=\dim R/\mathfrak p$ (the $U$-closure is dense open in the $V$-closure, hence of the same dimension), and $\dim V=\operatorname{trdeg}_k k(V)=\dim R$, (\ast) follows.

STEP 1 (The fibre at a closed point is a closed subscheme, cut out by one parameter). Because $s$ is closed, $\{s\}\subset\mathbf P^1_k$ is closed with reduced induced structure $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)$, so $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)\to\mathbf P^1_k$ is a closed immersion; let $\mathcal J\subset\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^1_k}$ be its ideal sheaf. Since $\mathbf P^1_k$ is regular of dimension $1$ and $s$ is closed, $\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^1_k,s}$ is a discrete valuation ring; fix a uniformiser $t$, so $\mathcal J_s=(t)$. The scheme-theoretic fibre $S_s=S\times_{\mathbf P^1_k}\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)$ is the closed subscheme of $S$ defined by the ideal sheaf $\mathcal J\mathcal O_S$, and set-theoretically
$|S_s|=V(\mathcal J\mathcal O_S)=\{\xi\in|S|:(\mathcal J\mathcal O_S)_\xi\subset\mathfrak m_\xi\}=\{\xi\in|S|:\mathcal J_{f(\xi)}\subset\mathfrak m_{f(\xi)}\}=f^{-1}(\{s\})$,
with the subspace topology (the middle equality uses that the local map $\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^1_k,f(\xi)}\to\mathcal O_{S,\xi}$ is local). In particular $|S_s|$ is closed in $|S|$, $S_s$ is noetherian, and hence has only finitely many irreducible components.

STEP 2 (Every component has dimension exactly $1$). Let $Z$ be an irreducible component of $S_s$ and $\zeta$ its generic point; put $A:=\mathcal O_{S,\zeta}$, a noetherian local domain with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m:=\mathfrak m_\zeta$.

(2a) The local homomorphism $\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^1_k,s}\to A$ (induced by $f$, which is local because $f(\zeta)=s$) is injective. Indeed $S$ is integral and $f$ is dominant, so $f$ sends the generic point of $S$ to the generic point of $\mathbf P^1_k$ and induces an injective map of function fields $k(\mathbf P^1_k)\hookrightarrow k(S)$; the square $\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^1_k,s}\to A$, down to $k(\mathbf P^1_k)\hookrightarrow k(S)$ commutes and both vertical maps are injective (local rings of integral schemes embed in the function field). Hence $t$ maps to a NON-ZERO element of $A$, and since the map is local, $t\in\mathfrak m$, so it is a non-unit.

(2b) $\mathfrak m$ is a minimal prime of the principal ideal $tA$. Primes $\mathfrak q\subset A$ correspond bijectively to points $\xi\in|S|$ with $\zeta\in\overline{\{\xi\}}$, by $\mathfrak q\leftrightarrow\xi$, and then $\mathfrak q\subsetneq\mathfrak q'$ iff $\overline{\{\xi'\}}\subsetneq\overline{\{\xi\}}$. Since the ideal sheaf of $S_s$ in $S$ is $\mathcal J\mathcal O_S$ and $\mathcal J$ is generated by $t$ near $s=f(\zeta)$, the stalk at $\zeta$ is $tA$; thus the primes containing $tA$ are exactly those corresponding to points $\xi\in|S_s|$ with $\zeta\in\overline{\{\xi\}}$. If $\mathfrak m$ were not minimal over $tA$ there would be $\mathfrak q\subsetneq\mathfrak m$ with $t\in\mathfrak q$, giving $\xi\in|S_s|$ with $\overline{\{\xi\}}\supsetneq\overline{\{\zeta\}}=Z$. As $f$ is continuous, $f(\overline{\{\xi\}})\subset\overline{\{f(\xi)\}}=\{s\}$, so $\overline{\{\xi\}}$ is an irreducible closed subset of $|S_s|$ strictly containing $Z$ — contradicting that $Z$ is an irreducible component of $S_s$. Hence $\mathfrak m$ is minimal over $tA$.

(2c) By Krull's principal ideal theorem, a prime minimal over a principal ideal in a noetherian ring has height $\le1$; so $\dim A=\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak m\le1$. Since $A$ is a domain and $t\in\mathfrak m$ is non-zero, $\mathfrak m\ne(0)$, so $\dim\mathcal O_{S,\zeta}=\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak m=1$.

(2d) Apply (\ast) to $V=S$, $\xi=\zeta$: $\dim Z=\dim\overline{\{\zeta\}}=\dim S-\dim\mathcal O_{S,\zeta}=2-1=1$. (The inequality $\dim Z\le1$ is also immediate directly: $f$ is dominant and $s$ is closed, so $|S_s|=f^{-1}(\{s\})\ne|S|$, hence $Z\ne S$ and $Z$ is a proper closed irreducible subset of the irreducible noetherian space $|S|$ of dimension $2$.) Thus every irreducible component of $S_s$ has dimension $1$; i.e. $S_s$ is of pure dimension $1$, and since $S_s\ne\varnothing$, $\dim|S_s|=1$.

STEP 3 (The image in $X\times_k X$ is closed). Since $s$ is closed in $\mathbf P^1_k$, $\kappa(s)/k$ is FINITE: cover $\mathbf P^1_k$ by the two standard charts $\mathbf A^1_k=\operatorname{Spec}k[u]$; $s$ lies in one of them, and in that chart $\kappa(s)\cong k[u]/(g)$ with $g$ the monic irreducible polynomial of $s$, a $k$-vector space of dimension $\deg g<\infty$. Hence $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is finite, and so is its base change
$q:(X\times_k X)\times_k\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)\longrightarrow X\times_k X$.
Let $\varphi:S_s\to X\times_k X$ be the composite of the closed immersion $S_s\hookrightarrow (X\times_k X)\times_k\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)$ (base change of $i$) with $q$. Both maps are closed (a closed immersion is a homeomorphism onto a closed subset; finite morphisms are proper, hence closed), so $\varphi$ is a closed map; equivalently $\varphi$ is proper, being the composite $S_s\hookrightarrow S\hookrightarrow X\times_k X\times_k\mathbf P^1_k\xrightarrow{\;\pi_3\;}X\times_k X$ of two closed immersions and the projective, hence proper, projection. Set $T:=\varphi(|S_s|)\subset|X\times_k X|$; $T$ is closed because $\varphi$ is closed.

STEP 4 (Definition of $Y_1,Y_2$; they are closed). Let $p_i:X\times_k X\to X$ be the projections and put $Y_i:=p_i(T)\subset X$. Each $p_i$ is projective (base change of $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$), hence proper, hence closed; as $T$ is closed, $Y_i$ is closed in $X$. Equivalently $Y_i=(p_i\circ\varphi)(|S_s|)$ with $p_i\circ\varphi$ proper.

STEP 5 ($\dim Y_i\le1$). We use an elementary fact.
CLAIM. If $g:W\to W'$ is a surjective closed continuous map of noetherian topological spaces, then $\dim W'\le\dim W$.
Proof of the claim. Let $Z_0\subsetneq Z_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq Z_n$ be a chain of distinct irreducible closed subsets of $W'$. We construct inductively irreducible closed $W_i\subset W$ with $g(W_i)=Z_i$ and $W_{i-1}\subsetneq W_i$. Start: $g^{-1}(Z_n)$ is closed in $W$; write it as a finite union of irreducible components $C_1\cup\cdots\cup C_r$ (possible since $W$ is noetherian). Each $C_j$ is closed in $W$, so $g(C_j)$ is closed in $W'$ (here closedness of $g$ is used); the $g(C_j)$ are irreducible and cover $Z_n$, so irreducibility of $Z_n$ forces $g(C_j)=Z_n$ for some $j$; set $W_n:=C_j$. Inductive step: given $W_i$ with $g(W_i)=Z_i$, the set $E:=W_i\cap g^{-1}(Z_{i-1})$ is closed in $W$, is non-empty since $g(W_i)=Z_i\supset Z_{i-1}$, and satisfies $g(E)=Z_{i-1}\cap g(W_i)=Z_{i-1}$. Write $E=C_1\cup\cdots\cup C_r$ into irreducible components; each $C_j$ is closed in $W$, so $g(C_j)$ is closed in $W'$ and contained in $Z_{i-1}$; as $Z_{i-1}=\bigcup_j g(C_j)$ is irreducible, some $g(C_j)=Z_{i-1}$; set $W_{i-1}:=C_j$. Then $W_{i-1}\subset W_i$ strictly, because $g(W_{i-1})=Z_{i-1}\subsetneq Z_i=g(W_i)$. Thus $W_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq W_n$ is a strict chain of irreducible closed subsets of $W$, so $n\le\dim W$; taking the supremum over all chains gives $\dim W'\le\dim W$. $\square$

Apply the claim to $g:|S_s|\twoheadrightarrow Y_i$, the corestriction of $p_i\circ\varphi$. It is surjective by definition of $Y_i$ and continuous. It is closed: for $C\subset|S_s|$ closed, $(p_i\circ\varphi)(C)$ is closed in $X$ (as $\varphi(C)$ is closed in $X\times_k X$ since $\varphi$ is closed, and $p_i$ is closed), and $(p_i\circ\varphi)(C)\subset Y_i$, hence it is closed in the subspace $Y_i$. Both spaces are noetherian ($S_s$ is noetherian; $Y_i$ is closed in the noetherian space $|X|$). By Step 2d, $\dim|S_s|=1$, so the claim gives $\dim Y_i\le1$. (Since $d=\dim X\ge2$ and $X$ is integral, this also shows $Y_i\ne X$, i.e. each $Y_i$ is a proper closed subset, though only $\dim Y_i\le1$ is required.)

STEP 6 (The containment in $|Y_1\times_k Y_2|$). The morphism $Y_1\times_k Y_2\to X\times_k X$ is a closed immersion (successive base change of the closed immersions $Y_i\hookrightarrow X$), so we identify $|Y_1\times_k Y_2|$ with its image. We check
$|Y_1\times_k Y_2|=p_1^{-1}(|Y_1|)\cap p_2^{-1}(|Y_2|)$ as subsets of $|X\times_k X|$.
For the inclusion $\supset$: let $w\in|X\times_k X|$ with $p_j(w)\in|Y_j|$ for $j=1,2$. The map $X\times_k Y_2\to X\times_k X$ is the base change of $Y_2\to X$ along $p_2$, and for any cartesian square the map on underlying points $|A\times_C B|\to|A|\times_{|C|}|B|$ is surjective; equivalently, the fibre over $w$ is $\operatorname{Spec}(\kappa(w)\otimes_{\kappa(p_2(w))}\kappa(p_2(w)))\simeq\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(w)\ne\varnothing$ (the fibre of $Y_2\to X$ over $p_2(w)\in|Y_2|$ is $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(p_2(w))$). Hence $w\in|X\times_k Y_2|$, and applying the same argument to the first factor gives $w\in|Y_1\times_k Y_2|$. The reverse inclusion is immediate from the functoriality of the projections.
Finally, for $P\in|S_s|$ we have $\varphi(P)\in T$ and $p_i(\varphi(P))\in p_i(T)=|Y_i|$ for $i=1,2$; hence $\varphi(P)\in p_1^{-1}(|Y_1|)\cap p_2^{-1}(|Y_2|)=|Y_1\times_k Y_2|$. Therefore $\varphi(|S_s|)\subset|Y_1\times_k Y_2|$, which is precisely the assertion that the image of the topological space $|S_s|$ in $X\times_k X$ is contained in $|Y_1\times_k Y_2|$.

Steps 2 and 4-6 give, for every closed point $s\in\mathbf P^1_k$, that all irreducible components of $S_s$ have dimension $1$ and that closed subsets $Y_1,Y_2\subset X$ of dimension $\le1$ with the required containment exist. This proves the lemma. \qed

statement: Let X/k be a smooth projective variety of dimension d, let A be a finitely generated k-algebra which is an integral domain with fraction field L, and let Z be a d-dimensional cycle on X ×_k X. If the image of Z in CH^d(X_L ×_L X_L) is zero, then there exists a nonzero element f in A such that the image of Z in CH^d(X_{A_f} ×_{A_f} X_{A_f}) is zero, where X_{A_f} = X ×_k Spec A_f.
proof:
Proof. Put Y = X ×_k X. For a k-algebra R write Y_R = Y ×_k Spec R = X_R ×_R X_R, and let p_R: Y_R -> Y be the base-change morphism. Since R is a vector space over the field k, p_R is flat. Let a = dim A = trdeg_k L.

If a = 0, then A is a finitely generated k-algebra domain of dimension 0, hence a field; therefore A = L, and f = 1 works. If Z = 0, again f = 1 works. If d = 0, then Y_L is 0-dimensional, so CH_0(Y_L) = Z_0(Y_L); rational equivalence is trivial because there are no integral closed subschemes of dimension 1. Thus the hypothesis says that p_L^![Z] is the zero cycle. For a closed point y of Y, p_L^![y] is a positive linear combination of the closed points of Spec(κ(y) ⊗_k L), and these supports are disjoint for distinct y. Hence p_L^![Z] = 0 forces Z = 0, and f = 1 works. We now assume d ≥ 1, a ≥ 1, and Z ≠ 0.

We first record the needed spreading-out and divisor facts.

Fact 1 (product dimensions). If B and S are finitely generated domains over k, then every irreducible component of Spec(B ⊗_k S) has dimension dim B + dim S. Indeed, let p be a minimal prime of B ⊗_k S. If b ∈ B is nonzero, then multiplication by b on B is injective; tensoring over k with the vector space S is exact, and B/bB is nonzero, so b is a non-zero-divisor on B ⊗_k S. Hence p ∩ B = 0. The morphism Spec(B ⊗_k S) -> Spec B is flat and finite type. For a flat finite type morphism with irreducible base, every irreducible component dominates the base and has dimension equal to dim base plus the dimension of the generic fibre. The generic fibre is an irreducible component of Spec(Frac(B) ⊗_k S). For a finitely generated domain S over k and any field extension K/k, every irreducible component of Spec(K ⊗_k S) has dimension dim S; this follows, for example, from Noether normalization and finiteness after base change. Therefore dim V(p) = dim B + dim S.

Fact 2 (descent of closed subschemes). Let A be a noetherian domain with fraction field L, let V be a scheme of finite type over Spec A, and let T ⊂ V_L be a closed subscheme. Then there exist 0 ≠ f ∈ A and a closed subscheme T̄ ⊂ V_{A_f} such that T̄ ×_{A_f} Spec L = T. Proof. Cover V by finitely many affine opens V_i = Spec R_i. On (V_i)_L, the closed subscheme T is defined by a finitely generated ideal I_i ⊂ L ⊗_A R_i. Choose finitely many generators of I_i and clear denominators; this gives 0 ≠ f_i ∈ A such that the generators lie in (A_{f_i} ⊗_A R_i). Let f_1 be the product of the f_i and let J_i ⊂ A_{f_1} ⊗_A R_i be the ideal generated by those elements. Then J_i ⊗_A L = I_i. On overlaps, the ideals J_i and J_j define the same closed subscheme after tensoring with L. Since the rings are noetherian and the ideals are finitely generated, equality of their L-localizations implies equality after further localization at some nonzero element of A. Taking the product over finitely many overlaps gives 0 ≠ f ∈ A and closed subschemes over (V_i)_{A_f} which agree on overlaps, hence glue to T̄ ⊂ V_{A_f}. Its generic fibre is T.

Fact 3 (divisors by difference of lengths). Let W be an integral scheme of finite type over a field k. For v ∈ W^{(1)}, let R = O_{W,v}, a one-dimensional noetherian local domain. For x ∈ R \ {0}, set ℓ_R(x) = length_R(R/xR). This length is finite because R/xR is a noetherian local ring of dimension 0. We claim ℓ_R(xy) = ℓ_R(x) + ℓ_R(y). Let R^ν be the normalization of R. Since R is excellent (W is finite type over a field), R^ν is finite over R and is a semilocal Dedekind domain. Put M = R^ν/R, a finite length R-module. Multiplication by x on 0 -> R -> R^ν -> M -> 0 gives, by the snake lemma, an exact sequence
0 -> M[x] -> R/xR -> R^ν/xR^ν -> M/xM -> 0.
For a finite length module M, length_R(M[x]) = length_R(M/xM), because both equal length_R(M) - length_R(xM). Hence ℓ_R(x) = length_R(R^ν/xR^ν). In a semilocal Dedekind domain the latter is additive in x, since (x) factors uniquely into powers of maximal ideals and length is the sum of the corresponding valuation contributions. Thus ℓ_R is additive.
For f ∈ Frac(W)^× and v ∈ W^{(1)}, choose a,b ∈ R nonzero with f = a/b and define
ord_v(f) = ℓ_R(a) - ℓ_R(b).
Additivity of ℓ_R shows this is independent of the representation a/b. There is a nonempty open subset of W on which f and f^{-1} are units, so only finitely many codimension-one points have nonzero order. Define
div_W(f) = Σ_{v ∈ W^{(1)}} ord_v(f) [closure(v)].
If j: U -> W is an open immersion, then codimension-one points of U are precisely the codimension-one points of W lying in U, with the same local rings, so j^* div_W(f) = div_U(f). If i: W -> Y is a closed immersion, then i_* div_W(f) is the same cycle viewed on Y. Finally, if ν: W^ν -> W is the normalization, then for v ∈ W^{(1)} one has
ord_v(f) = Σ_{w | v} v_w(f) [κ(w):κ(v)],
where v_w is the normalized valuation of the DVR O_{W^ν,w}. Hence div_W(f) = ν_* div_{W^ν}(f). Thus these are exactly the divisors used in the usual definition of Chow groups.

For an integral closed subscheme W ⊂ Y of dimension d and a finitely generated k-domain R of dimension r, define the flat pullback of [W] by
p_R^![W] = Σ_V length_{O_{W_R,ξ_V}}(O_{W_R,ξ_V}) [V],
where V runs over the irreducible components of W_R = W ×_k Spec R and ξ_V is the generic point of V. Fact 1 shows dim V = d + r, and the local ring at ξ_V is artinian local, so the length is finite. Extend linearly to cycles. This is the usual flat pullback under p_R.

Write Z = Σ_j n_j [W_j] with W_j ⊂ Y integral closed of dimension d. The hypothesis says p_L^![Z] = 0 in CH_d(Y_L). By definition of the Chow group, there exist finitely many integral closed subschemes T_i ⊂ Y_L of dimension d+1 and rational functions g_i ∈ k(T_i)^× such that
Σ_i div_{T_i}(g_i) = p_L^![Z]
as d-dimensional cycles on Y_L. If p_L^![Z] is already the zero cycle, take the empty sum.

Apply Fact 2 to V = Y_A and to each closed subscheme T_i ⊂ Y_L. We obtain 0 ≠ f_i ∈ A and closed subschemes T̄_i ⊂ Y_{A_{f_i}} with generic fibre T_i. Let f_0 = Π_i f_i. Then all T̄_i are closed subschemes of Y_{A_{f_0}} and (T̄_i)_L = T_i.

For each i, the generic fibre T̄_i,L = T_i is integral. Hence among the minimal primes of T̄_i there is exactly one whose contraction to A_{f_0} is (0). Let η_i be that minimal prime, and let W_i be the reduced closure of η_i in T̄_i. Then W_i is an integral closed subscheme of Y_{A_{f_0}}, it dominates Spec A_{f_0}, and its generic fibre is T_i. Its function field is k(T_i), so by the dimension formula for finite type domains over a field,
dim W_i = dim A_{f_0} + trdeg_L k(T_i) = a + (d+1).
Moreover Frac(W_i) = k(T_i), so each g_i may be regarded as an element of Frac(W_i)^×.

Let ν_i: W_i -> Y_{A_{f_0}} be the closed immersion, and consider the (d+a)-dimensional cycle
C = Σ_i (ν_i)_* div_{W_i}(g_i) - p_{A_{f_0}}^![Z]
on Y_{A_{f_0}}.
We claim that the restriction of C to the generic fibre is zero. Define the generic-fibre restriction of a cycle by sending an integral closed subscheme V ⊂ Y_{A_{f_0}} to [V_L] if V meets Y_L, and to 0 otherwise, extended linearly.

For the divisor terms, the codimension-one points of W_i are of two types. If v is horizontal, then v ∩ (A_{f_0} \ {0}) = ∅, so every element of A_{f_0} \ {0} is already a unit in O_{W_i,v}. Such v correspond bijectively to codimension-one points w of T_i, and O_{W_i,v} = O_{T_i,w}. Hence the coefficient ord_v(g_i) is exactly ord_w(g_i). Vertical codimension-one points disappear after restricting to the generic fibre. Therefore
res_η((ν_i)_* div_{W_i}(g_i)) = div_{T_i}(g_i).

For the flat pullback term, write Z = Σ_j n_j [W_j]. For each component V of W_{j,A_{f_0}} with generic point ξ, if ξ is vertical then V disappears in the generic fibre. If ξ is horizontal, then ξ lies over (0) ∈ Spec A_{f_0}. Thus every nonzero element of A_{f_0} is already a unit in O_{W_{j,A_{f_0}},ξ}. The corresponding component of W_{j,L} has generic point w, and
O_{W_{j,L},w} = O_{W_{j,A_{f_0}},ξ}.
This equality is for the local ring of W_{j,A_{f_0}} at ξ, including nilpotent information; it is not the local ring of the reduced component. Hence the multiplicity length_{O_{W_{j,A_{f_0}},ξ}}(O_{W_{j,A_{f_0}},ξ}) is unchanged after passing to the generic fibre. Therefore
res_η(p_{A_{f_0}}^![W_j]) = p_L^![W_j],
and hence res_η(p_{A_{f_0}}^![Z]) = p_L^![Z].
Combining the two restrictions gives
res_η(C) = Σ_i div_{T_i}(g_i) - p_L^![Z] = 0.

Write C = Σ_l m_l [V_l] with V_l integral closed subschemes of Y_{A_{f_0}} of dimension d+a. If V_l is horizontal, then V_{l,L} is integral and dense in V_l, so V_l is the closure of V_{l,L}. Distinct horizontal integral closed subschemes have distinct generic fibres: if V_{l,L} = V_{l',L}, then their closures in Y_{A_{f_0}} are equal. Since res_η(C) = Σ_{l horizontal} m_l [V_{l,L}] = 0, all coefficients m_l of horizontal components vanish. Thus C is supported on vertical components.

For each vertical component V_l, its image in Spec A_{f_0} is a proper closed subset. Hence there exists 0 ≠ h_l ∈ A_{f_0} whose vanishing locus contains that image. Let h = Π_l h_l. Write h = a/f_0^N with 0 ≠ a ∈ A. Then C restricts to the zero cycle on Y_{A_{f_0a}}.

Set f = f_0 a. Since restriction to the open Y_{A_f} commutes with flat pullback and with the divisor construction on horizontal open subsets, the equation C|_{Y_{A_f}} = 0 gives
p_{A_f}^![Z] = Σ_i (ν_i')_* div_{U_i}(g_i'),
where U_i = W_i ×_{A_{f_0}} Spec A_f and g_i' is the restriction of g_i to U_i. Each U_i is an integral closed subscheme of Y_{A_f} of dimension d+1+a, and g_i' ∈ Frac(U_i)^×. Hence p_{A_f}^![Z] is rationally equivalent to zero in CH_{d+a}(Y_{A_f}).

Finally, Y_{A_f} is equidimensional of dimension 2d+a: Y is smooth of dimension 2d over k, A_f is a finitely generated k-domain of dimension a, and Fact 1 applies to affine covers. Therefore CH^d(X_{A_f} ×_{A_f} X_{A_f}) = CH^d(Y_{A_f}) = CH_{d+a}(Y_{A_f}). The vanishing of p_{A_f}^![Z] in CH_{d+a}(Y_{A_f}) is exactly the vanishing of the image of Z in CH^d(X_{A_f} ×_{A_f} X_{A_f}). Since f = f_0 a is nonzero in the domain A, this proves the lemma. QED.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let E/k be a finite field extension of degree n, and let α ∈ CH^d(X×_k X) be a class whose image under flat base change in CH^d(X_E×_E X_E) is zero, where X_E = X×_k Spec E. Then n·α = 0 in CH^d(X×_k X). In particular the kernel of CH^d(X×_k X) → CH^d(X_E×_E X_E) is a torsion subgroup.
proof:
Write W := X \times_k X, so dim W = 2d and CH^d(W) = CH_d(W) (codimension-d cycles on the 2d-dimensional variety W are exactly the d-dimensional cycles). Let t: Spec E \to Spec k be the structure morphism of the finite extension E/k, let f: W_E := W \times_k Spec E \to W be its base change, and let \pi_E: W_E \to Spec E be the projection.

Step 1 (Identification of the target). By the universal property of fibre products there is a canonical k-isomorphism
   (X \times_k Spec E) \times_E (X \times_k Spec E) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } (X \times_k X) \times_k Spec E = W_E,
  ((x,e),(x',e)) \mapsto ((x,x'),e);
indeed both sides represent the functor of pairs of maps into X from a Spec E-scheme. Under this identification the "flat base change" map of the statement is precisely the flat pullback
   f^*: CH_d(W) \longrightarrow CH_d(W_E).

Step 2 (f is finite locally free of rank n). Since E/k is a finite extension of degree n, E is a free k-module of rank n (any basis e_1,...,e_n of E over k gives E \cong k^{\oplus n} as k-modules). Hence t is finite locally free of rank n, and so is its base change f: W_E \to W (finite locally free morphisms are stable under base change). In particular f is flat of relative dimension 0 and proper.

Step 3 (The two homomorphisms).
(a) Flat pullback. Because f is flat of relative dimension 0, flat pullback sends d-dimensional cycles to d-dimensional cycles: for V \subset W integral of dimension d, the scheme-theoretic inverse image V_E := V \times_k Spec E = f^{-1}V is finite over V, and each of its irreducible components W_i, viewed as an integral closed subscheme of W_E, has function field \kappa(W_i) finite over \kappa(V); hence trdeg_k \kappa(W_i) = trdeg_k \kappa(V) = d, so dim W_i = d. By definition (Fulton, Ch. 1, \S 1.4),
   f^*[V] = \sum_i m_i [W_i], \qquad m_i := length_{O_{V_E,\eta_i}}(O_{V_E,\eta_i}),
where \eta_1,...,\eta_r are the generic points of the irreducible components of V_E (equivalently of V_E \times_V \{\eta\}, \eta the generic point of V), and m_i is the length of that Artin local ring as a module over itself. Flat pullback commutes with rational equivalence (pulling back the graph of a rational function on an integral (d+1)-dimensional subvariety T \subset W gives the graph of the pulled-back rational function on the components of T_E), so f^* is a well-defined homomorphism CH_d(W) \to CH_d(W_E).
(b) Proper pushforward. Since f is finite, it is a closed map, and for Z \subset W_E integral of dimension d the image f(Z) is closed of dimension d (the induced map Z \to f(Z) is finite and surjective, so the corresponding ring extension is integral and dimensions agree), and f|_Z is generically finite of degree [\kappa(Z):\kappa(f(Z))]. Hence
   f_*[Z] = [\kappa(Z):\kappa(f(Z))]\,[f(Z)].
Proper pushforward commutes with rational equivalence: for T \subset W_E integral of dimension d+1 and r \in \kappa(T)^*, writing T' = f(T) and using that the norm N = N_{\kappa(T)/\kappa(T')} is compatible with the discrete valuations attached to codimension-1 points (for each codimension-1 point v of T' the sum of the extensions w|_v has the correct multiplicity), one gets f_*(div_T(r)) = div_{T'}(N(r)). Thus f_* is a well-defined homomorphism CH_d(W_E) \to CH_d(W). Both maps are \mathbb Z-linear.

Step 4 (Key claim: f_* \circ f^* = n \cdot id on Z_d(W)). Since both maps are \mathbb Z-linear, it suffices to treat an integral closed subscheme V \subset W of dimension d. Consider the finite \kappa(V)-algebra
   A := \kappa(V) \otimes_k E.
The fibre V_E = V \times_k Spec E is the affine scheme Spec A: over the affine open U = Spec B \subset V containing \eta we have V_E \times_V U = Spec(B \otimes_k E), and localising at the multiplicative set B \setminus \{0\} gives A; since V_E is finite over V (E/k finite), V_E is covered by such affines and its generic structure is Spec A. Concretely, the irreducible components of V_E are the closures of the points of V_E lying over \eta, i.e. the integral closed subschemes Spec(A/\mathfrak p) as \mathfrak p runs over the minimal primes of A.

Subclaim 4.1. A is an Artinian ring of dimension n over \kappa(V), its prime ideals \mathfrak p_1,...,\mathfrak p_r are exactly its minimal (equivalently maximal) ideals, and for each i the contraction \mathfrak p_i \cap \kappa(V) is (0).
Proof. E is an n-dimensional k-vector space, so A \cong \kappa(V) \otimes_k k^{\oplus n} \cong \kappa(V)^{\oplus n} as \kappa(V)-vector spaces, hence dim_{\kappa(V)} A = n. A finite-dimensional algebra over a field is Artinian, so every prime is maximal, and the primes are the finitely many minimal primes. Since A is integral over the field \kappa(V) (each element satisfies its characteristic polynomial of multiplication), the contraction of any prime is a prime of the field \kappa(V), and it cannot be \kappa(V) since 1 \notin \mathfrak p_i. Hence the contraction is (0). \square

Write W_i := Spec(A/\mathfrak p_i) \subset W_E (reduced induced structure on the i-th irreducible component of V_E); by Subclaim 4.1 each A/\mathfrak p_i is a domain finite-dimensional over the field \kappa(V), hence a field, so W_i is integral with \kappa(W_i) = A/\mathfrak p_i, and W_i maps onto V with generic point \eta_i corresponding to \mathfrak p_i. Thus W_1,...,W_r are exactly the integral closed subschemes of W_E occurring in f^*[V], and
   O_{V_E,\eta_i} = A_{\mathfrak p_i}, so m_i = length_{A_{\mathfrak p_i}}(A_{\mathfrak p_i}),
   f_*[W_i] = [A/\mathfrak p_i : \kappa(V)]\,[V].
Therefore
   f_* f^*[V] = \Big(\sum_{i=1}^r length_{A_{\mathfrak p_i}}(A_{\mathfrak p_i})\,[A/\mathfrak p_i : \kappa(V)]\Big)\,[V].   (*)

Subclaim 4.2. For any finite-dimensional commutative algebra A over a field F with dim_F A = n and minimal/maximal primes \mathfrak p_1,...,\mathfrak p_r,
   n = \sum_{i=1}^r length_{A_{\mathfrak p_i}}(A_{\mathfrak p_i})\,[Frac(A/\mathfrak p_i) : F].
Proof. An Artinian ring decomposes as the product of its localisations at its maximal ideals: A \xrightarrow{\sim} \prod_i A_{\mathfrak p_i} (Chinese remainder theorem, using that the \mathfrak p_i are pairwise comaximal and \prod_i \mathfrak p_i \subseteq \cap_i \mathfrak p_i = nil(A) = 0 after localising; equivalently A is a product of Artin local rings). Hence dim_F A = \sum_i dim_F A_{\mathfrak p_i}. Each R := A_{\mathfrak p_i} is an Artin local F-algebra, finite-dimensional over F, with maximal ideal \mathfrak m := \mathfrak p_i A_{\mathfrak p_i}, nilpotent of index s+1, and residue field R/\mathfrak m = S^{-1}(A/\mathfrak p_i) = Frac(A/\mathfrak p_i) (localising the domain A/\mathfrak p_i at its non-zero elements). The filtration R \supseteq \mathfrak m \supseteq \mathfrak m^2 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq \mathfrak m^{s+1} = 0 gives dim_F R = \sum_{j=0}^{s} dim_F(\mathfrak m^j/\mathfrak m^{j+1}). Each \mathfrak m^j/\mathfrak m^{j+1} is annihilated by \mathfrak m, hence is a vector space over R/\mathfrak m, and its R-submodules are exactly its (R/\mathfrak m)-subspaces, so length_R(\mathfrak m^j/\mathfrak m^{j+1}) = dim_{R/\mathfrak m}(\mathfrak m^j/\mathfrak m^{j+1}); consequently dim_F(\mathfrak m^j/\mathfrak m^{j+1}) = length_R(\mathfrak m^j/\mathfrak m^{j+1})\cdot[R/\mathfrak m : F]. Summing over j and using additivity of length, dim_F R = length_R(R)\cdot[R/\mathfrak m:F] = length_{A_{\mathfrak p_i}}(A_{\mathfrak p_i})\,[Frac(A/\mathfrak p_i):F]. Summing over i proves the subclaim. \square

Applying Subclaim 4.2 with F = \kappa(V) and using dim_{\kappa(V)} A = n together with (*), we obtain
   f_* f^*[V] = n\,[V]
for every integral d-dimensional closed subscheme V \subset W. By \mathbb Z-linearity, f_* f^*[Z] = n\,[Z] for every d-dimensional cycle Z on W.

Step 5 (Conclusion for the class \alpha). The identity of Step 4 holds on cycles, hence descends to Chow groups: for every \gamma \in CH_d(W),
   f_*(f^*\gamma) = n\,\gamma.
(This is the standard projection-formula property of a finite locally free morphism of rank n, here verified from first principles.) By hypothesis the image of \alpha under flat base change, i.e. f^*\alpha \in CH_d(W_E) = CH^d(X_E \times_E X_E), is zero. Hence
   n\,\alpha = f_*(f^*\alpha) = f_*(0) = 0,
using \mathbb Z-linearity of f_*. This proves the main assertion.

Step 6 (The "in particular"). The map CH^d(X \times_k X) \to CH^d(X_E \times_E X_E) is a group homomorphism (flat pullback is additive), so its kernel K_E is a subgroup. Step 5 shows n\,\alpha = 0 for every \alpha \in K_E; thus every element of K_E is torsion, i.e. K_E is a torsion subgroup, in fact of exponent dividing n = [E:k].

Step 7 (Edge cases and completeness of the case analysis).
(i) d = 0: then W is 0-dimensional, every integral closed subscheme V \subset W is a closed point, V_E = Spec(\kappa(V)\otimes_k E) = Spec A is already affine Artinian, and Steps 3-4 apply verbatim (the dimension count dim W_i = d = 0 is the statement that \kappa(W_i)/\kappa(V) is algebraic, which holds since A is finite over \kappa(V)).
(ii) E/k purely inseparable or otherwise giving non-reduced fibres: this is exactly the reason the multiplicities m_i = length_{A_{\mathfrak p_i}}(A_{\mathfrak p_i}) appear; Subclaim 4.2 counts them correctly (e.g. if A is a field purely inseparable of degree n over \kappa(V), then r = 1, m_1 = 1 and [A:\kappa(V)] = n, giving n[V]).
(iii) X (hence W) not integral: no reduction is needed, since the argument is carried out componentwise on each integral d-dimensional closed subscheme V \subset W, and \kappa(V) is a field by definition of "integral".
(iv) The argument uses only the additive structure of the Chow group of W = X \times_k X, not the composition of correspondences, so it applies a fortiori in the correspondence ring.

Thus n\cdot\alpha = 0 in CH^d(X \times_k X), and the kernel of CH^d(X \times_k X) \to CH^d(X_E \times_E X_E) is a torsion subgroup of exponent dividing n = [E:k]. \blacksquare

statement: Let R be a discrete valuation ring with fraction field K and residue field k, and let \mathcal{Y} be a scheme that is smooth and projective over R of pure relative dimension m. Denote by j: Y_\eta \to \mathcal{Y} the generic fibre and by i: Y_s \to \mathcal{Y} the special fibre. For n \ge 0 and W an integral closed subscheme of Y_\eta of codimension n, let \overline W be the closure of W in \mathcal{Y}. Then the assignment [W] \mapsto i^![\overline W], where i^! is the refined Gysin homomorphism of the regular embedding i, induces a well-defined group homomorphism \mathrm{CH}^n(Y_\eta) \to \mathrm{CH}^n(Y_s).
proof:
Proof. Let pi be a uniformizer of R. We use the convention CH_t(X)=0 for t<0 or t>dim X. Since the morphism Ycal -> Spec R is smooth of pure relative dimension m, the generic fibre Y_eta is smooth of pure dimension m over K and the special fibre Y_s is smooth of pure dimension m over k (if one of the fibres is empty then the corresponding Chow groups are zero and the assertion is trivial). Hence for every n>=0 we identify CH^n(Y_eta)=CH_{m-n}(Y_eta) and CH^n(Y_s)=CH_{m-n}(Y_s). Put r=m-n. If r<0, both groups are zero, so assume r>=0.

Basic intersection-theoretic facts. Because Ycal is flat over the DVR R, multiplication by pi on Ycal is injective; hence Y_s=V(pi) is an effective Cartier divisor and i:Y_s -> Ycal is a regular embedding of codimension 1. The ideal sheaf of Y_s is generated by the global non-zero-divisor pi, so O_Ycal(Y_s) is trivial. The conormal sheaf I/I^2=(pi)/(pi)^2 is free of rank one generated by the class of pi, hence the normal bundle N_{Y_s/Ycal} is trivial and c_1(N_{Y_s/Ycal})=0. Fulton's refined Gysin homomorphism for the regular embedding i gives additive maps i^!:CH_t(Ycal)->CH_{t-1}(Y_s) for all t (Fulton, Intersection Theory, Ch. 17.1; see also Ch. 1.7). If a cycle alpha on Ycal is rationally equivalent to zero, then i^!alpha=0 in CH_{t-1}(Y_s), because i^! descends to Chow groups. If alpha is supported on Y_s, say alpha=i_*beta with beta in CH_t(Y_s), then the self-intersection formula for a regular embedding gives i^!alpha=i^!i_*beta=c_1(N_{Y_s/Ycal}) cap beta=0 (Fulton, Ch. 6, Thm 6.2; or Ch. 17.1).

Dimension lemma. Let A be a domain of finite type over R such that pi is nonzero in A and pi is not a unit in A. Put d=dim A[1/pi]. Then dim A=d+1 and dim A/(pi)=d. Proof: By relative Noether normalization over a DVR (Liu, Algebraic Geometry and Arithmetic Curves, Thm 8.2.8; Stacks Project, More on Algebra, Noether normalization), there exist elements x_1,...,x_d in A, algebraically independent over R, such that A is finite over B=R[x_1,...,x_d]. The hypothesis that pi is not a unit is exactly the nonempty-special-fibre hypothesis needed for the version over the whole DVR. Since dim R=1, dim B=d+1. Finite integral extensions preserve Krull dimension, so dim A=d+1. Localizing at pi gives a finite nonzero extension A[1/pi] over K[x_1,...,x_d]; hence dim A[1/pi]=dim K[x_1,...,x_d]=d. Since pi is not a unit, A/(pi) is nonzero and finite over k[x_1,...,x_d]; hence dim A/(pi)=d. This proves the lemma.

Closure properties. Let W be an integral closed subscheme of Y_eta of dimension r, and let X=overline W be its closure in Ycal with the reduced induced structure. Then X is integral. Since Y_eta is open in Ycal, W=X cap Y_eta: indeed, if x in X cap Y_eta were not in W, an open neighbourhood of x in Y_eta disjoint from W would be open in Ycal and disjoint from W, contradicting x in the closure of W. Thus W is a dense open subscheme of X. The morphism X -> Spec R is closed because X is closed in the R-projective scheme Ycal, and its image contains the generic point because W is nonempty; hence the image is all of Spec R. In particular X_s is nonempty. For flatness and dimension, let U=Spec A be an affine open of X. Since X is integral and dominant over Spec R, pi is nonzero in A. If U meets X_s, then pi is not a unit in A, and the dimension lemma gives dim U=dim U_eta+1. If U is contained in Y_eta, then pi is a unit and dim U<=dim W=r. Choose an affine open U meeting X_s; then U is dense in the irreducible scheme X, so U_eta is a nonempty open subset of W, hence dim U_eta=r, and the dimension lemma gives dim U=r+1. Therefore dim X=r+1. Since X is an integral scheme over the PID R and pi is nonzero in every affine coordinate ring, X is torsion-free over R, hence flat.
