The same argument applied to an integral closed subscheme V of Y_eta of dimension r+1 shows that X=overline V is integral, dominant, flat over R, has dimension r+2, and contains V as a dense open subscheme.

Definition on cycles. Define a homomorphism of free abelian groups Phi:Z_r(Y_eta)->CH_r(Y_s) by sending the generator [W], where W is integral closed of dimension r in Y_eta, to i^![overline W] in CH_r(Y_s), and extending linearly. Additivity is built into the definition. We must show that Phi vanishes on cycles rationally equivalent to zero.

Rational equivalence. A cycle in Z_r(Y_eta) is rationally equivalent to zero if it is a finite sum of cycles div_V(f), where V is an integral closed subscheme of Y_eta of dimension r+1 and f is a nonzero rational function on V (Fulton, Ch. 1). If r=m, there are no integral closed subschemes of Y_eta of dimension m+1, so rational equivalence in dimension m is trivial; in this case a cycle rationally equivalent to zero is already zero, and Phi is automatically well-defined. Assume now r<m. It suffices to prove Phi(div_V(f))=0 for one such V and f.

Let X=overline V in Ycal. By the closure properties above, X is integral, dominant, flat over R, dim X=r+2, and V=X cap Y_eta is a dense open subscheme. Hence K(X)=K(V), so f may be regarded as a rational function on X. Let D=(f) be the Cartier divisor on X determined by f, and let (f)_X be its associated (r+1)-cycle on X, pushed forward to Ycal. The cycle (f)_X is rationally equivalent to zero in CH_{r+1}(Ycal), because it is the principal divisor on the integral closed subscheme X (Fulton, Ch. 1). Therefore i^![(f)_X]=0 in CH_r(Y_s).

We compare (f)_X with div_V(f). Since V is a dense open subscheme of X and X\V=X_s, the Cartier divisor cycle decomposes into horizontal and vertical parts. More precisely, the components of (f)_X whose generic points lie in V correspond bijectively to the codimension-one points of V that occur in div_V(f). For such a point xi, the local rings O_{X,xi} and O_{V,xi} are equal because V is open in X; hence the Cartier coefficient of xi in (f)_X equals the coefficient of xi in div_V(f). If T is the integral closed subscheme of V (equivalently of Y_eta) obtained as the closure of xi, then the closure of xi in X is exactly overline T in Ycal: indeed T is dense in the irreducible closed subset closure_X(xi), and X is closed in Ycal. Thus the horizontal part of (f)_X is the cycle sum_T n_T [overline T], where sum_T n_T [T]=div_V(f) in Z_r(Y_eta). Applying i^! to this horizontal part gives exactly Phi(div_V(f)).

Let Z be the vertical part of (f)_X, i.e. the sum of the components contained in X_s. Then in CH_r(Y_s) we have Phi(div_V(f)) = i^![(f)_X] - i^![Z]. The first term is zero. For the second term, each integral component T of Z is contained in Y_s, and as a cycle on Ycal it is i_*[T]. By the self-intersection formula and the triviality of N_{Y_s/Ycal}, i^![T]=i^!i_*[T]=c_1(N_{Y_s/Ycal}) cap [T]=0. Hence i^![Z]=0. Therefore Phi(div_V(f))=0.

Since Phi kills every generator of the rational equivalence relation, it kills all cycles rationally equivalent to zero and therefore factors through CH_r(Y_eta). The induced homomorphism CH_r(Y_eta)->CH_r(Y_s) sends the class of [W] to i^![overline W]. Under the identifications CH^n(Y_eta)=CH_{m-n}(Y_eta) and CH^n(Y_s)=CH_{m-n}(Y_s), this is precisely the map asserted in the lemma. The cases r<0 (n>m) and r=m (n=0) were handled above. This completes the proof.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective geometrically integral of dimension d ≥ 1, and let α ∈ CH^d(X ×_k X) have zero image in CH^d(X_{k(t)} ×_{k(t)} X_{k(t)}). Then there exists a closed subscheme Y⊊X such that α ∘ α has a cycle representative supported on Y ×_k Y, where ∘ denotes composition of correspondences.
proof: We identify CH^d(X x X) with CH_d(X x X), since dim(X x X)=2d. Write F=k(X) for the function field of X. A cycle representative means an algebraic cycle whose class is the given Chow class. The zero cycle is regarded as supported on every closed subscheme. If alpha=0, choose a closed point y in X; such a point exists because X is nonempty and of finite type over k, and y is proper in X because dim(X)=d>=1. Taking Y to be the reduced closed subscheme y, the zero cycle alpha o alpha is supported on Y x Y. Hence assume alpha != 0. We prove two support statements: (S1) there exists a proper closed subscheme Z subset X such that alpha has a cycle representative supported on Z x X; (S2) there exists a proper closed subscheme Z' subset X such that alpha has a cycle representative supported on X x Z'. Once these are known, apply lemma_63 (Spark) to alpha with A=Z, B=X, C=X, D=Z'. Since alpha has representatives supported on A x B=Z x X and on C x D=X x Z', lemma_63 gives that alpha o alpha has a cycle representative supported on A x D=Z x Z'. Let Y be the reduced closed subscheme Z union Z'. Because X is integral and Z and Z' are proper closed subsets, Y is proper in X. Also Z x Z' subset Y x Y, so alpha o alpha is supported on Y x Y. It remains to prove (S1) and (S2). The proof of (S2) will be the same as that of (S1) applied to the transpose alpha^t, using lemma_42 (Spark). We first prove several auxiliary lemmas. Auxiliary Lemma 1 (generic fiber of Cartier divisors). Let X/k be integral of dimension d, let F=k(X), and let T subset X x X be integral of dimension d+1, with projection to the first factor. If T does not dominate X, put T_eta=empty. If T dominates X, then T_eta=T x_X Spec F is an integral curve over F. For f in k(T)^*, let f_eta be its image in k(T_eta). Then (div_T f)_eta = div_{T_eta}(f_eta) as 0-cycles on T_eta. Proof. The morphism Spec F -> X is flat, since F is the localization of any affine coordinate ring of X at its nonzero elements. Hence T_eta -> T is flat. The Cartier divisor div_T(f) pulls back to the Cartier divisor div_{T_eta}(f_eta). For Cartier divisors, associated cycles commute with flat pullback. To see the multiplicity statement directly, work locally: let X=Spec A and T=Spec B, with B an integral domain and F=S^{-1}A for S=A\{0}. A codimension-one point xi of T_eta corresponds to a prime Q subset B disjoint from S, of height one in S^{-1}B. The multiplicity of xi in the pullback of div_T(f) is length_{B_Q}(B_Q/f B_Q). On the other hand, the generic fiber of the cycle associated to div_T(f) is obtained by taking the sum over height-one primes P subset B with v_P(f) nonzero and P disjoint from S, with coefficient v_P(f), and then taking the fundamental cycle of (V(P))_eta. At xi, the contribution is the sum of v_P(f) times the length of the local ring at xi of (V(P))_eta over all such P contained in Q. This is exactly the length filtration of the one-dimensional Noetherian local ring B_Q/f B_Q, so the two multiplicities agree. If T does not dominate X, then T_eta is empty and both sides are zero. Auxiliary Lemma 2 (generic fiber map and descent). Let X/k be integral projective of dimension d and F=k(X). For gamma in CH_d(X x X) define gamma_eta in CH_0(X_F) as follows. Choose a d-cycle Z=sum n_i[W_i] representing gamma, with each W_i integral of dimension d. If W_i dominates X, then W_i_eta=W_i x_X Spec F is an integral zero-dimensional finite type F-scheme, hence the spectrum of a finite field extension of F; take its fundamental cycle. If W_i does not dominate X, take 0. Set Z_eta=sum n_i[W_i_eta]_fund. By Auxiliary Lemma 1 this is independent of the chosen representative and depends only on the rational equivalence class of Z, so it defines gamma_eta. Moreover, gamma_eta=0 in CH_0(X_F) if and only if there exists a dense open U subset X such that gamma|_{U x X}=0 in CH_d(U x X). Proof. If gamma restricts to zero on U x X, then its generic fiber is zero. Conversely, suppose gamma_eta=0. Choose a d-cycle Z representing gamma. Since the class of Z_eta is zero, by the definition of rational equivalence for 0-cycles there exist integral curves C_j subset X_F and rational functions f_j in k(C_j)^* such that Z_eta=sum div_{C_j}(f_j) as cycles. Let scriptC_j subset X x X be the scheme-theoretic closure of C_j. Then scriptC_j is integral of dimension d+1, dominates X, has generic fiber C_j, and k(scriptC_j)=k(C_j); hence f_j extends to an element of k(scriptC_j)^*. Put D=Z-sum div_{scriptC_j}(f_j). By Auxiliary Lemma 1, D_eta=0 as a cycle. Suppose an integral component V of D dominates X. Since dim V=d and V dominates X, V_eta is an integral zero-dimensional finite type F-scheme, hence a closed point of X_F. Distinct integral components of D that dominate X have distinct generic points in X_F, because a generic point of X x X determines its closure uniquely; components not dominating X contribute nothing to D_eta. Therefore the coefficient of the point V_eta in D_eta is a nonzero integer, contradicting D_eta=0. Thus no component of D dominates X. Since D has finitely many components and the first projection X x X -> X is proper, the images of these components under the first projection are proper closed subsets of X. Let Z_0 be their union. Then D is supported on Z_0 x X. Hence Z is rationally equivalent to a cycle supported on Z_0 x X. Taking U=X\Z_0 gives gamma|_{U x X}=0. Auxiliary Lemma 3 (support from vanishing on an open). Let U subset X be dense open and let delta in CH_d(X x X) satisfy delta|_{U x X}=0. Then delta has a cycle representative supported on (X\U) x X. Proof. Choose a d-cycle Z representing delta. Its restriction Z_U to U x X is rationally trivial. Hence there exist integral closed subschemes T_j subset U x X of dimension d+1 and rational functions f_j in k(T_j)^* such that Z_U=sum div_{T_j}(f_j) as cycles. Let overline{T_j} be the closure of T_j in X x X. Then overline{T_j} is integral, k(overline{T_j})=k(T_j), and f_j extends to a rational function on overline{T_j}. Define D=Z-sum div_{overline{T_j}}(f_j). Restricting to U x X gives D|_{U x X}=Z_U-sum div_{T_j}(f_j)=0 as a cycle. Therefore every component of D is contained in (X\U) x X, so D is a cycle representative of delta supported on (X\U) x X. Auxiliary Lemma 4 (injectivity over a rational function field). Let E be a field and let Y/E be smooth projective. The base-change map CH_0(Y) -> CH_0(Y_{E(t)}) is injective. Proof. Let z in CH_0(Y) map to zero in CH_0(Y_{E(t)}). Choose a 0-cycle Z on Y representing z. Since z_{E(t)}=0, there exist integral normal curves C_j subset Y_{E(t)}, morphisms nu_j:C_j -> Y_{E(t)}, and functions f_j in k(C_j)^* such that Z_{E(t)}=sum (nu_j)_* div(f_j) as cycles. This representation is standard: rational equivalence for 0-cycles is generated by principal divisors on integral curves, and normalizing a curve preserves pushforwards of principal divisors. Choose a nonzero g in E[t] and set A=E[1/g]. By spreading out the finitely many curves C_j, maps nu_j, functions f_j, and the finite 0-cycle Z, and by using generic flatness and normalization, we may assume that there exist normal integral curves scriptC_j proper and flat over Spec A, morphisms nu_j:scriptC_j -> Y x Spec A, functions f_{j,A} in k(scriptC_j)^*, and a finite flat A-scheme scriptZ subset Y x Spec A, such that the generic fibers are C_j, nu_j, f_j, and Z_{E(t)}, and after possibly replacing A by E[1/g'] with g' dividing g, the equality scriptZ=sum (nu_j)_* div(f_{j,A}) holds as cycles on Y x Spec A. For each j, the Cartier divisor div(f_{j,A}) has only finitely many vertical components. Remove from Spec A the finitely many closed points a for which some component of the fiber scriptC_{j,a} is contained in the support of div(f_{j,A}) or of its pole divisor. Let V be the remaining open subset of Spec A. For a closed point a in V, let R=A_{(a)} be the DVR at a, with uniformizer pi and residue field kappa(a). Base change scriptC_j and f_{j,A} to R. If necessary, normalize the resulting curve over R; normalization is finite and flat over the DVR R, does not change the function field or the pushforward of principal divisors, and yields a normal integral surface S flat over R whose special fiber S_0 has no embedded primes (normality gives S_2, and the fiber is an effective Cartier divisor, hence S_1). The function f=f_{j,R} is a unit at every generic point of S_0 by the choice of a. We claim that (div_S f)_0 = div_{S_0}(f_0) as 0-cycles on S_0. Indeed, in the Cartier divisor group of the normal surface S, (f)*(pi)=(pi)*(f). The left side is the principal divisor of f_0 on S_0, because (pi) is the Cartier divisor of the special fiber and f is a unit at the generic points of S_0. The right side is the fiber of div_S f: if D is a codimension-one integral subscheme of S with v_D(f) nonzero, then D cannot be vertical by the unit condition, so D -> Spec R is finite flat, and its contribution is v_D(f)[D_0]_fund. Thus the claim holds. Applying this to every j and using the spread-out equality gives Z_{kappa(a)}=sum (nu_{j,a})_* div(f_{j,a}) in Z_0(Y_{kappa(a)}). Hence z_{kappa(a)}=0 in CH_0(Y_{kappa(a)}). For a finite extension kappa/E, let pi:Y_kappa -> Y be the base-change projection. The norm formula pi_* pi^*=[kappa:E] id on CH_0(Y) holds. To verify it, let y be a closed point of Y with residue field L. Then pi^*[y]=sum_w length_{(L tensor_E kappa)_w}(L tensor_E kappa)[w], where w runs over the generic points of Spec(L tensor_E kappa), and pi_*[w]=[kappa(w):L][y]. The total coefficient of [y] is sum_w length_{(L tensor_E kappa)_w}(L tensor_E kappa)=dim_L(L tensor_E kappa)=[kappa:E]. Applying this with kappa=kappa(a), the equality z_{kappa(a)}=0 implies [kappa(a):E] z=0 in CH_0(Y). It remains to choose enough good closed points a. The bad closed points removed from Spec A form a finite set. If E is infinite, choose a good E-rational point a of A; this is possible because only finitely many elements c in E give bad closed points. Then kappa(a)=E and z=0. If E is finite, the number of monic irreducible polynomials of degree n over E tends to infinity with n, while the bad set is finite. Choose good closed points a_1 and a_2 of degrees n and n+1 for n sufficiently large. Then gcd(n,n+1)=1, and Bezout gives z=0. This proves injectivity. We now prove (S1). Since X/k is geometrically integral, X_{k(t)} is integral. Indeed, for an affine open Spec A subset X, A tensor_k k(t) is a domain, and its fraction field is Frac(A)(t); gluing gives function field F(t). Let eta' be the generic point of X_{k(t)}. Apply the generic fiber construction of Auxiliary Lemma 2 to the integral projective variety X_{k(t)}/k(t). Since alpha_{k(t)}=0 in CH_d(X_{k(t)} x X_{k(t)}), its generic fiber (alpha_{k(t)})_{eta'} is zero in CH_0(X_{F(t)}). If Z is a d-cycle representative of alpha on X x X, then for each integral component W of Z we have (W_{k(t)})_{eta'}=(W_eta)_{F(t)} as 0-cycles on X_{F(t)}: if W does not dominate X both sides are empty, and if W dominates X then W_eta is a finite F-scheme and the two sides are the same finite F(t)-scheme with its fundamental cycle. Hence (alpha_{k(t)})_{eta'}=(alpha_eta)_{F(t)} in CH_0(X_{F(t)}). Therefore (alpha_eta)_{F(t)}=0. By Auxiliary Lemma 4 applied to E=F and Y=X_F, we obtain alpha_eta=0 in CH_0(X_F). By the converse direction in Auxiliary Lemma 2, there exists a dense open U subset X such that alpha|_{U x X}=0 in CH_d(U x X). By Auxiliary Lemma 3, alpha has a cycle representative supported on Z_1 x X, where Z_1=X\U is proper closed in X. This proves (S1). For (S2), let alpha^t be the transpose of alpha. By lemma_42 (Spark), alpha^t also has zero image in CH_d(X_{k(t)} x X_{k(t)}). Applying the preceding paragraph to alpha^t gives a dense open V subset X and a proper closed subscheme Z_2=X\V such that alpha^t has a cycle representative supported on Z_2 x X. Transposing this representative gives a cycle representative of alpha supported on X x Z_2. This proves (S2). Finally, apply lemma_63 (Spark) as explained above. Let Y=Z_1 union Z_2 with its reduced closed subscheme structure. Since X is integral and Z_1 and Z_2 are proper closed subsets, Y is a proper closed subscheme of X. The cycle representative of alpha o alpha supplied by lemma_63 is supported on Z_1 x Z_2, which is contained in Y x Y. This completes the proof.

statement: Let E/k be a finite field extension of degree n and let t be an indeterminate over k. Then E⊗_k k(t) is a field, finite of degree n over k(t), and has transcendence degree one over k; moreover the canonical maps E→E⊗_k k(t) and k(t)→E⊗_k k(t) are injective.
proof:
Proof (self-contained commutative algebra; no external results are used).

NOTATION. Let S := k[t] \ {0} ⊂ k[t]. Then S is a multiplicative set: 1 ∈ S, 0 ∉ S, and S is closed under products (k[t] is a domain, since k is a field and a product of nonzero polynomials of degrees r, s has degree r + s with leading coefficient the product of the two nonzero leading coefficients). Let Ω := S^{-1}E[t] be the localization of the polynomial ring E[t] at S. We first build Ω, then identify it with E ⊗_k k(t), then prove it is a field of degree n over k(t).

PRELIMINARIES.
(P1) E[t] is an integral domain: if f, g ∈ E[t] are nonzero of degrees r, s with leading coefficients a, b ∈ E^×, then fg has degree r + s and leading coefficient ab ≠ 0, so fg ≠ 0.
(P2) The inclusion k[t] ⊂ E[t] (coefficients in k ⊂ E) is injective, since equality of polynomials is tested coefficientwise and k → E is injective. Hence every element of S is a nonzero element of E[t], and by (P1) a non-zero-divisor of E[t].

STEP 1: THE LOCALIZATION Ω.
Define a relation ~ on E[t] × S by (a, t₁) ~ (b, t₂) ⟺ there exists v ∈ S with v(a t₂ − b t₁) = 0 in E[t].
• Reflexive: (a,t) ~ (a,t) because 1·(at − at) = 0 and 1 ∈ S.
• Symmetric: v(a t₂ − b t₁) = 0 implies v(b t₁ − a t₂) = 0.
• Transitive: assume (a,t₁) ~ (b,t₂) via v ∈ S and (b,t₂) ~ (c,t₃) via w ∈ S, i.e. v(a t₂ − b t₁) = 0 and w(b t₃ − c t₂) = 0. Multiply the first identity by w t₃ and the second by v t₁ and add:
0 = w t₃·v(a t₂ − b t₁) + v t₁·w(b t₃ − c t₂) = v w(a t₂t₃ − b t₁t₃ + b t₁t₃ − c t₁t₂) = v w(a t₂t₃ − c t₁t₂) = v w t₂(a t₃ − c t₁).
Since t₂ ∈ S and S is multiplicative, v w t₂ ∈ S, so (a,t₁) ~ (c,t₃). (The common factor extracted is t₂, not t₃.)
Thus ~ is an equivalence relation; write f/s for the class of (f,s). Define (f/t) + (g/u) := (f u + g t)/(t u) and (f/s)(g/u) := (fg)/(su).
Well-definedness of addition: if (f,t) ~ (f′,t′) via v and (g,u) ~ (g′,u′) via w, then
v w[(f u + g t)t′u′ − (f′u′ + g′t′)tu] = v w[u u′(f t′ − f′t) + t t′(g u′ − g′u)] = u u′·[v(f t′ − f′t)]·w + t t′·[w(g u′ − g′u)]·v = u u′·0·w + t t′·0·v = 0,
and v w t t′ u u′ ∈ S, so the sums agree.
Well-definedness of products: with the same hypotheses,
(fg)t′u′ − (f′g′)tu = (f t′ − f′t)·g u′ + f′·(g u′ − g′u)·t,
as is checked by expanding the right side: f t′g u′ − f′t g u′ + f′g u′t − f′g′ut = f g t′u′ − f′g′tu (the middle terms cancel). Multiplying by v w gives 0, and v w ∈ S.
The ring axioms (associativity, commutativity, distributivity, 0 = 0/1, 1 = 1/1, −(f/s) = (−f)/s) follow directly from the corresponding identities in the commutative ring E[t]. The map j: E[t] → Ω, f ↦ f/1, is a ring homomorphism, and j(s) = s/1 is a unit with inverse 1/s for every s ∈ S.
Zero test: f/s = 0/1 ⟺ ∃v ∈ S with v(f·1 − 0·s) = v f = 0 ⟺ f = 0, using (P1), (P2) (v ≠ 0 in the domain E[t]). In particular 1/1 ≠ 0/1, so Ω is not the zero ring. Also Ω is a domain: (f/s)(g/u) = 0 ⇒ fg = 0 ⇒ f = 0 or g = 0.

STEP 2: Ω ≅ E ⊗_k k(t) AS k(t)-ALGEBRAS.
Let A := E ⊗_k k(t). Define ι: E[t] → A to be the unique k-algebra homomorphism with ι(e) = e ⊗ 1 for e ∈ E and ι(t) = 1 ⊗ t (existence/uniqueness by the universal property of the polynomial ring applied to the k-algebra A; the images of E and of k[t] commute in A). Explicitly ι(Σ_i e_i t^i) = Σ_i e_i ⊗ t^i, and in particular ι(e p) = (e ⊗ 1)(1 ⊗ p) = e ⊗ p for e ∈ E, p ∈ k[t].
For s ∈ S, ι(s) = 1 ⊗ s is a unit of A with inverse 1 ⊗ (1/s), since (1 ⊗ s)(1 ⊗ 1/s) = 1 ⊗ (s·(1/s)) = 1 ⊗ 1. Hence by the universal property of the localization there is a unique ring homomorphism Ψ: Ω → A with Ψ(f/s) = ι(f)·(1 ⊗ 1/s).
Conversely, define β: E × k(t) → Ω by β(e, p/s) := (e p)/s (p ∈ k[t], s ∈ S).
– Independence of the representation of ξ = p/s: if p/s = p′/s′ in k(t), there is 0 ≠ w ∈ k[t] with w(p s′ − p′s) = 0 in k[t]; as k[t] is a domain and w ≠ 0, p s′ = p′s in k[t], hence in E[t], so (ep)s′ = (ep′)s in E[t] and (ep)/s = (ep′)/s′ in Ω (equality criterion with multiplier 1).
– Additivity in the first variable: β(e + e′, p/s) = ((e + e′)p)/s = (ep + e′p)/s = (ep)/s + (e′p)/s.
– Additivity in the second variable: with ξ = p/s and ξ′ = p′/s′, ξ + ξ′ = (p s′ + p′s)/(s s′), so
β(e, ξ + ξ′) = (e(p s′ + p′s))/(s s′) = (ep·s′ + ep′·s)/(s s′),
while β(e,ξ) + β(e,ξ′) = (ep)/s + (ep′)/s′ = (ep·s′)/(s s′) + (ep′·s)/(s s′) = (ep·s′ + ep′·s)/(s s′). These agree (note the cross-multiplied numerators ep·s′ and ep′·s).
– k-homogeneity: for λ ∈ k, with λ·(q/r) := (λq)/r the k-algebra structure on Ω, β(λe, p/s) = ((λe)p)/s = (λ(ep))/s = λ·(ep)/s and β(e, λp/s) = (e(λp))/s = (λ(ep))/s, using commutativity of E.
So β is k-bilinear and induces a k-linear map Φ: A → Ω with Φ(e ⊗ ξ) = β(e, ξ).
Φ is a ring homomorphism: Φ(1 ⊗ 1) = 1/1 = 1_Ω, and for ξ = p/s, ξ′ = p′/s′,
Φ((e ⊗ ξ)(e′ ⊗ ξ′)) = Φ(ee′ ⊗ (p p′)/(s s′)) = (ee′p p′)/(s s′) = (ep)/s · (e′p′)/s′ = Φ(e ⊗ ξ)·Φ(e′ ⊗ ξ′).
They are mutually inverse:
ΨΦ(e ⊗ p/s) = Ψ((ep)/s) = ι(ep)·(1 ⊗ 1/s) = (e ⊗ p)(1 ⊗ 1/s) = e ⊗ (p/s).
ΦΨ(f/s): write f = Σ_i e_i t^i with e_i ∈ E; then Ψ(f/s) = ι(f)(1 ⊗ 1/s) = Σ_i e_i ⊗ (t^i/s), and by k-linearity of Φ this maps to Σ_i (e_i t^i)/s = (Σ_i e_i t^i)/s = f/s.
Hence Φ is a ring isomorphism Ω ≅ E ⊗_k k(t). Moreover Φ(e ⊗ 1) = (e·1)/1 = e/1 = j(e) and Φ(1 ⊗ p/s) = (1·p)/s = p/s; i.e. the canonical maps e ↦ e ⊗ 1 and ξ ↦ 1 ⊗ ξ correspond under Φ to the restrictions of j to E ⊂ E[t] and to k[t], followed by the localization.

STEP 3: Ω IS A FIELD.
Division lemma. Let v₁ = 1, v₂, …, v_n be a k-basis of E (n = [E:k]). Then (v₁,…,v_n) is a k[t]-basis of E[t]:
– Existence: f = Σ_j e_j t^j with e_j ∈ E; write e_j = Σ_i c_{ij} v_i with c_{ij} ∈ k; then f = Σ_i (Σ_j c_{ij} t^j) v_i with Σ_j c_{ij}t^j ∈ k[t].
– Uniqueness: if Σ_i h_i v_i = 0 with h_i = Σ_j c_{ij}t^j ∈ k[t], then Σ_{i,j} c_{ij} t^j v_i = 0 in E[t}; comparing the coefficient of each t^j gives Σ_i c_{ij}v_i = 0 in E, so all c_{ij} = 0 by k-linear independence, hence all h_i = 0.
Now fix 0 ≠ f ∈ E[t]. Multiplication by f is k[t]-linear on E[t] (f·(a h) = a·(f h) by commutativity), so there are c_{ji} ∈ k[t] with f v_i = Σ_j c_{ji} v_j; set C := (c_{ji}) ∈ M_n(k[t]). For x = (x_i) ∈ k[t]^n one has f(Σ_i x_i v_i) = Σ_j (Σ_i c_{ji}x_i) v_j.
Claim: det C ≠ 0. If det C = 0, then C is not invertible over the field k(t), so there is a nonzero x ∈ k(t)^n with Cx = 0; multiplying by a common denominator s ∈ k[t]\{0} yields y := s x ∈ k[t]^n nonzero with Cy = 0. Then h := Σ_i y_i v_i ≠ 0 in E[t] (uniqueness above), yet f h = Σ_j (Cy)_j v_j = 0, contradicting (P1) and f ≠ 0.
Let A := adj(C) = (a_{ij}) be the classical adjugate, so C·adj(C) = det(C)·I_n. Indeed the (i,j)-entry of C·adj(C) is Σ_ℓ c_{iℓ} a_{ℓj} = Σ_ℓ c_{iℓ} cof_{jℓ}(C), where cof_{jℓ}(C) is the (j,ℓ)-cofactor and ℓ is a summation index distinct from the entry indices i, j; this sum is det C when i = j (Laplace expansion of det C along the i-th row) and 0 when i ≠ j (Laplace expansion along row i of the matrix obtained from C by replacing its j-th row by its i-th row, which then has two equal rows).
Put D := det C ∈ k[t]\{0}, so D ∈ S, and g := Σ_i a_{i1} v_i ∈ E[t]. Then
f g = Σ_i a_{i1} f v_i = Σ_i a_{i1} Σ_j c_{ji} v_j = Σ_j (Σ_i c_{ji} a_{i1}) v_j = Σ_j (C A)_{j1} v_j = D·v₁ = D,
since (CA)_{j1} = δ_{j1} det C and v₁ = 1. Thus: for every 0 ≠ f ∈ E[t] there exist g ∈ E[t] and D ∈ S with f g = D.
Units. Let 0 ≠ f/s ∈ Ω. By the zero test of Step 1, f ≠ 0 in E[t]. Choose g ∈ E[t] and D ∈ S with fg = D. Note that D ∈ S, so h := (s g)/D is a legitimate element of Ω (its denominator lies in S). Then by the definition of multiplication in Ω,
(f/s)·h = (f·(s g))/(s·D) = (f s g)/(s D),
and in the domain E[t] the numerator equals f s g = s(f g) = s D, which is exactly the denominator; hence (f s g)/(s D) = (s D)/(s D) = 1/1 by the equality criterion with multiplier 1, because (sD)·1 − 1·(sD) = 0. Thus (f/s)h = 1_Ω, and by commutativity h(f/s) = 1_Ω. (The non-vanishing g ≠ 0 is automatic from fg = D ≠ 0 in the domain E[t], and is not needed.) Since 1_Ω ≠ 0_Ω by Step 1, every nonzero element of Ω is invertible: Ω is a field.

STEP 4: THE CANONICAL MAPS ARE INJECTIVE AND [Ω : k(t)] = n.
Injectivity of E → Ω, e ↦ e/1: e/1 = 0 forces e = 0 by the zero test. (Equivalently: Ω is a nonzero ring and E a field, so a unital ring map from E has kernel a proper ideal of E, hence 0.)
Injectivity of k(t) → Ω, p/s ↦ p/s: if p/s = 0 in Ω, the zero test gives p = 0 in E[t], hence p = 0 in k[t] by (P2), hence p/s = 0 in k(t). (Same alternative argument.)
Via the isomorphism Φ of Step 2 these are exactly the canonical maps E → E ⊗_k k(t), e ↦ e ⊗ 1, and k(t) → E ⊗_k k(t), ξ ↦ 1 ⊗ ξ; hence both are injective. In particular Ω is a field extension of (the image of) k(t), and E ⊗_k k(t) is not the zero ring.
k(t)-basis. Give Ω its k(t)-vector space structure through the injective map k(t) → Ω. We show (v₁,…,v_n) is a k(t)-basis.
– Spanning: let f/s ∈ Ω and write f = Σ_i h_i(t) v_i with h_i ∈ k[t] (basis fact above). Then
f/s = Σ_i (h_i/s)·(v_i/1),
because (h_i/s)(v_i/1) = (h_i v_i)/s and Σ_i (h_i v_i)/s = (Σ_i h_i v_i)/s = f/s (addition with the common denominator s). Each h_i/s lies in the image of k(t).
– Independence: suppose Σ_i (p_i/s_i)·(v_i/1) = 0 with p_i ∈ k[t], s_i ∈ S. Let s := Π_j s_j ∈ S and q_i := p_i Π_{j≠i} s_j ∈ k[t]; then p_i/s_i = q_i/s in k(t) and hence in Ω, so 0 = Σ_i (q_i/s)(v_i/1) = (Σ_i q_i v_i)/s. By the zero test, Σ_i q_i v_i = 0 in E[t], and uniqueness of the k[t]-basis representation gives q_i = 0 in k[t] for every i; then p_i/s_i = 0 in k(t).
Therefore Ω is a k(t)-vector space of dimension n, i.e. Ω/k(t) is a finite field extension of degree n = [E:k].

STEP 5: TRANSCENDENCE DEGREE.
Via k → k(t) → Ω (both injective) Ω is a field extension of k. Since Ω/k(t) is finite (Step 4), every element of Ω is algebraic over k(t). The element t ∈ Ω (namely t/1) is transcendental over k: if Σ_i λ_i t^i = 0 in Ω with λ_i ∈ k, then (Σ_i λ_i t^i)/1 = 0, so the zero test gives Σ_i λ_i t^i = 0 in E[t], hence all λ_i = 0 in E and therefore in k (this is exactly the statement that t is an indeterminate over k). Thus {t} is algebraically independent over k, and Ω is algebraic over k(t); hence {t} is a transcendence basis of Ω over k and trdeg_k Ω = 1.

CONCLUSION. E ⊗_k k(t) ≅ Ω is a field; it is a finite extension of k(t) of degree n = [E:k]; it has transcendence degree one over k; and the canonical maps E → E ⊗_k k(t) and k(t) → E ⊗_k k(t) are injective. ∎

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, and let p_{12}, p_{23}, p_{13}: X^3 -> X x X be the projections. For alpha,beta in CH^d(X x X), let Z_alpha and Z_beta be cycle representatives with supports S_alpha and S_beta. Then alpha o beta = p_{13*}(p_{12}^* alpha . p_{23}^* beta) has a cycle representative supported on the image under p_{13} of {(x_1,x_2,x_3) in X^3 | (x_1,x_2) in S_alpha and (x_2,x_3) in S_beta}.
proof:
PROOF. Throughout, for a scheme $V$ of finite type over $k$ and $m\ge 0$, $Z_m(V)$ denotes the free abelian group on the integral closed subschemes of $V$ of dimension $m$; for $Z=\sum_i n_i[V_i]\in Z_m(V)$ we write $|Z|=\bigcup_{n_i\ne 0}|V_i|\subset V$ for its (closed) support. To say that a class $\gamma\in CH_m(V)$ is \emph{supported on} a closed subset $F\subset V$ means that $\gamma$ has a representative $Z\in Z_m(V)$ with $|Z|\subset F$.

If $X=\varnothing$ all Chow groups involved are $0$ and $W=\varnothing$, so the statement is trivial; assume henceforth $X\neq\varnothing$. If $Z_\alpha=0$ or $Z_\beta=0$ then $\alpha\circ\beta=0$ by $\mathbb Z$-bilinearity of $\circ$, and $0$ is represented by the empty cycle, supported on $p_{13}(W)=\varnothing$; so we may also assume $Z_\alpha,Z_\beta\ne 0$. The case $d=0$ is covered by the same arguments (flat of relative dimension $0$).

\subsection*{Notation}
Put $S_\alpha:=|Z_\alpha|$, $S_\beta:=|Z_\beta|$ (closed subsets of $X\times_k X$) and
$$W:=p_{12}^{-1}(S_\alpha)\cap p_{23}^{-1}(S_\beta)\ \subset X^3 .$$
Set-theoretically, a point $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ of $X^3$ (i.e. a morphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to X^3$) lies in $W$ if and only if $p_{12}(x)=(x_1,x_2)\in S_\alpha$ and $p_{23}(x)=(x_2,x_3)\in S_\beta$; thus $W$ is exactly the set displayed in the statement of the lemma. It is closed, being the intersection of two inverse images of closed sets.

\subsection*{Step 1. The three projections}
Each of $p_{12},p_{23},p_{13}\colon X^3\to X\times_k X$ is the base change of the structure morphism $\pi\colon X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ along the structure morphism of $X\times_k X$: e.g.~the square with top arrow $\operatorname{pr}_3\colon X^3\to X$, left arrow $p_{12}$, right arrow $\pi$ and bottom arrow $X\times_k X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is cartesian because $X^3\cong (X\times_k X)\times_k X$. Since $X/k$ is smooth projective of pure dimension $d$, $\pi$ is flat of relative dimension $d$ and proper; flatness, relative dimension and properness are preserved by base change. Hence each $p_{ij}$ is \emph{flat projective of relative dimension $d$}.

\subsection*{Step 2. Support of a flat pullback}
\emph{Claim 1.} If $f\colon Y\to V$ is flat of relative dimension $r$ between schemes of finite type over $k$, and $Z\in Z_m(V)$, then $f^*Z\in Z_{m+r}(Y)$ is defined and $|f^*Z|=f^{-1}(|Z|)$.

\emph{Proof of Claim 1.} By linearity it suffices that $Z=[\mathcal V]$ for $\mathcal V\subset V$ integral closed. For a flat morphism the pullback of $[\mathcal V]$ is defined (Fulton, \emph{Intersection Theory}, \S1.7) as the cycle associated with the scheme-theoretic inverse image: $f^*[\mathcal V]=\sum_\xi \operatorname{length}_{\mathcal O_{f^{-1}\mathcal V,\xi}}(\mathcal O_{f^{-1}\mathcal V,\xi})\,[\overline\xi]$, the sum running over the generic points $\xi$ of $f^{-1}\mathcal V$. That this is a legal element of $Z_{m+r}(Y)$ is the standard dimension theorem for flat morphisms: $g\colon f^{-1}\mathcal V\to\mathcal V$ is flat of finite presentation with every fibre of pure dimension $r$ (fibres of $g$ are fibres of $f$), and $\mathcal V$ is catenary (variety over a field), so every irreducible component of $f^{-1}\mathcal V$ has dimension $\dim\mathcal V+r=m+r$ (going-down for flat maps lifts chains from the base, and the fibre dimension adds; see e.g.\ Stacks Project, Tags 00O5, 02VG). Each coefficient $\operatorname{length}_{\mathcal O_{f^{-1}\mathcal V,\xi}}\mathcal O_{f^{-1}\mathcal V,\xi}$ is the length of a non-zero zero-dimensional local ring, hence $\ge 1>0$; therefore every irreducible component of $f^{-1}\mathcal V$ occurs in $f^*[\mathcal V]$, and
$$|f^*[\mathcal V]|=|f^{-1}\mathcal V|=f^{-1}(|\mathcal V|).$$
Writing $Z=\sum n_i[\mathcal V_i]$ gives $|f^*Z|=\bigcup_{n_i\ne0}|f^*[\mathcal V_i]|=\bigcup_{n_i\ne0}f^{-1}|\mathcal V_i|=f^{-1}|Z|$. Flat pullback also descends to Chow groups (Fulton \S1.7: for a rational function $u$ on an integral $(m{+}1)$-dimensional $T\subset V$, flat base change identifies $f^*\operatorname{div}(u)$ with $\operatorname{div}(u\circ\operatorname{pr})$ on $T\times_V Y$, using that flat pullback commutes with Cartier divisors). $\square$

Applying Claim 1 to $f=p_{12}$, $r=d$, $Z=Z_\alpha$ and to $f=p_{23}$, $Z=Z_\beta$:
$$A:=p_{12}^*[Z_\alpha]\in Z_{2d}(X^3)\ \text{represents}\ p_{12}^*\alpha,\qquad |A|=p_{12}^{-1}S_\alpha,$$
$$B:=p_{23}^*[Z_\beta]\in Z_{2d}(X^3)\ \text{represents}\ p_{23}^*\beta,\qquad |B|=p_{23}^{-1}S_\beta.$$
(In particular $p_{12}^*\alpha,p_{23}^*\beta\in CH^{d}(X^3)$: flat pullback by a morphism of relative dimension $d$ preserves codimension, since $\dim X^3=3d=2d+d$.)

\subsection*{Step 3. Support of an intersection product on a smooth scheme}
\emph{Claim 2.} Let $Y/k$ be smooth of pure dimension $n$, let $a\in CH^{r}(Y)$, $b\in CH^{s}(Y)$ be represented by cycles $A,B$ on $Y$. Then $a\cdot b\in CH^{r+s}(Y)$ has a representative supported on $|A|\cap|B|$.

\emph{Proof of Claim 2.} The intersection product on the smooth $k$-scheme $Y$ is defined by
$$a\cdot b=\Delta^!(a\times b),$$
where $\times$ is the exterior (cross) product and $\Delta\colon Y\hookrightarrow Y\times_k Y$ is the diagonal, a regular embedding of codimension $n$ (smoothness of $Y/k$ makes $\Delta$ a local complete intersection closed immersion of codimension $\dim Y$); this is the standard definition of the ring structure on $CH(Y)$ (Fulton, Ch.~8, \S8.1).

\emph{(a) The cross product.} For integral closed $\mathcal V,\mathcal W\subset Y$, $[\mathcal V]\times[\mathcal W]$ is the cycle associated with $\mathcal V\times_k\mathcal W$ pushed forward by the closed immersion $\mathcal V\times_k\mathcal W\hookrightarrow Y\times_k Y$. Its support is the image of $|\mathcal V\times_k\mathcal W|$, which equals $|\mathcal V|\times|\mathcal W|$: the map $|\mathcal V\times_k\mathcal W|\to|\mathcal V|\times|\mathcal W|$ is surjective because the fibre over $(v,w)$ is $\operatorname{Spec}(\kappa(v)\otimes_k\kappa(w))$, non-empty since $\kappa(v)\otimes_k\kappa(w)\ne0$ (both fields are free, hence flat, $k$-modules, so non-zero elements tensor to a non-zero element, and a non-zero ring has a prime ideal). Writing $A=\sum_i n_i[\mathcal V_i]$, $B=\sum_j m_j[\mathcal W_j]$, bilinearity gives a representative of $a\times b$ which is the pushforward of a cycle $\tau\in Z_{2n-r-s}(T)$, where $T:=(|A|\times|B|)_{\mathrm{red}}\subset Y\times_k Y$ is the reduced closed subscheme on $|A|\times|B|$, and $j\colon T\hookrightarrow Y\times_k Y$ is the closed immersion.

\emph{(b) The refined Gysin map.} For the regular embedding $\Delta$ of codimension $n$ and any morphism $g\colon\Sigma\to Y\times_k Y$ there is a homomorphism $\Delta^!\colon CH_m\Sigma\to CH_{m-n}(\Sigma\times_{Y\times_k Y}Y)$ (Fulton, Ch.~VI, \S1), characterized/constructed so that:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] (proper intersection formula) if $\Sigma$ is integral and every component of $\Sigma\times_{Y\times_k Y}Y$ has codimension $n$ in $\Sigma$, then $\Delta^![\Sigma]=\sum_\xi\operatorname{length}_{\mathcal O_{\Sigma,\xi}}\big(\mathcal O_{\Sigma\times_{Y\times_k Y}Y,\xi}\big)[\overline\xi]$, a cycle \emph{on} $\Sigma\times_{Y\times_k Y}Y$;
\item[(ii)] (compatibility with proper pushforward, Fulton Ch.~VI, Thm.~6.2(a)) for a commutative diagram with cartesian right square and $h\colon\Sigma'\to\Sigma$ proper over $Y\times_k Y$, one has $\Delta^!h_*=h'_*\Delta^!$, where $h'$ is the base change of $h$.
\end{itemize}
(Both are immediate from the construction via the deformation to the normal cone, which takes place entirely over $\Sigma\times_{Y\times_k Y}Y$; (i) is the classical proper intersection product, so the definition recovers the usual product when intersections are proper.)

Applying (ii) to the proper map $j\colon T\to Y\times_k Y$ and the cartesian square
$$\begin{array}{ccc} T\times_{Y\times_k Y}Y & \longrightarrow & T\\ \downarrow && \downarrow j\\ Y & \xrightarrow{\ \Delta\ } & Y\times_k Y,\end{array}$$
we obtain $a\cdot b=\Delta^!(j_*\tau)=j'_*(\Delta_T^!\tau)$, where $\Delta_T\colon T\times_{Y\times_k Y}Y\hookrightarrow T$ is the base-change regular embedding and $j'\colon T\times_{Y\times_k Y}Y\to Y$ is the base change of $j$. Thus $a\cdot b$ is the pushforward of a cycle living on $T\times_{Y\times_k Y}Y$.

\emph{(c) Identifying the fibre product.} Via $\Delta\simeq\mathrm{id}_Y$, the scheme $T\times_{Y\times_k Y}Y$ is the closed subscheme $\Delta^{-1}(T)\subset Y$, whose underlying set is $\{y\in Y:(y,y)\in |A|\times|B|\}=|A|\cap|B|$. Hence $j'_*(\Delta_T^!\tau)$ is a cycle on $Y$ supported on $|A|\cap|B|$, representing $a\cdot b$. $\square$

\emph{Remark (independence of the definition).} The equivalent formula $a\cdot b=\Delta^!(\operatorname{pr}_1^*a\cdot\operatorname{pr}_2^*b)$ (Fulton, Ex.~8.1.1) gives the same support conclusion: applying Claim 2 to the smooth scheme $Y\times_k Y$ shows $\operatorname{pr}_1^*a\cdot\operatorname{pr}_2^*b$ is supported on $\operatorname{pr}_1^{-1}|A|\cap\operatorname{pr}_2^{-1}|B|$, and the argument of (b)--(c) then puts the product in $|A|\cap|B|$ again. So the conclusion does not depend on which standard definition of the product on $CH(Y)$ is adopted.

\subsection*{Step 4. Support of a proper pushforward}
\emph{Claim 3.} If $f\colon Y\to V$ is proper and $C\in Z_m(Y)$, then $f_*C\in Z_m(V)$ is defined and $|f_*C|\subset f(|C|)$.

\emph{Proof of Claim 3.} For $\mathcal V\subset Y$ integral closed, $f_*[\mathcal V]=0$ if $\dim f(|\mathcal V|)<\dim\mathcal V$, and $f_*[\mathcal V]=[\kappa(\mathcal V):\kappa(f(\mathcal V))]\,[f(|\mathcal V|)]$ if $\dim f(|\mathcal V|)=\dim\mathcal V$ (Fulton, \S1.4); in either case the support of $f_*[\mathcal V]$ is either empty or equal to $f(|\mathcal V|)\subset f(|\mathcal V|)$. Linearity gives the claim. $\square$

\subsection*{Step 5. Assembly}
Apply Claim 2 with $Y=X^3$ (smooth of dimension $3d$ over $k$), $a=p_{12}^*\alpha$, $b=p_{23}^*\beta$, $r=s=d$, using the representatives $A=p_{12}^*[Z_\alpha]$ and $B=p_{23}^*[Z_\beta]$ of Step 2. We obtain a cycle
$$C\in Z_{d}(X^3)\qquad\text{with}\qquad [C]=p_{12}^*\alpha\cdot p_{23}^*\beta\in CH^{2d}(X^3),\qquad |C|\subset |A|\cap|B|=p_{12}^{-1}S_\alpha\cap p_{23}^{-1}S_\beta=W .$$
Now apply Claim 3 to the proper morphism $p_{13}$ (Step 1) and to $C$: $p_{13*}C\in Z_d(X\times_k X)$ represents
$$p_{13*}\big(p_{12}^*\alpha\cdot p_{23}^*\beta\big)=\alpha\circ\beta,$$
and its support satisfies
$$|p_{13*}C|\subset p_{13}(|C|)\subset p_{13}(W).$$
Since $p_{13}$ is proper and $W$ is closed in $X^3$, $p_{13}(W)$ is a closed subset of $X\times_k X$. Thus $\alpha\circ\beta=p_{13*}(p_{12}^*\alpha\cdot p_{23}^*\beta)$ is represented by the cycle $p_{13*}C$, supported on $p_{13}(W)=p_{13}\big(\{(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in X^3:(x_1,x_2)\in S_\alpha,\ (x_2,x_3)\in S_\beta\}\big)$, which is exactly the required conclusion.

All steps have been justified: Step 1 (base change of $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$), Claim 1 (flat pullback: equidimensionality and positivity of multiplicities), Claim 2 (cross product support + refined Gysin target and proper-pushforward compatibility), Claim 3 (proper pushforward), and the set-theoretic identification $W=p_{12}^{-1}S_\alpha\cap p_{23}^{-1}S_\beta$ with the displayed subset. $\blacksquare$

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let E/k be a finite field extension of degree n, let X_E=X×_k Spec E, and let π:X_E×_E X_E→X×_k X be the natural projection. Then π is finite flat of degree n, and for every γ∈CH^d(X×_k X) the equality π_*π^*γ=nγ holds, where π^* is flat pullback and π_* is proper pushforward on Chow groups.
proof:
We write S := X \times_k X and S_E := X_E \times_E X_E with X_E := X \times_k \mathrm{Spec}\,E, so that \pi : S_E \to S is the natural projection. Throughout, E/k is a finite field extension of degree n, and e_1,...,e_n is a fixed k-basis of E.

STEP 0 (empty case). If X = \emptyset then S = S_E = \emptyset, CH^d(S) = 0, and \pi : \emptyset \to \emptyset is finite flat of rank n (there are no affine opens to check, and \pi_*O_{S_E} = 0 = O_S^{\oplus n}); the identity \pi_*\pi^*\gamma = n\gamma reads 0 = 0. Henceforth assume X \neq \emptyset.

STEP 1 (identification of S_E, and finite flatness of \pi of rank n).
1(a) Canonical identification. For k-schemes X, Y and a k-scheme T one has a canonical isomorphism (X \times_k T) \times_T (Y \times_k T) \xrightarrow{\sim} X \times_k Y \times_k T: by the universal property of the fibre product, a T-morphism Z \to (X\times_k T)\times_T(Y\times_k T) is the same as a pair of morphisms Z \to X\times_k T and Z \to Y\times_k T over T, i.e. morphisms Z\to X, Z\to Y, Z\to T such that the two composites Z\to T agree, which is the same as a k-morphism Z \to X\times_k Y\times_k T. Taking T = \mathrm{Spec}\,E and Y = X gives
   S_E = (X\times_k \mathrm{Spec}\,E)\times_{\mathrm{Spec}\,E}(X\times_k \mathrm{Spec}\,E) \cong X\times_k X\times_k \mathrm{Spec}\,E = S\times_k \mathrm{Spec}\,E,
and under this identification \pi is the base change of the structural morphism p : \mathrm{Spec}\,E \to \mathrm{Spec}\,k.
1(b) Finiteness and flatness. Since E/k is a finite extension of degree n, E is a free k-module of rank n with basis e_1,\dots,e_n. For any k-algebra B, the map
   \theta_B : B\otimes_k E \longrightarrow B^{\oplus n},\quad b\otimes\Big(\sum_i \lambda_i e_i\Big) \longmapsto (b\lambda_1,\dots,b\lambda_n),
is a B-module isomorphism, with inverse (b_1,\dots,b_n) \mapsto \sum_i b_i\otimes e_i. Hence B\otimes_k E is generated as B-module by 1\otimes e_1,\dots,1\otimes e_n, so it is a finite B-module, and it is a free B-module of rank n, hence flat. If U_\lambda = \mathrm{Spec}\,B_\lambda is an affine open of S, then \pi^{-1}U_\lambda = \mathrm{Spec}(B_\lambda\otimes_k E), so \pi is affine, finite and flat, and \Gamma(U_\lambda,\pi_*O_{S_E}) = B_\lambda^{\oplus n}. Since \theta_B is natural in B, the isomorphisms \theta_{B_\lambda} glue over the affine opens of S to an isomorphism of O_S-modules
   \pi_*O_{S_E} \;\cong\; O_S^{\oplus n}.
Thus \pi is finite, flat, and \pi_*O_{S_E} is locally free of constant rank n; this rank n is what we mean by "finite flat of degree n". (We deliberately make no assertion about the length of the fibre algebras E\otimes_k\kappa(s) as modules over themselves: such an Artinian \kappa(s)-algebra has \kappa(s)-dimension n, but its self-length need not be n, since its simple modules are its residue fields, which can have degree >1 over \kappa(s). All numerical uses of the degree below go through ranks/dimension over a field, culminating in the identity (*) of Step 5.)
1(c) Relative dimension. Every fibre of \pi is \mathrm{Spec}(E\otimes_k\kappa(s)) for a point s\in S, the spectrum of an Artinian ring, hence 0-dimensional. So \pi is flat of relative dimension 0 in the sense of Fulton, Intersection Theory, Ch. 1, \S 1.7, and the same holds for every base change of \pi.

STEP 2 (equidimensionality and reduction to integral d-dimensional subschemes).
2(a) By convention "smooth projective of dimension d" means of pure dimension d. Since X is smooth over k it is regular, hence normal; a noetherian normal scheme is a disjoint union of its irreducible components, which are open and closed. Write X = \bigsqcup_j X_j with X_j integral, smooth and projective of dimension d over k. Then S = \bigsqcup_{j,j'} (X_j\times_k X_{j'}), and each X_j\times_k X_{j'} \to \mathrm{Spec}\,k is smooth of relative dimension 2d (smoothness and relative dimension are preserved under base change and products), hence of pure dimension 2d: smooth morphisms over a field are open and have equidimensional fibres of the relative dimension. Thus S is equidimensional of dimension 2d, and consequently codimension-d cycles on S are exactly d-dimensional cycles, i.e. CH^d(S) = CH_d(S). Likewise X_E is smooth projective of dimension d over E (base change of X), so S_E = X_E\times_E X_E is equidimensional of dimension 2d and CH^d(S_E) = CH_d(S_E).
2(b) Reduction. Flat pullback gives a homomorphism \pi^* : CH_d(S) \to CH_d(S_E) (flat of relative dimension 0 preserves the dimension of cycles; Fulton 1.7), and \pi is finite, hence proper, so proper pushforward gives \pi_* : CH_d(S_E) \to CH_d(S) (Fulton 1.4). Both are group homomorphisms, so the map \gamma \mapsto \pi_*\pi^*\gamma - n\gamma is additive on CH_d(S). Since CH_d(S) is generated by the classes [V] of integral closed subschemes V \subset S of dimension d, it suffices to prove
   \pi_*\pi^*[V] = n\,[V] \quad\text{in } Z_d(S)
for every such V. (We prove it at the level of cycles, so it automatically descends to Chow groups.)

STEP 3 (restriction to V and the flat-pullback formula). Fix an integral closed subscheme V \subset S of dimension d, put K := \kappa(V) (the function field, i.e. the residue field at the generic point \eta of V), and set Y := \pi^{-1}V = V\times_k\mathrm{Spec}\,E with f := \pi|_Y : Y \to V. By Step 1 applied over V (base change of \mathrm{Spec}\,E\to\mathrm{Spec}\,k), f is finite flat with f_*O_Y \cong O_V^{\oplus n}, of relative dimension 0. By the definition of flat pullback on cycles (Fulton Ch. 1, Def. 1.7 and Ex. 1.7.1),
   \pi^*[V] = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \ell_i\,[W_i], \qquad \ell_i := \mathrm{length}_{O_{Y,\xi_i}}(O_{Y,\xi_i}),
where W_1,\dots,W_r are the irreducible components of Y of dimension d = \dim V + 0 and \xi_i is the generic point of W_i (the summand is viewed as a cycle on S_E via the closed immersion Y \hookrightarrow S_E). Step 4 will show that every irreducible component of Y has dimension d, so that W_1,\dots,W_r are all the components of Y.

STEP 4 (every component of Y dominates V).
Lemma 4'. Let V be integral of dimension d and f : Y = V\times_k\mathrm{Spec}\,E \to V the finite flat morphism above. Then every irreducible component W of Y maps onto V.
Proof. Cover V by its non-empty affine opens U_\lambda = \mathrm{Spec}\,B_\lambda; each B_\lambda is a domain (open subscheme of the integral scheme V). Then \pi^{-1}U_\lambda = \mathrm{Spec}\,A_\lambda with A_\lambda = B_\lambda\otimes_k E, which is free of rank n \geq 1 over B_\lambda by Step 1(b); a free module of positive finite rank over a nonzero ring is faithfully flat, so B_\lambda \to A_\lambda is flat, and flat ring maps satisfy going down (Atiyah--Macdonald, Prop. 3.16). Let q be a minimal prime of A_\lambda and set p := q\cap B_\lambda. In B_\lambda we have the inclusion (0) \subset p, and q is a prime of A_\lambda lying over p; going down applied to this chain yields a prime q' \subset q of A_\lambda with q'\cap B_\lambda = (0). Minimality of q forces q' = q, hence q\cap B_\lambda = (0). Thus the generic point of every irreducible component C of \pi^{-1}U_\lambda maps to the generic point of U_\lambda, i.e. C dominates U_\lambda and f(C) is dense in U_\lambda. Since f is finite, f is a closed map, and C is closed in \pi^{-1}U_\lambda (components of a noetherian space are closed); hence f(C) is closed in U_\lambda and dense, so f(C) = U_\lambda.
Now let W be an irreducible component of Y. The opens \pi^{-1}U_\lambda cover Y and W \neq \emptyset, so W\cap\pi^{-1}U_\lambda \neq \emptyset for some \lambda. This intersection is open in W, hence irreducible, hence contained in a single irreducible component C of \pi^{-1}U_\lambda. The closure \overline{C} of C in Y is irreducible closed and contains W\cap\pi^{-1}U_\lambda, which is dense in W; therefore W = \mathrm{cl}_Y(W\cap\pi^{-1}U_\lambda) \subset \overline{C}, and maximality of W among irreducible closed subsets gives W = \overline{C}. Then f(W) \supset f(C) = U_\lambda, and f(W) is closed in V (W is closed in Y and f is finite, hence closed); a closed subset of V containing the dense open U_\lambda is all of V. Hence f(W) = V. \qed

Consequences of Lemma 4'.
(4a) Each generic point \xi_i lies over \eta = \mathrm{Spec}\,K.
(4b) \dim W_i = \dim V = d. Indeed, take any non-empty affine open U = \mathrm{Spec}\,B \subset V; then W_i\cap f^{-1}U is a non-empty open subscheme of the integral scheme W_i, isomorphic to \mathrm{Spec}(A/q_i) where A := B\otimes_k E and q_i is a minimal prime of A. As A is a finite B-module (Step 1(b)), A/q_i is a finite, hence integral, extension of B/(q_i\cap B) = B/(0) = B; for an integral extension of domains, going up and lying over give \dim(A/q_i) = \dim B = d, and the dimension of an irreducible noetherian space equals that of any non-empty open. So \dim W_i = d. In particular the components W_i are exactly the d-dimensional components entering the formula of Step 3, and Y is equidimensional of dimension d.
(4c) A/q_i is a domain finite over B, so A_\eta/Q_i := S^{-1}(A/q_i) (with S = B\setminus\{0\}, see Step 5) is a finite-dimensional K-algebra which is a domain, hence a field; it is the fraction field of A/q_i. Thus \kappa(W_i) := \kappa(\xi_i) = \mathrm{Frac}(A/q_i) is a finite extension of K.
(4d) \ell_i < \infty. Indeed O_{Y,\xi_i} is noetherian local, and its prime ideals correspond to the primes of A contained in q_i, of which q_i is the only one; so O_{Y,\xi_i} is noetherian local of dimension 0, hence Artinian, hence of finite length over itself.

STEP 5 (the numerical identity). We keep the affine open U = \mathrm{Spec}\,B \subset V, A := B\otimes_k E, Y_U := f^{-1}U = \mathrm{Spec}\,A, S := B\setminus\{0\}, K = S^{-1}B = \mathrm{Frac}(B).
5(a) Localising at the generic point. Since each W_i dominates V, W_i\cap Y_U is a non-empty open of W_i, hence contains \xi_i; so all \xi_i lie in Y_U and O_{Y,\xi_i} = O_{Y_U,\xi_i} = A_{q_i}. Moreover the C_i := W_i\cap Y_U are exactly the irreducible components of Y_U: by the argument of Lemma 4', each W_i\cap Y_U is contained in a component C of Y_U with \overline{C} = W_i, and if C_i \subsetneq C' \subset Y_U with C' a component then C' \subset \mathrm{cl}_Y(C_i) = W_i, whence C' \subset W_i\cap Y_U = C_i, contradiction. Thus Min(A) = \{q_1,\dots,q_r\}, each q_i\cap B = (0) (hence q_i\cap S = \emptyset) by the going-down argument in Lemma 4', and \ell_i = \mathrm{length}_{A_{q_i}}(A_{q_i}).
5(b) The generic fibre. We have A\otimes_B K = (B\otimes_k E)\otimes_B K = K\otimes_k E =: A_\eta, and Y\times_V\mathrm{Spec}\,K = \mathrm{Spec}\,A_\eta; topologically, the points of the generic fibre are exactly the points of Y lying over \eta, and for such a point y the local rings agree, O_{Y_\eta,y} = O_{Y,y}\otimes_{O_{V,\eta}}\kappa(\eta) = O_{Y,y}, because O_{V,\eta} = \kappa(\eta) = K (V integral). We record the following elementary bijection: q \mapsto S^{-1}q gives a bijection Min(A) \xrightarrow{\sim} Min(A_\eta) with A_q \cong (A_\eta)_{S^{-1}q}.
Proof. Primes of A_\eta = S^{-1}A are S^{-1}p with p a prime of A, p\cap S = \emptyset. If S^{-1}q_i \supset S^{-1}q' with q'\cap S = \emptyset, then q' \subset q_i, so q' = q_i by minimality of q_i; thus S^{-1}q_i is minimal. Conversely, let P = S^{-1}q' be minimal in A_\eta, so q' is minimal among the primes disjoint from S. If q \subset q' is any prime of A, then q\cap B \subset q'\cap B = (0), so q\cap S = \emptyset and S^{-1}q \subset P; minimality gives S^{-1}q = P, hence q = q', so q' \in Min(A). For the local rings: (S^{-1}A)_{S^{-1}q_i} is the localization of A at the multiplicative set \{s\cdot a : s\in S,\ a\notin q_i\} = S\cdot(A\setminus q_i), which equals (A_{q_i}) localized at the image of S; but S \subset A\setminus q_i, so the image of S in A_{q_i} consists of units and the localization does nothing. Hence (A_\eta)_{S^{-1}q_i} \cong A_{q_i}.
5(c) Counting over K. As a K-vector space, A_\eta = K\otimes_k E \cong \bigoplus_{i=1}^{n} K\,(1\otimes e_i), so \dim_K A_\eta = n. Being a finite-dimensional commutative K-algebra, A_\eta is Artinian (descending chains of ideals are descending chains of K-subspaces). By the structure theorem for Artinian rings, A_\eta has only finitely many prime ideals, all maximal — these are exactly Q_i := S^{-1}q_i, i=1,\dots,r — and the natural map is an isomorphism
   A_\eta \;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \prod_{i=1}^{r} (A_\eta)_{Q_i}.
Each R_i := (A_\eta)_{Q_i} is Artinian local with maximal ideal Q_iR_i and residue field R_i/Q_iR_i \cong A_\eta/Q_i. By 5(b), R_i \cong A_{q_i}, so \mathrm{length}_{R_i}(R_i) = \ell_i. By 4(c), A_\eta/Q_i = S^{-1}(A/q_i) is a field equal to \mathrm{Frac}(A/q_i) = \kappa(W_i), a finite extension of K; indeed A_\eta/Q_i is a finite-dimensional K-algebra and a domain, hence a field, and it is a subring of \mathrm{Frac}(A/q_i) containing A/q_i, hence equal to \mathrm{Frac}(A/q_i). In the local ring R_i the unique simple module is R_i/Q_iR_i = \kappa(W_i); taking a composition series of R_i as an R_i-module, all \ell_i factors are isomorphic to \kappa(W_i), and comparing K-dimensions gives
   \dim_K R_i = \ell_i\cdot[\kappa(W_i):K].
Summing over i and using the product decomposition and \dim_K A_\eta = n,
   n \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{r} \dim_K R_i \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{r} \ell_i\,[\kappa(W_i):K]. \qquad (*)
This is the correct form of the "degree n" count: rank n of f_*O_Y equals the sum of the local multiplicities \ell_i weighted by the residue-field degrees.

STEP 6 (pushforward of the components). For each i, f(W_i) = V by Lemma 4' and \dim W_i = \dim V = d by 4(b). By the definition of the proper pushforward of a cycle (Fulton Ch. 1, Def. 1.4), a proper map sending an integral closed subscheme W onto an integral closed subscheme V' with \dim W = \dim V' pushes [W] forward to [\kappa(W):\kappa(V')]\,[V'] (and to 0 if the dimensions differ). Hence
   \pi_*[W_i] = [\kappa(W_i):\kappa(V)]\,[V] = [\kappa(W_i):K]\,[V],
and therefore, using the expression of Step 3 and linearity,
   \pi_*\pi^*[V] = \sum_{i=1}^{r}\ell_i\,\pi_*[W_i] = \Big(\sum_{i=1}^{r}\ell_i\,[\kappa(W_i):K]\Big)[V] \overset{(*)}{=} n\,[V].

STEP 7 (descent to Chow groups, and the ambient group). By additivity, \pi_*\pi^*Z = nZ for every d-cycle Z on S. Flat pullback and proper pushforward preserve rational equivalence (Fulton Ch. 1, Prop. 1.7 and Prop. 1.4), so both descend to Chow groups, and we obtain for every \gamma \in CH_d(S)
   \pi_*\pi^*\gamma = n\,\gamma.
Here \pi^* : CH_d(S) \to CH_d(S_E) and \pi_* : CH_d(S_E) \to CH_d(S); the equality is an equality in CH_d(S) = CH^d(S) = CH^d(X\times_k X), obtained after pushing forward to S — not an equality in CH_d(S_E).

STEP 8 (conclusion). Steps 1 and 7 give exactly the two required assertions: \pi : X_E\times_E X_E \to X\times_k X is finite flat of degree n (equivalently, finite with \pi_*O_{S_E} \cong O_S^{\oplus n}), and \pi_*\pi^*\gamma = n\gamma in CH^d(X\times_k X) for every \gamma \in CH^d(X\times_k X). \qed

statement: Let Y/k be a scheme of finite type, let p: Y\times_k \mathbb{A}^1_k \to \mathbb{A}^1_k be the projection, let i_0: Y \xrightarrow{\sim} Y\times_k\{0\} \hookrightarrow Y\times_k \mathbb{A}^1_k be the zero section, and for each closed point s of \mathbb{A}^1_k let i_s: Y_{\kappa(s)} \hookrightarrow Y\times_k \mathbb{A}^1_k be the base change of Spec \kappa(s) \hookrightarrow \mathbb{A}^1_k. Let i_0^!: \mathrm{CH}_m(Y\times_k \mathbb{A}^1_k) \to \mathrm{CH}_{m-1}(Y) denote the refined Gysin pullback along the effective Cartier divisor Y\times_k\{0\} of Y\times_k \mathbb{A}^1_k. Then i_0^! \circ i_{s*} = 0 for every closed point s of \mathbb{A}^1_k and every m \ge 0.
proof:
Notation. Write $\mathbb A^1_k=\operatorname{Spec} k[t]$ with standard coordinate $t$, put $X:=Y\times_k\mathbb A^1_k$ and $\pi:=\mathrm{pr}_1:X\to Y$, $p:=\mathrm{pr}_2:X\to\mathbb A^1_k$. Let $f:=p^{\#}(t)\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be the pullback of $t$, and let $D:=Y\times_k\{0\}\subset X$; thus $D=V(f)$ and $i_0:Y\xrightarrow{\sim}D\hookrightarrow X$ is the zero section of the trivial line bundle $\pi:X\to Y$. For a closed point $s\in\mathbb A^1_k$ with residue field $\kappa(s)$ and closed immersion $j_s:\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1_k$, the map $i_s:Y_{\kappa(s)}=Y\times_k\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)\hookrightarrow X$ is the base change of $j_s$; its image is the fibre $Y\times_k\{s\}$ (as a closed subscheme).

$D$ is an effective Cartier divisor: on an affine open $\operatorname{Spec} B\subset Y$ we have $\mathcal O_X= B[t]$ and multiplication by $t$ on $B[t]$ is injective, so $f$ is a non-zero-divisor on $X$ and $\mathcal I_D=f\cdot\mathcal O_X$.

We use three standard facts about the refined Gysin homomorphism of an effective Cartier divisor, which we recall/verify.

(F1) Cycle formula away from $D$. Let $W\subset X$ be an integral closed subscheme of dimension $m$ with $W\not\subset D$. Then, as cycles on $D$,
$$i_0^![W]=\operatorname{div}(f|_W)=\sum_{\xi} \operatorname{length}_{\mathcal O_{W,\xi}}\bigl(\mathcal O_{W,\xi}/(f)\bigr)\,[\bar\xi],$$
where $\xi$ runs over the codimension-$1$ points of $W$ at which $f$ lies in the maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_\xi$, and $\bar\xi$ is the corresponding integral closed subscheme of $D$. This is the definition of the refined Gysin pullback along a Cartier divisor for cycles not contained in the divisor (equivalently, the Cartier-divisor intersection product $D\cdot[W]$; it agrees with the refined Gysin homomorphism of the regular embedding $i_0$, since an effective Cartier divisor is a regular embedding of codimension $1$). In particular $\operatorname{Supp}(i_0^![W])=W\cap D$; hence if $W\cap D=\varnothing$ then every local ring $\mathcal O_{W,\xi}/(f)$ is $0$ and $i_0^![W]=0$ as a cycle.

(F2) First Chern class of a trivial line bundle. If $M\cong\mathcal O_Z$ is a trivial line bundle on a scheme $Z$ and $\beta\in\mathrm{CH}_m(Z)$, then $c_1(M)\cap\beta=0$. Indeed, by the definition of the cap product with $c_1$ through rational sections (Fulton, Intersection Theory, Ch. 2, §2.1), for an integral closed $V\subset Z$ of dimension $m$ one sets $c_1(M|_V)\cap[V]:=\operatorname{div}(\sigma)$ for any rational section $\sigma$ of $M|_V$; taking $\sigma$ to be the nowhere-vanishing section coming from the trivialisation gives $\operatorname{div}(\sigma)=0$ (there is no codimension-$1$ point where $\sigma$ vanishes or has a pole), so $c_1(M)\cap[V]=0$ as a cycle, and the general case follows from additivity of the cap product.

(F3) Self-intersection formula. If $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ is a regular embedding of pure codimension $d$ with normal bundle $N_{Z/X}:=(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)^{\vee}$, then on Chow groups $i^!\circ i_* = c_d(N_{Z/X})\cap(-)$ (Fulton, Intersection Theory, Ch. 6, §6.6, self-intersection formula). We apply this with $d=1$ and $i=i_0$, whose refined Gysin homomorphism is exactly the one in the statement.

Reduction to integral cycles. The pushforward $i_{s*}$ is defined on cycles by $\mathbb Z$-linear extension from integral subschemes, and $i_0^!$ is a group homomorphism on Chow groups (as stated). Hence it suffices to prove $i_0^!\bigl(i_{s*}[W]\bigr)=0$ in $\mathrm{CH}_{m-1}(Y)$ for every integral closed subscheme $W\subset Y_{\kappa(s)}$ of dimension $m$. If $m=0$ then $\mathrm{CH}_{-1}(Y)=0$ by convention, so the claim is trivial; assume $m\ge 1$. Since $i_s$ is a closed immersion (base change of a closed immersion), $W\to i_s(W)$ is an isomorphism onto its image with the reduced structure: indeed a closed immersion $W\to Z$ that is a homeomorphism onto $Z=\overline{i_s(W)}$ (reduced) is an isomorphism, because the defining ideal $\mathcal I\subset\mathcal O_Z$ satisfies $V(\mathcal I)=|Z|$, so $\mathcal I\subset\sqrt{0}=0$ as $Z$ is reduced. Thus $\kappa(W)\cong\kappa(i_s(W))$, the degree in the pushforward formula is $1$, and
$$i_{s*}[W]=[i_s(W)]\in Z_m(X),\qquad i_s(W)\subset Y\times_k\{s\}.$$

Case 1: $s\neq 0$. Closed points of $\mathbb A^1_k=\operatorname{Spec}k[t]$ correspond to monic irreducible polynomials: $s\leftrightarrow(p(t))$ with $\kappa(s)=k[t]/(p)$, and $0\leftrightarrow(t)$. Since $s\neq 0$, $p\neq t$, and $(p),(t)$ are distinct maximal ideals of the PID $k[t]$, hence comaximal; equivalently $t\notin (p)$, so the class $\bar t\in\kappa(s)$ is non-zero, hence a unit. Therefore
$$\{s\}\times_{\mathbb A^1_k}\{0\}=\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(\kappa(s)\otimes_{k[t]}k\bigr)=\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(\kappa(s)/(t)\bigr)=\operatorname{Spec}(0)=\varnothing,$$
and consequently, base-changing along $Y\to\operatorname{Spec}k$,
$$(Y\times_k\{s\})\cap D=(Y\times_k\{s\})\times_X(Y\times_k\{0\})=Y\times_k\bigl(\{s\}\times_{\mathbb A^1_k}\{0\}\bigr)=\varnothing.$$
In particular $i_s(W)\not\subset D$ (its support is disjoint from $D$), so (F1) applies. Concretely, the function $f$ restricted to $Y\times_k\{s\}=Y\times_k\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)$ is the image of $t$ under $k[t]\twoheadrightarrow\kappa(s)\hookrightarrow\Gamma(Y_{\kappa(s)},\mathcal O)$, i.e. the constant function $\bar t\in\kappa(s)^{\times}$, which is a unit; hence $f|_{i_s(W)}$ is a unit of $\Gamma(i_s(W),\mathcal O)$ and $\mathcal O_{i_s(W),\xi}/(f)=0$ for every codimension-$1$ point $\xi$. Thus $\operatorname{div}(f|_{i_s(W)})=0$ and by (F1)
$$i_0^!\bigl(i_{s*}[W]\bigr)=i_0^![i_s(W)]=0\ \ \text{as a cycle on } D,$$
hence its class in $\mathrm{CH}_{m-1}(Y)$ (identifying $\mathrm{CH}_\bullet(D)\cong\mathrm{CH}_\bullet(Y)$ through $i_0:Y\xrightarrow{\sim}D$) is $0$.

Case 2: $s=0$. Then $\kappa(s)=k[t]/(t)=k$, so $Y_{\kappa(s)}=Y\times_k\operatorname{Spec}k=Y$ and $i_s=i_0$. By (F3) applied to the regular embedding $i_0:Y\hookrightarrow X$ of codimension $1$,
$$i_0^!\bigl(i_{0*}[W]\bigr)=c_1\bigl(N_{D/X}\bigr)\cap[i_0(W)]\ \ \text{in } \mathrm{CH}_{m-1}(D)\cong\mathrm{CH}_{m-1}(Y).$$
It remains to compute the normal bundle. The ideal sheaf of $D$ is $\mathcal I=f\cdot\mathcal O_X$; since $f$ is a non-zero-divisor, $\varphi:\mathcal O_X\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal I$, $a\mapsto af$, is an $\mathcal O_X$-linear isomorphism, and $\varphi(\mathcal I)=\mathcal I^2$ because $\varphi(f\cdot b)=f^2b$. Hence $\varphi$ induces an $\mathcal O_D$-linear isomorphism
$$\bar\varphi:\mathcal O_D=\mathcal O_X/\mathcal I\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \mathcal I/\mathcal I^2,\qquad \bar 1\longmapsto \bar f .$$
So $\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2$ is a free $\mathcal O_D$-module of rank $1$, i.e. the trivial line bundle, and therefore $N_{D/X}=(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)^{\vee}\cong\mathcal O_D$ is trivial as well (the dual of $\bar\varphi$ identifies it with $\mathcal O_D$). By (F2) with $Z=D$ and $M=N_{D/X}$, we obtain $c_1(N_{D/X})\cap\beta=0$ for every $\beta\in\mathrm{CH}_m(D)$; applying this to $\beta=[i_0(W)]$ gives
$$i_0^!\bigl(i_{0*}[W]\bigr)=0\ \ \text{in } \mathrm{CH}_{m-1}(Y).$$

(Alternative justification of Case 2, reducing it to Case 1: the two effective Cartier divisors $D_0=V(t)$ and $D_a=V(t-a)$ on $X$, $a\in k^{\times}$, are linearly equivalent, since their difference is the divisor of the rational function $t/(t-a)$; linearly equivalent Cartier divisors induce the same refined Gysin homomorphism $\mathrm{CH}_m(X)\to\mathrm{CH}_{m-1}(Y)$ (for a cycle $W$ met properly by both, the two cycle-level answers differ by $\operatorname{div}(g|_W)$ with $g$ the ratio of local equations, which is rationally equivalent to $0$ on $W$ by the definition of rational equivalence via rational functions, and the general case follows by the standard bilinearity/deformation properties). Since $\operatorname{Supp}(i_{0*}[W])\cap D_a=\varnothing$, Case 1 gives $i_a^!i_{0*}[W]=0$, whence $i_0^!i_{0*}[W]=0$.)

Conclusion. In both cases, for every closed point $s$ of $\mathbb A^1_k$ and every integral closed $W\subset Y_{\kappa(s)}$ of dimension $m\ge 1$ we have $i_0^!i_{s*}[W]=0$ in $\mathrm{CH}_{m-1}(Y)$; for $m=0$ the target group is $0$. By additivity of $i_{s*}$ on cycles and of $i_0^!$ on Chow groups, $i_0^!\circ i_{s*}=0$ as a homomorphism $\mathrm{CH}_m(Y_{\kappa(s)})\to\mathrm{CH}_{m-1}(Y)$ for every closed point $s$ and every $m\ge 0$. (If $Y=\varnothing$, or if $Y_{\kappa(s)}$ has no $m$-dimensional integral subschemes, all groups involved are $0$ and the claim is immediate.) This completes the proof.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let t be an indeterminate over k, and let alpha in CH^d(X x_k X) have zero image under flat base change in CH^d(X_{k(t)} x_{k(t)} X_{k(t)}). Then alpha = 0.
proof:
Notation. Write Y_0 := X \times_k X (smooth projective of dimension 2d over k), K := k(t), and let pr: V := Y_0 \times_k \mathbb A^1_k = Y_0 \times_k \mathrm{Spec}\,k[t] \to Y_0 be the projection. For a k-subscheme T \subset \mathbb A^1_k we write Y_T := Y_0 \times_k T. Since dim V = 2d+1, CH^d(V) = CH_{d+1}(V), and similarly for the other varieties below; we freely pass between codimensional and dimensional notation. Recall also that for any k-algebra A, X_A \times_A X_A \cong (X\times_k X)\times_k \mathrm{Spec}\,A = Y_0\times_k \mathrm{Spec}\,A, since a fibre product over \mathrm{Spec}\,A of two base changes is the base change of the fibre product over k.

We must show: if the flat pullback of \alpha \in CH^d(Y_0) to CH^d(Y_0\times_k \mathrm{Spec}\,k(t)) is zero, then \alpha = 0.

STEP 1 (Spreading out; the only non-standard input, lemma_65). Choose a d-dimensional cycle Z on Y_0 representing \alpha. By hypothesis its image in CH^d(X_K \times_K X_K) = CH^d(Y_0\times_k \mathrm{Spec}\,K) is zero. Apply Spark's lemma_65 to the smooth projective k-variety X of dimension d, to the finitely generated k-algebra A := k[t] (an integral domain with fraction field K = k(t)), and to the d-dimensional cycle Z on X\times_k X = Y_0. It yields a nonzero element g \in k[t] such that the image of Z in CH^d(X_{k[t,1/g]}\times_{k[t,1/g]} X_{k[t,1/g]}) is zero. With U := \mathrm{Spec}\,k[t,1/g] \subset \mathbb A^1_k this says
   (1.1)   pr_U^*[Z] = 0  in  CH^d(Y_U) = CH_{d+1}(Y_U),
where pr_U: Y_U \to Y_0 is the (flat, relative dimension 1) base change of pr.

STEP 2 (Localisation on the affine line). Two cases.
Case g \in k^*: then U = \mathbb A^1_k, so (1.1) reads pr^*[Z] = 0 in CH_{d+1}(V), and Step 4 below (homotopy invariance) gives [Z] = 0, i.e. \alpha = 0.
Case deg g \ge 1: let Z(g) := \mathrm{Spec}\,k[t]/(g) \subset \mathbb A^1_k, a closed subscheme of pure codimension 1, with closed complement Y := Y_0\times_k Z(g) of Y_U. The localisation sequence of Chow groups for the closed immersion i_Y: Y \hookrightarrow V with open complement Y_U (Fulton, Intersection Theory, Ex. 1.8.1) is exact:
   CH_{d+1}(Y) \xrightarrow{(i_Y)_*} CH_{d+1}(V) \xrightarrow{\,j^*\,} CH_{d+1}(Y_U) \to 0.
By (1.1), j^*(pr^*[Z]) = pr_U^*[Z] = 0 (flat pull-back commutes with restriction to open subschemes). Hence there exists \gamma \in CH_{d+1}(Y) with
   (2.1)   pr^*[Z] = (i_Y)_* \gamma.

STEP 3 (The push-forward from a fibre over a closed point of \mathbb A^1 is zero).
3a. Decomposition into fibres. Write g = c\prod_{i=1}^r m_i^{e_i} with c\in k^* and m_1,\dots,m_r distinct monic irreducible polynomials. Since the m_i are pairwise coprime, the Chinese remainder theorem gives k[t]/(g)_{red} \cong \prod_{i=1}^r k[t]/(m_i); set \kappa(s_i) := k[t]/(m_i), a finite field extension of k, and D_i := Y_0\times_k \mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(s_i) = Y_0\times_k\{s_i\}. Chow groups of a scheme of finite type over a field depend only on the reduced structure: integral closed subschemes are the same for W and W_{red} (a reduced scheme maps into the nilpotent thickening W_{red}\hookrightarrow W through its reduction, and rational equivalence is computed from function fields \kappa(W_j)=\kappa(W_{j,red}), which are unchanged). Moreover Y_0\times_k Z(g)_{red} \to Y_0\times_k Z(g) is a base change of the nilpotent closed immersion Z(g)_{red}\hookrightarrow Z(g), hence a universal homeomorphism, so its reduction is (Y_0\times_k Z(g))_{red} and it identifies cycle groups. Since Z(g)_{red} = \bigsqcup_i \mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(s_i) is a disjoint union of points, we get
   CH_{d+1}(Y) = CH_{d+1}((Y_0\times_k Z(g))_{red}) = \bigoplus_{i=1}^r CH_{d+1}(D_i),
and under this identification (i_Y)_* = \sum_i (i_i)_*, where i_i: D_i \hookrightarrow V is the closed immersion. Thus it suffices to prove:
   (3.1)  for every closed point s \in \mathbb A^1_k with residue field \kappa(s), the push-forward (i_s)_*: CH_{d+1}(Y_0\times_k\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(s)) \to CH_{d+1}(V) is zero,
where i_s: Y_0\times_k\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(s) \hookrightarrow V is the closed immersion.

3b. Proof of (3.1). Fix such an s, given by a monic irreducible m \in k[t]; write \bar t \in \kappa(s) = k[t]/(m) for the image of t, and n := [\kappa(s):k]. Put D := Y_0\times_k\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(s) (smooth projective of dimension 2d over \kappa(s)), and let V' := D\times_{\kappa(s)}\mathbb A^1_{\kappa(s)} = \mathrm{Spec}(k[D][u]) with fibre coordinate u; let p': V'\to D be the projection and s_0: D \hookrightarrow V' the zero section u=0 (a closed immersion, the zero section of the trivial line bundle).

Define a k-morphism \varphi: V' \to V by the k-algebra homomorphism
   \varphi^\#: k[Y_0][t] \longrightarrow k[D][u], \qquad a \mapsto \bar a\ (\text{the image of } a \in k[Y_0] \text{ in } k[D]=k[Y_0]\otimes_k\kappa(s)), \qquad t \mapsto \bar t + u.
This is well defined because t is an indeterminate. Concretely, \varphi is the base change along the projection V = Y_0\times_k\mathbb A^1_k \to \mathbb A^1_k of the k-morphism \psi: \mathbb A^1_{\kappa(s)} \to \mathbb A^1_k given by \psi^\#(t) = \bar t + u; indeed V\times_{\mathbb A^1_k,\psi}\mathbb A^1_{\kappa(s)} = \mathrm{Spec}(k[Y_0]\otimes_k k[t]\otimes_{k[t]}\kappa(s)[u]) = \mathrm{Spec}(k[Y_0]\otimes_k\kappa(s)[u]) = V'.

\psi is finite: set z := \bar t + u, so that \kappa(s)[u] = \kappa(s)[z] (as u = z - \bar t). Choosing a k-basis e_1,\dots,e_n of \kappa(s), we have \kappa(s)[z] = \bigoplus_{i\ge 0}\kappa(s)z^i = \bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=1}^n k e_j z^i, and the k[t]-module structure is via k[t] \xrightarrow{\sim} k[z], t\mapsto z, acting by multiplication on z and by k-scalar multiplication on the e_j. Hence \kappa(s)[z] \cong \bigoplus_{j=1}^n k[z] e_j \cong (k[t])^{n} as k[t]-modules, i.e. \psi is finite locally free of rank n. Therefore \varphi, being a base change of a finite morphism, is finite, hence proper.

Next, \varphi\circ s_0 = i_s. Indeed, on rings the composite (\varphi\circ s_0)^\# sends a \in k[Y_0] to \bar a \in k[D] (since s_0^\#: k[D][u]\to k[D] is the identity on k[D]) and sends t to \bar t + u \mapsto \bar t + 0 = \bar t; this is exactly the comorphism of the closed immersion D = Y_0\times_k\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(s) \hookrightarrow Y_0\times_k\mathbb A^1_k = V.

By functoriality of proper push-forward (Fulton, Ch. 1, Prop. 1.4),
   (i_s)_* = (\varphi\circ s_0)_* = \varphi_* \circ (s_0)_*.
It remains to show (s_0)_* = 0. Let D_0 := s_0(D) \subset V', let \sigma: D \xrightarrow{\sim} D_0 be the isomorphism with s_0 = i_0\circ\sigma where i_0: D_0\hookrightarrow V' is the closed inclusion, and let \beta \in CH_{d+1}(D) with corresponding class \beta' := \sigma_*\beta \in CH_{d+1}(D_0).

(i) Homotopy invariance for vector bundles (Fulton, Ch. 1, Prop. 1.8): p'^*: CH_{k}(D) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } CH_{k+1}(V') is an isomorphism whose inverse is the refined Gysin homomorphism s_0^! of the regular embedding s_0. Hence s_0^!\,p'^* = id.
(ii) D_0 is the zero scheme in V' of the single global function u \in \Gamma(V',\mathcal O_{V'}) = k[D][u]. Multiplication by u is injective on k[D][u] (u is transcendental over k[D]), so u is a non-zero-divisor and D_0 is an effective Cartier divisor of V', defined by the global section u of \mathcal O_{V'}. The ideal sheaf of D_0 is (u)\cdot\mathcal O_{V'}, and multiplication by u gives an isomorphism \mathcal O_{V'} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathcal O_{V'}(D_0); so \mathcal O_{V'}(D_0) is trivial and c_1(\mathcal O_{V'}(D_0))\cap - = 0.
(iii) For an effective Cartier divisor, the refined Gysin homomorphism of the closed immersion i_0 coincides with the Gysin homomorphism of the Cartier divisor (Fulton, Ch. 1, Prop. 1.7(a)), and the divisor-intersection formula (Fulton, Ch. 2, Prop. 2.3) gives i_{0*}\,i_0^!\,\xi = c_1(\mathcal O_{V'}(D_0))\cap \xi for all \xi \in CH_*(V'). By (ii) the right-hand side is 0, so i_{0*}\,i_0^! = 0.
(iv) Since s_0 = i_0\circ\sigma and \sigma is an isomorphism, functoriality of refined Gysin maps gives s_0^! = \sigma^! i_0^! = \sigma^* i_0^!, hence i_0^! p'^*\beta = \sigma_*(s_0^!p'^*\beta) = \sigma_*\beta = \beta' by (i). Therefore
   (s_0)_*\beta = i_{0*}\beta' = i_{0*}i_0^! p'^*\beta = 0
by (iii). As \beta was arbitrary, (s_0)_* = 0, whence (i_s)_* = \varphi_*\circ 0 = 0, proving (3.1). Note that no separability of m was used: \psi is finite locally free of rank n for every monic irreducible m, and the vanishing comes from the triviality of the Cartier divisor div(u), not from any multiplicity/torsion argument.

3c. Conclusion of Steps 2--3. By (2.1) and the decomposition in 3a, pr^*[Z] = \sum_i (i_i)_*\gamma_i with \gamma_i \in CH_{d+1}(D_i), and each (i_i)_*\gamma_i = 0 by (3.1). Hence
   (3.2)   pr^*[Z] = 0 \quad\text{in}\quad CH_{d+1}(V) = CH^d(V).

STEP 4 (Homotopy invariance). pr: V = Y_0\times_k\mathbb A^1_k \to Y_0 is the projection of the trivial line bundle over Y_0, so by homotopy invariance of Chow groups (Fulton, Ch. 1, Prop. 1.8) the flat pull-back pr^*: CH^d(Y_0) \to CH^d(V) is an isomorphism. From (3.2) we obtain [Z] = 0 in CH^d(Y_0), i.e. \alpha = 0.

Steps 1--4 cover all cases (g a unit, and deg g \ge 1 with arbitrary factorisation, including inseparable irreducible factors), and every step is justified above. Hence the base-change map CH^d(X\times_k X) \to CH^d(X_{k(t)}\times_{k(t)} X_{k(t)}) is injective. \square

statement: Let V be an integral scheme of finite type over a field k, let t be an indeterminate over k, and let K=k(t). Then the base change V_K=V\times_k\operatorname{Spec}K is integral and \dim V_K=\dim V.
proof:
CONVENTIONS. All schemes and tensor products are over k unless stated otherwise. For a scheme W we write dim W for the Krull dimension, i.e. the supremum of the lengths n of chains Z_0 proper_subset ... proper_subset Z_n of irreducible closed subsets (irreducible subsets are non-empty by definition). 'Integral' means non-empty, irreducible and reduced. Write K = k(t) = S^{-1}k[t] where S = k[t] \ {0}. For a k-scheme W put W_K = W x_k Spec K and denote by pi_W : W_K -> W the projection. We prove that V_K is integral and that dim V_K = dim V.

STEP 1 (AFFINE CORE). Let A be a finitely generated k-algebra which is an integral domain, X = Spec A, m = dim A.

1a. A_K := A tensor_k K is isomorphic to S^{-1}A[t] as A-algebras. Indeed, let theta : A[t] -> A tensor_k K be the k-algebra homomorphism with theta|_A = (a |-> a tensor 1) and theta(t) = 1 tensor t; it exists and is unique because A[t] is the free k-module with basis {t^i}. For g in S, theta(g) = g(1 tensor t) = 1 tensor g is a unit of A tensor_k K with inverse 1 tensor g^{-1}; hence theta extends to psi : S^{-1}A[t] -> A tensor_k K, psi(h/g) = theta(h)(1 tensor g)^{-1}. Conversely, A x K -> S^{-1}A[t], (a, f/g) |-> (af)/g, is k-bilinear and induces phi : A tensor_k K -> S^{-1}A[t]. Both phi and psi are k-algebra maps and phi o psi and psi o phi are the identity on the k-generating sets {a tensor 1 : a in A} union {1 tensor t} union {1 tensor (1/g) : g in S}: psi(a tensor 1) = a/1 and phi(a/1) = a tensor 1; psi(1 tensor t) = t/1 and phi(t/1) = 1 tensor t; psi(1 tensor g^{-1}) = (1/g)/1 and phi((1/g)/1) = 1 tensor g^{-1}. Hence phi, psi are mutually inverse isomorphisms.

1b. A_K is a non-zero domain. (i) A[t] is a domain: if f = sum_{i<=r} a_i t^i != 0 and g = sum_{j<=s} b_j t^j != 0 with a_r != 0, b_s != 0, then the coefficient of t^{r+s} in fg is a_r b_s != 0 since A is a domain, so fg != 0. (ii) k -> A is injective (A != 0 is a domain and 1 maps to 1 != 0), so k[t] -> A[t] is injective; thus S contains no zero divisor of A[t] and does not contain 0. (iii) A localisation of a domain away from 0 is a non-zero domain: 0 not in S gives 1/1 != 0, and (f/s)(g/u) = 0 means fgv = 0 for some v in S, whence fg = 0 by (i), whence f = 0 or g = 0. Therefore A_K is a non-zero domain. Consequently Spec A_K is non-empty (the zero ideal is prime), irreducible (its nilradical (0) is prime, and Spec of a ring is irreducible iff its nilradical is prime), and reduced (a localisation of a reduced ring is reduced: (f/s)^n = 0 gives f^n u = 0, hence fu = 0, hence f/s = 0).

1c. dim A_K = dim A.
(i) Noether normalisation (valid over an arbitrary base field): there exist y_1,...,y_m in A, algebraically independent over k, such that A is integral, equivalently finite, over B := k[y_1,...,y_m]. For infinite k this is the usual generic linear change of variables; for a finite field k of cardinality q one replaces in that proof the scalar multiples a_i + c a_n by a_i + a_n^{q^i}, which gives the same conclusion; the case m = 0 is Zariski's lemma (a field which is a finitely generated k-algebra is finite algebraic over k). Since A is integral over B, lying over gives dim A >= dim B and incomparability gives dim A <= dim B: for the first, a chain q_0 proper_subset ... proper_subset q_n in B is lifted inductively to Q_0 proper_subset ... proper_subset Q_n in A by applying lying over to the integral injections B/q_l -> A/Q_l; for the second, contractions of a chain in A are strictly increasing because two primes of A with the same contraction cannot be strictly nested. Hence dim A = dim B. Finally dim B = m: the chain (0) proper_subset (T_1) proper_subset ... proper_subset (T_1,...,T_m) in k[T_1,...,T_m] gives >= m, and the principal ideal theorem (height of a prime minimal over r elements is at most r, applied to the maximal ideals of the affine domain k[T_1,...,T_m]) gives <= m. Thus m = dim A, consistently with the hypothesis.
(ii) Base change of the extension. By 1a applied to A and to B, A_K = S^{-1}A[t] and B_K = S^{-1}B[t], and B_K -> A_K is injective because localisation is exact. If A = sum_i B u_i then S^{-1}A[t] = sum_i S^{-1}B[t] u_i, so A_K is a finite, hence integral, B_K-module.
(iii) B_K = S^{-1}(k[y_1,...,y_m][t]) = (S^{-1}k[t])[y_1,...,y_m] = K[y_1,...,y_m], a polynomial ring in m variables over the field K, so dim B_K = m by the classical computation quoted in (i).
(iv) Since B_K -> A_K is an injective integral extension, the same lying-over/incomparability argument as in (i) gives dim A_K = dim B_K = m = dim A. This finishes Step 1.

STEP 2 (FINITE AFFINE COVER). V is of finite type over k, hence quasi-compact, so V = X_1 union ... union X_r with X_i = Spec A_i affine open and each A_i a finitely generated k-algebra; discard empty members. Since V is integral, every non-empty open subscheme is integral (reducedness is local, and a non-empty open subspace of an irreducible space is irreducible), so each A_i is a domain. Then {(X_i)_K} is a finite affine open cover of V_K, (X_i)_K = Spec A_{i,K}, and by Step 1 each (X_i)_K is a non-empty integral affine scheme with dim (X_i)_K = dim A_{i,K} = dim A_i = dim X_i.

STEP 3 (V_K IS INTEGRAL).
3a. Non-empty: X_1 != empty and (X_1)_K != empty by Step 1b.
3b. Reduced: V_K = union_i (X_i)_K is covered by reduced open subschemes; a scheme is reduced iff it admits such a cover (equivalently iff all its local rings are reduced), so V_K is reduced.
3c. Irreducible. Put U := X_1. Then U is a non-empty open subset of the irreducible space V, hence dense in V. By Step 1, U_K is integral, in particular irreducible.
Density claim (*): U_K is dense in V_K. It suffices to prove that every non-empty open W of V_K meets U_K. Since V_K = union_i (X_i)_K, there is an index i with W cap (X_i)_K != empty; fix it. Then D := U cap X_i is a non-empty open subset of X_i (two non-empty opens of the irreducible space V meet), and D_K = U_K cap (X_i)_K, because (U cap X_i)_K = (U x_V V_K) x_{V_K} (X_i x_V V_K) = (U cap X_i) x_V V_K as open subschemes of V_K.
Subclaim: if X = Spec A with A a domain and D proper_subset X is a non-empty open subset, then D_K != empty. Proof: pick p in D and f in A with p in D(f) proper_subset D (principal opens form a basis). Then f not in p, and f != 0 because (0) subset p. The image f/1 of f in A_K = S^{-1}A[t] is non-zero: f/1 = 0 would give sf = 0 in A[t] for some s in S with s != 0, contradicting that A[t] is a domain (Step 1b(i)). The basic open D(f/1) of Spec A_K is non-empty since the prime (0) does not contain f/1. Finally (D(f))_K = D(f/1): both are the spectrum of the localisation of A[t] at the multiplicative set S . {f^n}, namely S^{-1}(A_f[t]) = (S^{-1}A[t])_f. Hence D_K contains (D(f))_K = D(f/1) != empty. Subclaim proved.
Applying the subclaim to X_i and D = U cap X_i, the subset U_K cap (X_i)_K = D_K is a non-empty open of (X_i)_K. Since (X_i)_K is irreducible (Step 1), two non-empty open subsets of it intersect, so empty != (W cap (X_i)_K) cap (U_K cap (X_i)_K) subset W cap U_K. This proves (*).
