Now V_K is irreducible: if V_K = F_1 union F_2 with F_j closed, then U_K = (F_1 cap U_K) union (F_2 cap U_K) is a union of two closed subsets of the irreducible space U_K, so U_k subset F_j for some j; then V_K = closure of U_K subset F_j by (*), i.e. F_j = V_K. Combining 3a, 3b, 3c, V_K is integral. (It is also of finite type over K, since base change preserves finite type.)

STEP 4 (DIMENSION).
4a. Surjectivity of pi := pi_V : V_K -> V. For v in V the scheme-theoretic fibre is pi^{-1}(v) = Spec(kappa(v) tensor_k K): indeed V_K x_V Spec kappa(v) = (V x_k Spec K) x_V Spec kappa(v) = Spec kappa(v) x_k Spec K. The map k -> kappa(v) is injective (kappa(v) is a field and 1 maps to 1 != 0), so k[t] -> kappa(v)[t] is injective and S avoids 0; by the same argument as in Step 1b, kappa(v) tensor_k K = S^{-1}kappa(v)[t] is a non-zero domain, whose spectrum contains the prime (0). Hence every fibre is non-empty and pi is surjective.
4b. Two facts about finite open covers. Let X be a topological space with a finite open cover X = U_1 union ... union U_s.
(F1) dim U_j <= dim X for each j. Given a chain C_0 proper_subset ... proper_subset C_n of irreducible closed subsets of U_j, the closures cl(C_l) in X are irreducible closed and form a strict chain: C_l = cl(C_l) cap U_j because C_l is closed in U_j, so cl(C_l) = cl(C_{l+1}) would force C_l = C_{l+1}. Thus n <= dim X.
(F2) dim X <= max_j dim U_j. Let Z_0 proper_subset ... proper_subset Z_n be a chain of irreducible closed subsets of X. Since Z_0 != empty and the U_j cover X, some U_j meets Z_0; fix such a j. Then for every l, Z_l cap U_j contains Z_0 cap U_j != empty, is closed in U_j, and is irreducible because it is a non-empty open subset of the irreducible space Z_l. We prove the inclusions Z_l cap U_j subset Z_{l+1} cap U_j are strict. Suppose equality holds, and call the common set C. Because Z_l proper_subset Z_{l+1} and Z_l is closed in X, the complement Z_{l+1} \ Z_l is a non-empty open subset of the irreducible space Z_{l+1}; and C = Z_{l+1} cap U_j is also a non-empty open subset of Z_{l+1}. Two non-empty open subsets of an irreducible space intersect, so (Z_{l+1} \ Z_l) cap U_j != empty. But the assumed equality gives C = Z_l cap U_j subset Z_l, hence (Z_{l+1} cap U_j) \ Z_l = empty, i.e. (Z_{l+1} \ Z_l) cap U_j = empty, a contradiction. Hence Z_l cap U_j proper_subset Z_{l+1} cap U_j for all l, which is a chain of n+1 distinct irreducible closed subsets of U_j; therefore n <= dim U_j <= max_j dim U_j. Taking the supremum over all chains yields (F2).
Applying (F1) and (F2) to X = V with the cover {X_i}, and to X = V_K with the cover {(X_i)_K}, gives
   dim V = max_i dim X_i   and   dim V_K = max_i dim (X_i)_K.
4c. Upper bound. Using 4b, Step 2 and Step 1c,
   dim V_K = max_i dim (X_i)_K = max_i dim A_{i,K} = max_i dim A_i = max_i dim X_i = dim V.
In particular dim V_K <= dim V, and dim V < infinity (each dim A_i is finite by Noether normalisation, Step 1c(i)).
4d. Lower bound. First, dim V is a finite integer, as just noted; hence the set of lengths of chains of irreducible closed subsets of V is a set of non-negative integers with finite supremum dim V, and that supremum is attained: if no chain had length dim V, all chain lengths would be at most dim V - 1, forcing sup <= dim V - 1 < dim V, a contradiction. Choose a chain Z_0 proper_subset ... proper_subset Z_n of irreducible closed subsets of V with n = dim V.
Give each Z_l the reduced induced closed subscheme structure, and write Z_l^red for the resulting closed subscheme (defined by the radical ideal sheaf of Z_l). This does not change the underlying topological space, so Z_0^red proper_subset ... proper_subset Z_n^red is still a chain of n+1 distinct closed subsets with the same length n, and each Z_l^red is integral: non-empty (irreducible spaces are non-empty), reduced by construction, irreducible as a space; it is of finite type over k as a closed subscheme of the finite type k-scheme V. By Steps 1-3 applied to Z_l^red, (Z_l^red)_K is non-empty and integral.
Base changing the closed immersion Z_l^red -> V gives a closed immersion j_l : (Z_l^red)_K -> V_K; identify (Z_l^red)_K with its image. We compute the image set-theoretically: on the affine open X_i = Spec A_i the ideal of Z_l^red is generated by f_1,...,f_s in A_i, so the image inside (X_i)_K = Spec A_{i,K} is Spec A_{i,K}/(f_1,...,f_s)A_{i,K} = { q in Spec A_{i,K} : f_1,...,f_s in q } = pi^{-1}({ p in Spec A_i : f_1,...,f_s in p }) cap (X_i)_K = pi^{-1}(|Z_l|) cap (X_i)_K; patching over i gives |im j_l| = pi^{-1}(|Z_l|).
The inclusions are strict: Z_l proper_subset Z_{l+1} means Z_{l+1} \ Z_l != empty, and pi is surjective by 4a, so pi^{-1}(Z_{l+1} \ Z_l) != empty; since pi^{-1}(Z_{l+1} \ Z_l) = pi^{-1}(Z_{l+1}) \ pi^{-1}(Z_l), we obtain |im j_l| proper_subset |im j_{l+1}|.
Each |im j_l| is closed in V_K and irreducible, because j_l is a homeomorphism onto its image and (Z_l^red)_K is integral, hence irreducible. Thus |im j_0| proper_subset ... proper_subset |im j_n| is a chain of n+1 irreducible closed subsets of V_K, and dim V_K >= n = dim V.
4e. Conclusion. 4c and 4d give dim V_K = dim V, and Step 3 shows V_K is integral (and of finite type over K). This is exactly the statement of the lemma. QED

statement: Let X/k be a smooth projective variety of dimension d, let Y \subsetneq X be a proper closed subset, let Z = (X \times_k Y) \cup (Y \times_k X) \subset X \times_k X be given the reduced induced structure, and let j: (X \setminus Y) \times_k (X \setminus Y) \to X \times_k X be the open immersion. Then the classes of CH^d(X \times_k X) that admit a d-dimensional cycle representative supported on Z form an additive subgroup of CH^d(X \times_k X), equal to the image of CH_d(Z) \to CH_d(X \times_k X) and to the kernel of j^*: CH_d(X \times_k X) \to CH_d((X \setminus Y) \times_k (X \setminus Y)).
proof:
NOTATION AND SETUP. Write W := X \times_k X, U := X \setminus Y (open), V := U \times_k U, and let Z = (X \times_k Y) \cup (Y \times_k X) \subset W carry the reduced induced closed subscheme structure; write i: Z \hookrightarrow W for the closed immersion and j: V \hookrightarrow W for the open immersion. Set-theoretically |Z| = (X\times |Y|) \cup (|Y|\times X) and W \setminus |Z| = U \times U = V, because X\times X = (U \cup |Y|)\times (U \cup |Y|) = (U\times U) \cup (X\times |Y|) \cup (|Y|\times X). Define
  S_Z := { \alpha \in CH^d(W) : \alpha is represented by a d-dimensional cycle on W whose support lies in |Z| }.
We prove S_Z = im(i_*: CH_d(Z) \to CH_d(W)) = ker(j^*: CH_d(W) \to CH_d(V)), and then that this common set is an additive subgroup.

PRELIMINARIES.
(P1) Identification CH^d(W) = CH_d(W). Since X/k is a smooth projective variety of dimension d, X is integral and of pure dimension d. The projection p_1: W \to X is the base change of X \to Spec k, hence smooth of relative dimension d; its fibre over x \in X is X_{\kappa(x)}, smooth of pure dimension d over \kappa(x). A flat morphism of finite type whose fibres are equidimensional of dimension d over an irreducible base of dimension d has all irreducible components of dimension 2d, so W is of pure dimension 2d (it is smooth over k). For an equidimensional k-scheme of pure dimension 2d, codimension-p cycles coincide with (2d-p)-dimensional cycles, so CH^d(W) = CH_d(W) canonically; this is the identification used in the statement. (Projectivity of X is never used beyond finite type over k and separatedness, the latter only to ensure divisors of rational functions are finite sums.) Note also dim Z \le 2d-1, since dim Y \le d-1 and dim(X\times Y) = d + dim Y, dim(Y\times X) = dim Y + d.
(P2) Functoriality. i is a closed immersion, hence proper, so proper pushforward i_*: CH_d(Z) \to CH_d(W) is a well-defined group homomorphism (Fulton, Chap. 1, Prop. 1.4); on cycles it is given by the usual formula i_*[T] = [k(T):k(i(T)_{red})]\,[i(T)_{red}] when dim i(T) = dim T and 0 otherwise. j is an open immersion, hence flat of relative dimension 0, so flat pullback j^*: CH_d(W) \to CH_d(V) is a well-defined group homomorphism (Fulton, Chap. 1, Def. 1.7.1 and Prop. 1.7.3).
(P3) Dimension of open subsets. If T is an integral scheme of finite type over k and \emptyset \ne \Omega \subset T is open, then dim \Omega = dim T. Indeed dim \Omega \le dim T is clear; conversely choose an affine open Spec A \subset \Omega. Then A is a finitely generated k-algebra and a domain, and since T is integral and Spec A is dense in T, Frac(A) = k(T). Noether normalization gives dim A = trdeg_k Frac(A) = trdeg_k k(T) = dim T, so dim \Omega \ge dim T.
(P4) Flat pullback of prime cycles by an open immersion. If P \subset W is integral closed of dimension d, then P \times_W V = P \cap V. If P \cap V = \emptyset the flat pullback is 0 by definition (Fulton 1.7.1). If P \cap V \ne \emptyset, then P \cap V is integral of dimension d by (P3), the base change P\cap V \to P is an open immersion (flat of relative dimension 0) with a single generic point of residue-field degree 1 and local length 1, so j^*[P] = [P\cap V].
(P5) Principal divisors commute with open restriction. If T is integral of finite type over k, \Omega \subset T open, g \in k(T)^*, then div_T(g)|_\Omega = div_\Omega(g|_\Omega). Proof: the codimension-1 points of \Omega are exactly the codimension-1 points of T lying in \Omega; for such x one has O_{\Omega,x} = O_{T,x}, so the coefficient length_{O_{T,x}}(O_{T,x}/(g)) of [\overline{x}] in div_T(g) equals the coefficient of [\overline{x}^{\Omega}] in div_\Omega(g|_\Omega), and \overline{x}^{\Omega} = \overline{x}^{T} \cap \Omega. Since g is a unit on a dense open, only finitely many coefficients are non-zero (T is of finite type over k and separated), so both sides are well-defined cycles.

STEP 1. S_Z = im(i_*).
(1a) im(i_*) \subset S_Z. Let \beta \in CH_d(Z), \beta = [z'] with z' = \sum_\lambda n_\lambda [T_\lambda], T_\lambda integral closed of dimension d in Z. Then i_*\beta = [i_* z'] and i_*z' = \sum_\lambda n_\lambda [k(T_\lambda):k(i(T_\lambda)_{red})]\,[i(T_\lambda)_{red}], a d-cycle on W (a closed immersion is a homeomorphism onto its image, so dim i(T_\lambda) = dim T_\lambda = d and the formula applies) whose support is contained in |Z|. Hence i_*\beta \in S_Z.
(1b) S_Z \subset im(i_*). Let \alpha \in S_Z with representative z = \sum_\nu n_\nu [P_\nu], the P_\nu distinct integral closed d-dimensional subschemes of W with |P_\nu| \subset |Z|. Each P_\nu is reduced and its underlying set lies in |Z|, so by the universal property of the reduced induced closed subscheme structure the closed immersion P_\nu \to W factors (uniquely) through Z: P_\nu \xrightarrow{\;a_\nu\;} Z \xrightarrow{\;i\;} W. Since i is a closed immersion, hence a monomorphism of schemes, a_\nu is a closed immersion, and its image with the reduced structure is P_\nu itself (as a reduced closed subscheme of W); in particular [k(P_\nu):k(i(a_\nu(P_\nu))_{red})] = 1 and i_*[a_\nu(P_\nu)] = [P_\nu]. Viewing z' := \sum_\nu n_\nu [a_\nu(P_\nu)] \in Z_d(Z), we get i_* z' = z, so \alpha = [z] = [i_* z'] = i_*[z'] \in im(i_*).
Thus S_Z = im(i_*).

STEP 2. im(i_*) \subset ker(j^*).
It suffices to show j^* i_* = 0 on cycles. Let T \subset Z be integral closed of dimension d. Then |i(T)_{red}| = |T| \subset |Z| = W \setminus V, so i(T)_{red} \times_W V = \emptyset, and by (P4) (equivalently, by the definition of flat pullback, which assigns 0 to a subvariety whose inverse image is empty) j^*[i(T)_{red}] = 0. Hence j^* i_*[T] = 0, and by linearity and (P2), j^* \circ i_* = 0 on CH_d(Z). Therefore im(i_*) \subset ker(j^*).

STEP 3. ker(j^*) \subset im(i_*).
Let \alpha \in CH_d(W) with j^*\alpha = 0. Choose a d-cycle z = \sum_\nu n_\nu [W_\nu] on W with [z] = \alpha (W_\nu distinct integral closed subschemes of dimension d, n_\nu \ne 0). By (P4),
   j^* z = \sum_{\nu:\, W_\nu \cap V \ne \emptyset} n_\nu [W_\nu \cap V] \in Z_d(V).
Since j^*\alpha = 0 in CH_d(V), the cycle j^*z is rationally equivalent to zero on V. By the definition of rational equivalence there are finitely many integral closed subschemes T_\mu \subset V of dimension d+1 and rational functions g_\mu \in k(T_\mu)^* (possibly none) with
   j^* z = \textstyle\sum_\mu div_{T_\mu}(g_\mu) \quad \in Z_d(V).
For each \mu let \bar T_\mu \subset W be the scheme-theoretic closure of T_\mu (closure with the reduced induced structure). Then T_\mu is a dense open subscheme of \bar T_\mu; \bar T_\mu is integral of finite type over k, separated, and dim \bar T_\mu = dim T_\mu = d+1 by (P3); also k(\bar T_\mu) = k(T_\mu), so g_\mu \in k(\bar T_\mu)^*. Define the d-cycle on W
   D := \textstyle\sum_\mu (\bar T_\mu \hookrightarrow W)_*\, div_{\bar T_\mu}(g_\mu).
Each summand is the divisor of a single rational function on an integral closed subscheme of W of dimension d+1, hence is rationally equivalent to zero on W by definition of rational equivalence; therefore [D] = 0 in CH_d(W) and
   [z - D] = [z] = \alpha.   (\dagger)

Claim 3.1: j^* D = j^* z as cycles on V. Write div_{\bar T_\mu}(g_\mu) = \sum_\rho c_\rho [Q_\rho] with Q_\rho integral of dimension d in \bar T_\mu. By (P5) with T = \bar T_\mu and \Omega = \bar T_\mu \cap V = T_\mu, div_{\bar T_\mu}(g_\mu)|_{T_\mu} = div_{T_\mu}(g_\mu); the left side is \sum_\rho c_\rho [Q_\rho \cap T_\mu] (terms with Q_\rho \cap T_\mu = \emptyset contribute 0, and those are exactly the codimension-1 points of \bar T_\mu not meeting V, which do not occur in div_{T_\mu}(g_\mu)). On the other hand, pushing (\bar T_\mu \hookrightarrow W)_* div_{\bar T_\mu}(g_\mu) = \sum_\rho c_\rho [Q_\rho] forward to W and applying j^* gives \sum_\rho c_\rho [Q_\rho \cap V] by (P4), and Q_\rho \cap V = Q_\rho \cap T_\mu as subsets of V, with closure in V equal to Q_\rho \cap T_\mu (dense open in the integral Q_\rho when non-empty, by (P3)). Summing over \mu yields j^* D = \sum_\mu div_{T_\mu}(g_\mu) = j^* z.

Claim 3.2: z - D is supported on |Z|. Put w := z - D = \sum_\sigma m_\sigma [P_\sigma] with the P_\sigma distinct integral closed d-dimensional subschemes of W and m_\sigma \in \mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}. By Claim 3.1, 0 = j^*z - j^*D = j^*w = \sum_\sigma m_\sigma [P_\sigma \cap V]. If P_\sigma \cap V \ne \emptyset then P_\sigma \cap V is a non-empty open subscheme of the integral scheme P_\sigma, hence integral of dimension d by (P3), so [P_\sigma \cap V] is a non-zero prime d-cycle on V; moreover P_\sigma is the closure in W of P_\sigma \cap V (a non-empty open subset of an irreducible space is dense), so \sigma \mapsto [P_\sigma \cap V] is injective. A cycle is zero if and only if every coefficient of every prime component is zero, so m_\sigma = 0 for every \sigma with P_\sigma \cap V \ne \emptyset. Consequently every remaining component satisfies P_\sigma \cap V = \emptyset, i.e. |P_\sigma| \subset W \setminus V = |Z|, so w is a d-cycle on W supported on |Z|.

Conclusion of Step 3. By the cycle-level argument of Step 1b, w = i_* \eta for some \eta \in Z_d(Z). Hence by (\dagger), \alpha = [z] = [z-D] = [w] = [i_*\eta] = i_*[\eta] \in im(i_*).

CONCLUSION. Steps 1, 2, 3 give
   S_Z = im(i_*: CH_d(Z) \to CH_d(W)) = ker(j^*: CH_d(W) \to CH_d(V)),
with CH_d(W) = CH^d(X\times_k X) by (P1). Since i_* is a group homomorphism (P2), its image is an additive subgroup of CH^d(X\times_k X); thus S_Z is an additive subgroup, and it equals both the image of CH_d(Z) \to CH_d(X\times_k X) and the kernel of the flat restriction j^*. This is exactly the assertion.

EDGE CASES AND REMARKS. (i) If Y = \emptyset then Z = \emptyset, V = W and j = id_W; a cycle supported on \emptyset is the zero cycle, so S_\emptyset = \{0\} = im(CH_d(\emptyset) = 0) = ker(id), and the equalities hold. (ii) If d = 0, then a smooth projective variety of dimension 0 over k is a single closed point (finite separable over k), so necessarily Y = \emptyset and the previous case applies; equivalently CH_0(W) is free abelian on the closed points of W and all three groups vanish. (iii) The hypothesis Y \subsetneq X is used only to make Z a proper closed subset; the proof works verbatim for Y = \emptyset and breaks only in the vacuous case Y = X where Z = W, V = \emptyset and all three groups are CH_d(W). (iv) No smoothness beyond (P1) is used, and no intersection products or ideal properties are claimed: in particular this lemma asserts only the additive/localisation description of S_Z, not that S_Z is a left or right ideal for composition of correspondences.

statement: Let X/k be a smooth projective variety of dimension d, let A and B be closed subsets of X with dim A + dim B < d, and let \alpha \in CH^d(X \times_k X). If \alpha admits a d-dimensional cycle representative whose support is contained in A \times_k B, then \alpha = 0.
proof:
We prove the statement from elementary dimension theory; no auxiliary result from the list is needed.

SETUP AND INTERPRETATION. Since X/k is smooth of dimension d, X×_k X is smooth of dimension 2d, so CH^d(X×_k X) = CH_d(X×_k X): a class α ∈ CH^d(X×_k X) is, by definition, the class modulo rational equivalence of a d-dimensional cycle Z ∈ Z_d(X×_k X), i.e. a finite formal sum
    Z = Σ_i n_i [V_i],   n_i ∈ Z \ {0},
where the V_i ⊂ X×_k X are integral closed subschemes of dimension d. The support of Z is the closed subset |Z| = ∪_i |V_i| ⊂ |X×_k X|.

We give A and B the reduced induced closed subscheme structures (this does not change their dimensions, since dim T^red = dim T for any scheme T), and we write A×_k B for the fibre product of these closed subschemes. Since a fibre product of closed immersions is a closed immersion, A×_k B → X×_k X is a closed immersion; its underlying set is exactly the set of points of X×_k X whose two projections lie in A and in B, so "Supp(Z) ⊂ A×_k B" means |Z| ⊂ |A×_k B| inside |X×_k X|.

STEP 1: REDUCTION TO A DIMENSION BOUND. Let Z = Σ_i n_i[V_i] be a d-dimensional cycle representative of α with |Z| ⊂ |A×_k B|. Assume some V_i occurs. Then |V_i| ⊂ |A×_k B|, and since (A×_k B)^red is the closed subscheme of X×_k X cut out by the radical of the ideal sheaf of A×_k B, the reduced subscheme V_i^red is an integral closed subscheme of (A×_k B)^red. Hence
    d = dim V_i = dim V_i^red ≤ dim (A×_k B)^red = dim(A×_k B).
Therefore, if dim(A×_k B) < d, no index i can exist: the sum is empty, Z = 0 as a cycle, and consequently α = [Z] = 0 in CH^d(X×_k X).

Thus the lemma follows once we show dim(A×_k B) ≤ dim A + dim B, because the hypothesis dim A + dim B < d then gives dim(A×_k B) < d. If A = ∅ or B = ∅ then A×_k B = ∅, so |Z| = ∅, the sum above is empty, Z = 0 and α = 0; note this covers in particular d = 0, where dim A + dim B < 0 forces A = B = ∅ (a non-empty closed subset of a d-dimensional variety has dimension ≥ 0). We may therefore suppose A and B non-empty and prove the inequality in general.

STEP 2: THE DIMENSION INEQUALITY dim(Y×_k Z) ≤ dim Y + dim Z FOR FINITE TYPE k-SCHEMES.

Sublemma 2.1 (dimension = transcendence degree of the function field). If T is integral of finite type over a field F with generic point τ, then dim T = trdeg_F κ(τ).
Proof. Choose a non-empty affine open U = Spec A ⊂ T. Then A is a finitely generated F-domain, κ(τ) = Frac(A), and since T is irreducible noetherian and U is a dense open, dim T = dim A. By Noether normalisation there exist algebraically independent elements x_1,…,x_d ∈ A, with d = dim A, such that A is a finite k[x_1,…,x_d]-module; equivalently Frac(A) is a finite field extension of F(x_1,…,x_d). Hence trdeg_F κ(τ) = trdeg_F Frac(A) = trdeg_F F(x_1,…,x_d) = d = dim A = dim T. ∎

Sublemma 2.2 (extension of the ground field does not increase dimension). If Y is of finite type over k and K/k is any field extension, then dim(Y×_k Spec K) ≤ dim Y.
Proof. Cover Y by finitely many affine opens U_1,…,U_r; the (U_j)_K := U_j×_k Spec K cover Y_K := Y×_k Spec K. Let W ⊂ Y_K be irreducible closed. Some (U_j)_K meets W, and W∩(U_j)_K is a non-empty open subset of the irreducible noetherian space W, so dim W = dim \bar{W∩(U_j)_K} ≤ dim (U_j)_K. Write U_j = Spec A_j with A_j a finitely generated k-algebra, e_j := dim A_j ≤ dim Y. Noether normalisation gives that A_j is a finite module over a polynomial subring k[t_1,…,t_{e_j}] ⊂ A_j; base-changing along k → K, (A_j)_K = A_j⊗_k K is a finite module over K[t_1,…,t_{e_j}] = k[t_1,…,t_{e_j}]⊗_k K. An integral surjective map (lying over) sends any chain of primes of (A_j)_K to a chain of primes of K[t_1,…,t_{e_j}], so dim(A_j⊗_k K) ≤ dim K[t_1,…,t_{e_j}] = e_j ≤ dim Y. Taking the supremum over W and j gives dim Y_K ≤ dim Y. ∎

Sublemma 2.3 (reduction to integral factors). Every irreducible closed subset W ⊂ Y×_k Z is contained in Y'×_k Z' for some irreducible components Y' ⊂ Y, Z' ⊂ Z. Consequently dim(Y×_k Z) = max_{Y',Z'} dim(Y'×_k Z').
Proof. pr_1(W) is irreducible closed in Y, hence contained in an irreducible component Y'; similarly pr_2(W) ⊂ Z'. Then W ⊂ pr_1^{-1}(Y') ∩ pr_2^{-1}(Z') = Y'×_k Z'. The Y'×_k Z' are closed and cover Y×_k Z, so the dimension of Y×_k Z is the maximum of their dimensions. ∎

Proof of the inequality. By Sublemma 2.3 it suffices to treat Y, Z integral. Let W ⊂ Y×_k Z be irreducible closed with generic point w, and put a := pr_1(w) ∈ Y, b := pr_2(w) ∈ Z. Let Y' := \bar a^red ⊂ Y and Z' := \bar b^red ⊂ Z; these are integral closed subschemes for which a and b are the generic points, and W ⊂ Y'×_k Z' with dim Y' ≤ dim Y, dim Z' ≤ dim Z. Replacing (Y,Z) by (Y',Z'), we may (and do) assume that a and b are the generic points of Y and Z.

Restricting pr_2 to W gives, at w, a local homomorphism O_{Z,b} → κ(w). Since κ(w) is a field, the maximal ideal of the local ring O_{Z,b} maps to 0, so this homomorphism factors through the residue field, yielding an injective map of fields κ(b) ↪ κ(w). Form the generic fibre of pr_2|_W over b:
    W_b := W ×_Z Spec κ(b),
which is a closed subscheme of (Y×_k Z) ×_Z Spec κ(b) ≅ Y×_k Spec κ(b) =: Y_b. Because κ(w) is a κ(b)-algebra via the inclusion above, the fibre of W_b → W over w is Spec(κ(w)⊗_{κ(b)} κ(b)) = Spec κ(w); hence w has a unique lift w_b ∈ W_b with κ(w_b) = κ(w). Let T := \bar{w_b}^red ⊂ W_b ⊂ Y_b. Then T is integral of finite type over the field κ(b), with function field κ(w_b) = κ(w). Applying Sublemma 2.1 to T/κ(b) and then Sublemma 2.2,
    trdeg_{κ(b)} κ(w) = dim T ≤ dim W_b ≤ dim Y_b ≤ dim Y.   (∗)
Applying Sublemma 2.1 to Y/k (generic point a) and to Z/k (generic point b) gives trdeg_k κ(a) = dim Y and trdeg_k κ(b) = dim Z; applying it to W/k gives dim W = trdeg_k κ(w). The tower law for transcendence degree applied to k ⊂ κ(b) ⊂ κ(w) now yields, using (∗),
    dim W = trdeg_k κ(w) = trdeg_{κ(b)} κ(w) + trdeg_k κ(b) ≤ dim Y + dim Z.
Since W was an arbitrary irreducible closed subset of Y×_k Z, Sublemma 2.3 gives dim(Y×_k Z) ≤ dim Y + dim Z. ∎

STEP 3: CONCLUSION. Apply Step 2 with Y = A^red and Z = B^red, which are of finite type over k (closed subschemes of the projective variety X). Using dim T^red = dim T,
    dim(A×_k B) = dim(A^red ×_k B^red) ≤ dim A^red + dim B^red = dim A + dim B < d.
By Step 1, the cycle Z is the zero cycle, hence α = 0 in CH^d(X×_k X). This completes the proof.

(REMARK on content. The point of the lemma is that a d-dimensional cycle is a formal combination of d-dimensional integral subschemes, and A×_k B contains no such subscheme when dim A + dim B < d; so the hypothesis that α has a representative supported on A×_k B forces that representative to be the zero cycle, and α itself to vanish — no rational-equivalence argument is needed.)

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let Y ⊊ X be a proper closed subset of dimension e, and let m ≥ 1 be an integer with (m+1)e < d. If γ_1,…,γ_m ∈ CH^d(X\times_k X) each admit a d-dimensional cycle representative whose support is contained in Y\times_k Y, then the m-fold composition γ_1∘γ_2∘⋯∘γ_m is zero in CH^d(X\times_k X), where ∘ denotes composition of correspondences.
proof:
Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let Y ⊊ X be a closed subset of dimension e, let m ≥ 1 with (m+1)e < d, and let γ_1,…,γ_m ∈ CH^d(X ×_k X) each admit a d-dimensional cycle representative whose support is contained in |Y ×_k Y|. Write δ := γ_1 ∘ γ_2 ∘ ⋯ ∘ γ_m.

CONVENTIONS. For α, β ∈ CH^*(X ×_k X) the composition of correspondences is α ∘ β := p_{13*}(p_{12}^*α · p_{23}^*β), where p_{12}, p_{23}, p_{13}: X^3 → X ×_k X are the projections; this is the product used in Spark's lemma_63. The operation is biadditive, and CH^*(X ×_k X) is associative for it: for α,β,γ one has (α∘β)∘γ = α∘(β∘γ) = p_{14*}(p_{12}^*α · p_{23}^*β · p_{34}^*γ) on X^4, since both computations reduce to the same expression by two applications of the projection formula for the cartesian projections X^4 → X^3 (e.g. p_{13*}(p_{12}^*α·p_{23}^*β) pulled back to X^4 against p_{34}^*γ, and symmetrically). Hence the unparenthesized m-fold product δ is well defined, and we may compute it by the left-nested bracketing δ_j := γ_1 ∘ ⋯ ∘ γ_j.

STEP 1 (support of the iterated composition). We prove by induction on j = 1,…,m that δ_j has a d-dimensional cycle representative whose support is contained in |Y ×_k Y|.

j = 1: δ_1 = γ_1, which has such a representative by hypothesis.

Inductive step: assume δ_j has a d-dimensional cycle representative supported on |Y ×_k Y|, and γ_{j+1} has one supported on |Y ×_k Y|. Apply Spark's lemma_63 to α := δ_j, β := γ_{j+1}, with A = B = C = D := Y: since α has a representative supported on A × B = Y ×_k Y and β has one supported on C × D = Y ×_k Y, the composition α ∘ β = δ_{j+1} has a cycle representative supported on A × D = Y ×_k Y. (Note δ_j ∈ CH^d(X ×_k X) because the composition of two codimension-d correspondences on a d-fold is again of codimension d: p_{12}^*α·p_{23}^*β ∈ CH^{2d}(X^3) and p_{13} is proper of relative dimension d.) This completes the induction. In particular there is a d-dimensional cycle Z on X ×_k X with Supp(Z) ⊂ |Y ×_k Y| representing δ.

STEP 2 (dimension of Y ×_k Y). If Y = ∅, then dim(Y ×_k Y) = −1 and Step 2 is trivial; assume Y ≠ ∅, so e = dim Y ≥ 0. We claim dim(Y ×_k Y) ≤ 2e. It suffices to show that every integral closed subscheme T ⊂ Y ×_k Y satisfies dim T ≤ 2e.

Let p_1: Y ×_k Y → Y be the first projection and let Z_1 ⊂ Y be the reduced closed subscheme on the closure of p_1(T). Then Z_1 is integral, is a closed subscheme of Y, hence dim Z_1 ≤ e, and the induced morphism f: T → Z_1 is dominant. Thus κ(Z_1) embeds into κ(T), and both fields are finitely generated extensions of k. Using the standard identity dim V = trdeg_k κ(V) for integral schemes V of finite type over a field, and the additivity of transcendence degree in towers,
  dim T = trdeg_k κ(T) = trdeg_k κ(Z_1) + trdeg_{κ(Z_1)} κ(T) = dim Z_1 + trdeg_{κ(Z_1)} κ(T).
Let η ∈ Z_1 be the generic point, so κ(η) = κ(Z_1). The generic fibre T_η := T ×_{Z_1} Spec κ(η) is integral: indeed, taking an affine open Spec A ⊂ Z_1 over which T is covered by affines Spec B with B a domain (open subschemes of the integral scheme T are integral) and A ↪ B injective (dominance), one has T_η|_{Spec A} = Spec(S^{-1}B) with S = A \ {0}, a localization of a domain, hence a domain. It is of finite type over the field κ(η) and has function field κ(T), so by the same dimension/transcendence-degree identity, trdeg_{κ(Z_1)} κ(T) = dim T_η.

Next, T_η is a closed subscheme of (Y ×_k Y) ×_{Y,p_1} Spec κ(η) ≅ Spec κ(η) ×_k Y =: Y_{κ(η)} (base change of the closed immersion T ↪ Y ×_k Y along Spec κ(η) → Y). We show dim Y_{κ(η)} = dim Y = e. Cover Y by affine opens Spec B_i, B_i a finitely generated k-algebra; then Y_{κ(η)} is covered by Spec((B_i)_{κ(η)}), so dim Y_{κ(η)} = max_i dim (B_i)_{κ(η)} and dim Y = max_i dim B_i. For each i and each minimal prime p ⊂ B_i, Noether normalization gives a finite injective homomorphism k[x_1,…,x_r] ↪ B_i/p with r = dim B_i/p; tensoring with κ(η) (a flat extension, and finiteness/injectivity are preserved by base change, with incomparability for finite maps) gives a finite injective κ(η)[x_1,…,x_r] ↪ (B_i/p)_{κ(η)}, whence dim (B_i/p)_{κ(η)} = r = dim B_i/p. Since minimal primes of (B_i)_{κ(η)} lie over minimal primes of B_i (going-down for the flat map B_i → (B_i)_{κ(η)}), we get dim (B_i)_{κ(η)} = dim B_i, and hence dim Y_{κ(η)} = dim Y = e. Therefore dim T_η ≤ e, and
  dim T = dim Z_1 + dim T_η ≤ e + e = 2e,
proving the claim dim(Y ×_k Y) ≤ 2e.

STEP 3 (vanishing). Since m ≥ 1 we have m + 1 ≥ 2, and since Y ≠ ∅ we have e ≥ 0; hence 2e ≤ (m+1)e < d. Combined with Step 2, dim(Y ×_k Y) ≤ 2e < d.

The cycle Z from Step 1 is Z = Σ_i n_i [W_i] with n_i ≠ 0 and W_i ⊂ X ×_k X integral closed subschemes of dimension d, and Supp(Z) = ⋃_i W_i ⊂ |Y ×_k Y|. Thus each W_i is set-theoretically contained in |Y ×_k Y|, and endowing W_i with the reduced structure induced from Y ×_k Y exhibits it as an integral closed subscheme of Y ×_k Y of dimension d. By Step 2 no such subscheme exists (all integral closed subschemes of Y ×_k Y have dimension ≤ 2e < d). Hence the index set is empty, Z = 0 is the zero cycle, and therefore δ = 0 in CH^d(X ×_k X).

EDGE CASES. (i) If Y = ∅, then Y ×_k Y = ∅, so a d-dimensional cycle with support in ∅ is the zero cycle; each γ_i = 0, and by biadditivity of ∘ the product δ = 0. (ii) If d = 0 and Y ≠ ∅, then (m+1)e < 0 with e = dim Y ≥ 0 is impossible, so the hypothesis is void; if d = 0 and Y = ∅ this is case (i). (iii) If e = 0 (Y a non-empty finite scheme), the inequality reads 0 < d, and Step 3 applies since dim(Y ×_k Y) ≤ 0 < d. All cases are thus covered.

CONCLUSION. γ_1 ∘ γ_2 ∘ ⋯ ∘ γ_m = 0 in CH^d(X ×_k X). ∎

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective and integral of dimension d, let p_1: X ×_k X → X be the first projection, and let X_{k(X)} = X ×_k Spec k(X) be the base change of X to the function field of X. If α ∈ CH^d(X ×_k X) has zero image under the flat pullback CH^d(X ×_k X) → CH^d(X_{k(X)}) induced by the generic point Spec k(X) → X of the first factor, then there exists a proper closed subset Y ⊊ X such that α admits a d-dimensional cycle representative supported on Y ×_k X.
proof:
We prove the lemma from first principles of intersection theory (flat pullback, the definition of rational equivalence, generic flatness/dimension formula for flat maps, and the localization sequence for Chow groups). No result from the library other than these standard formal properties is used; in particular we do not use lemma_65, lemma_66 or lemma_74, and we make no assertion about projections of individual components of homotopy or boundary cycles.

=== 0. Setup and conventions ===

Let W := X \times_k X, let f := p_1: W \to X be the first projection, let \eta := Spec k(X) \xrightarrow{} X be the generic point (k(X) is the function field of X; it is a field because X is integral), let W_\eta := W \times_X Spec k(X) and let j_\eta: W_\eta \to W be the base change of \eta. Since X is smooth of relative dimension d over k, p_2: W \to X is smooth of relative dimension d; its fibre over x \in X is X_{\kappa(x)}, smooth of relative dimension d over the field \kappa(x), hence equidimensional of dimension d. As X is integral, catenary and of dimension d, and p_2 is flat with all fibres equidimensional of dimension d, the dimension formula for flat morphisms (Matsumura, CRT, Thm 15.1, applied at local rings of generic points) shows that every irreducible component of W has dimension 2d: indeed no component can be contained in a fibre of p_2, because p_2 is open (flat maps are open) and X is irreducible of positive dimension (the case d = 0 is treated separately in Step 5 below). Hence W is equidimensional of dimension 2d, and CH^d(X \times_k X) = CH_d(X \times_k X) by the codimension/dimension convention. Likewise, for every nonempty open V \subset X, V \times_k X is open in W, hence equidimensional of dimension 2d, and CH^d(V \times_k X) = CH_d(V \times_k X). Finally X_{k(X)} = W_\eta is smooth of relative dimension d over the field k(X), hence equidimensional of dimension d, and CH^d(X_{k(X)}) = CH_0(X_{k(X)}).

The morphism j_\eta is flat: it is the base change of Spec k(X) \to X, and k(X) = S^{-1}O_{X,\eta'}... more precisely k(X) is the localization of any affine open neighbourhood of \eta at the nonzero elements, hence a flat O_X-module. The map in the hypothesis, CH^d(X \times_k X) \to CH^d(X_{k(X)}), is exactly the flat pullback j_\eta^* (Fulton, Ch. 1, \S 1.7): for an integral closed subscheme Z \subset W,
   j_\eta^*[Z] = \sum_\xi length_{O_{Z_\eta,\xi}}(O_{Z_\eta,\xi}) \cdot [\overline{\xi}],
where Z_\eta := Z \times_X Spec k(X) = Z \times_W W_\eta and \xi runs over the generic points of Z_\eta. We record the explicit form of this formula.

(0.1) LEMMA. Let Z \subset W be integral closed of dimension n. Then either p_1(Z) \neq X, in which case Z_\eta = \emptyset and j_\eta^*[Z] = 0; or p_1(Z) = X, in which case Z_\eta is integral of dimension n - d and j_\eta^*[Z] = [Z_\eta].
Proof. If p_1(Z) \neq X then p_1(Z) is a proper closed subset of X, so it does not contain \eta and Z_\eta = \emptyset. Suppose p_1(Z) = X. Cover X by affine opens Spec A and Z by affine opens Spec B with B a finitely generated domain over k and A \to B injective. Then Z_\eta is covered by Spec(S^{-1}B) with S = A \setminus \{0\}; each S^{-1}B is a domain (localization of a domain), so Z_\eta is reduced and (since |Z_\eta| = |Z| \cap |W_\eta| is dense in the irreducible space |Z|: dominance of Z over X makes the preimage of the dense open V nonempty open, hence dense) irreducible; thus Z_\eta is integral. Its dimension is trdeg_{k(X)} k(Z) = trdeg_k k(Z) - d = n - d, using k(X) \subset k(Z). Since Z_\eta is integral with a single generic point \xi and O_{Z_\eta,\xi} = k(Z_\eta) has length 1 over itself, the displayed formula gives j_\eta^*[Z] = [Z_\eta]. Moreover dim Z_\eta = n - d = dim W_\eta - (2d - n), so codimension is preserved. QED

The same statement holds with X replaced by a nonempty open V \subset X: for the flat map j_{V,\eta}: W_\eta \to f^{-1}V = V \times_k X (base change of Spec k(X) \to V, flat) and Z \subset f^{-1}V integral of dimension n, (j_{V,\eta})^*[Z] = [Z_\eta] if Z dominates V and 0 otherwise; here dim Z_\eta = n - d because Z dominating V implies k(X) \subset k(Z).

=== 1. Chow groups of the generic fibre as a filtered colimit ===

Let \mathcal{V} be the directed set of nonempty open subschemes V \subset X, ordered by reverse inclusion (V' \le V iff V' \subset V); directedness holds since the intersection of two nonempty opens is nonempty. For V' \subset V the open immersion f^{-1}V' \hookrightarrow f^{-1}V is flat of relative dimension 0, so restriction of cycles gives a homomorphism CH^i(f^{-1}V) \to CH^i(f^{-1}V') (for open immersions restriction is just 'keep the components contained in the open'; it commutes with the divisor construction defining rational equivalence, because the local rings O_{T,D} of codimension-1 subvariety pairs are unchanged when T and D are contained in the open). These maps are compatible with j_\eta^* by functoriality of flat pullback, (g \circ h)^* = h^* g^*, since j_\eta = j_{V,\eta} \circ (open immersion). Hence there is a well-defined homomorphism
   \Phi_i : colim_{V \in \mathcal{V}} CH^i(f^{-1}V) \longrightarrow CH^i(W_\eta).
We prove \Phi_i is an isomorphism for every i \ge 0. Write m := d - i for the corresponding dimension index (for i > d both groups are 0).

Surjectivity. Let \beta \in Z^i(W_\eta) = Z_m(W_\eta), say \beta = \sum_j n_j [T_j] with T_j integral closed of dimension m in W_\eta. Let \overline{T_j} be the topological closure of T_j in W and let Q_j := (\overline{T_j})_{red}. Since T_j is closed in W_\eta we have |\overline{T_j}| \cap |W_\eta| = |T_j|; Q_j is integral (reduced, with dense irreducible subspace T_j); and (Q_j)_\eta = Q_j \times_X Spec k(X) is reduced (localizations of reduced rings are reduced) with underlying space |T_j|, hence (Q_j)_\eta = T_j as schemes (T_j is reduced). Also (Q_j)_\eta \neq \emptyset, so Q_j dominates X and dim Q_j = m + d = 2d - i, i.e. [Q_j] \in Z^i(W). By (0.1), j_\eta^*[Q_j] = [T_j]. Thus \sum_j n_j [Q_j] \in Z^i(W) = Z^i(f^{-1}X) maps to \beta, so \Phi_i is surjective on cycles, hence on Chow groups.

Injectivity. Let Z \in Z^i(f^{-1}V) represent an element of the colimit mapping to 0, i.e. (j_{V,\eta})^* Z \in Rat_m(f^{-1}V)\_\eta = Rat_m(W_\eta). By the definition of rational equivalence (Fulton, Ch. 1, \S 1.3) there are integral closed subschemes P_l \subset W_\eta \times_k \mathbb{P}^1_k of dimension m+1 and rational functions f_l \in k(P_l)^\times (l = 1,\dots,s) such that, with p_l: P_l \to W_\eta the projection (proper, as a closed subscheme of W_\eta \times \mathbb{P}^1 with \mathbb{P}^1 proper over k),
   (j_{V,\eta})^* Z = \textstyle\sum_l n_l\, p_{l*}[\mathrm{div}_{P_l}(f_l)]   \quad (\ast)
as an equality of m-dimensional cycles on W_\eta.

Lifting the data. For each l let \overline{P_l} be the closure of P_l in W \times_k \mathbb{P}^1_k and Q_l := (\overline{P_l})_{red}. As above, Q_l is integral, (Q_l)_\eta = P_l, and k(Q_l) = k(P_l), so f_l \in k(Q_l)^\times. Since (Q_l)_\eta \neq \emptyset, Q_l dominates X. Let q_l: Q_l \hookrightarrow W \times \mathbb{P}^1 \xrightarrow{pr_1} W be the (proper) projection, and set
   \widehat{Z} := \textstyle\sum_l n_l\, q_{l*}[\mathrm{div}_{Q_l}(f_l)] \in Z_m(W) = Z^i(W).

(1.1) SUBLEMMA. j_\eta^*[\mathrm{div}_{Q_l}(f_l)] = [\mathrm{div}_{P_l}(f_l)] for every l.
Proof. Write \mathrm{div}_{Q_l}(f_l) = \sum_D n_D [D], D running over the codimension-1 integral subschemes of Q_l, with n_D = length_{O_{Q_l,D}}(O_{Q_l,D}/a) - length_{O_{Q_l,D}}(O_{Q_l,D}/b) for any f_l = a/b, a,b \in O_{Q_l,D}\setminus\{0\} (Fulton, Ch. 1, \S 1.1; the lengths are finite since O_{Q_l,D} is a 1-dimensional noetherian local domain and a,b are non-zero-divisors). Split the D into type I (D dominates X) and type II (D does not). Type II: D_\eta = \emptyset, so j_\eta^*[D] = 0 by (0.1), and such D do not meet (Q_l)_\eta = P_l, hence do not occur in \mathrm{div}_{P_l}(f_l). Type I: D_\eta is integral of dimension dim D - d = (dim Q_l - 1) - d = dim P_l - 1 by (0.1), i.e. of codimension 1 in P_l; and D \mapsto D_\eta is a bijection from type-I codimension-1 subschemes of Q_l onto the codimension-1 integral subschemes of P_l, with inverse E \mapsto closure of E in Q_l (the closure has dimension dim E + d = dim P_l - 1 + d = dim Q_l - 1 by (0.1) applied in reverse, and is of codimension 1, hence of type I). It remains to check n_D = n_{D_\eta}. Put R := O_{Q_l,D} and R' := O_{P_l,D_\eta}. By construction R' = S^{-1}R where S is the image of the nonzero elements of the local ring of X at the generic point (the localization defining the generic fibre). R is a 1-dimensional noetherian local domain with maximal ideal m; since D_\eta \neq \emptyset we have m \cap S = \emptyset, so the primes of R' correspond to the primes of R disjoint from S, namely (0) and m; hence R' is a 1-dimensional noetherian local domain with maximal ideal m' = mR', and R/m \xrightarrow{\sim} R'/m' (both identify with the function field \kappa(D) of D: O_{Q_l,D}/m = \kappa(D), and O_{P_l,D_\eta}/m' = Frac(S^{-1}\kappa[D]) = \kappa(D) since D \to X is dominant). For 0 \neq a \in R, (R/aR) \otimes_R R' = R'/aR', and flatness of R \to R' with R'/m'R' = R'/m' of length 1 gives length_{R'}(R'/aR') = length_R(R/aR) \cdot length_{R'}(R'/m') = length_R(R/aR). Applying this to a and b gives n_{D_\eta}(f_l) = n_D(f_l). Therefore j_\eta^*[\mathrm{div}_{Q_l}(f_l)] = \sum_{D \text{ type I}} n_D [D_\eta] = \sum_{E \subset P_l, \mathrm{codim}\,1} n_E [E] = [\mathrm{div}_{P_l}(f_l)]. QED

(1.2) Conclusion of injectivity. The square
   P_l = (Q_l)_\eta  \to  Q_l
        \downarrow p_l      \downarrow q_l
        W_\eta      \to   W
cartesians, q_l is proper and j_\eta is flat, so flat base change for cycles (Fulton, Ch. 1, Prop. 1.7.3) gives j_\eta^* q_{l*} = p_{l*} (j_{\eta,l})^*. With (1.1) this yields j_\eta^*[\widehat{Z}] = \sum_l n_l p_{l*}[\mathrm{div}_{P_l}(f_l)] = (j_{V,\eta})^* Z by (\ast). Hence C := Z - \widehat{Z}|_V \in Z_m(f^{-1}V) satisfies (j_{V,\eta})^* C = 0 as a cycle. Write C = \sum_a c_a [C_a] in reduced form (C_a distinct integral closed subschemes of f^{-1}V, c_a \neq 0). By (0.1) (with X replaced by V), (j_{V,\eta})^*[C_a] = [(C_a)_\eta] if C_a dominates V and 0 otherwise; and (C_a)_\eta is integral by (0.1). If C_a, C_b are distinct dominant ones, then (C_a)_\eta \neq (C_b)_\eta: indeed if T := (C_a)_\eta = (C_b)_\eta, then the closure \overline{T} of T in f^{-1}V is integral, contained in both C_a and C_b, dominates V, and by (0.1) dim \overline{T} = dim T + d = dim C_a, forcing \overline{T} = C_a and likewise \overline{T} = C_b, contradiction. Thus the nonzero dominant terms give distinct integral subschemes of W_\eta, which are linearly independent in the free abelian group Z_m(W_\eta); from (j_{V,\eta})^* C = 0 we conclude that no C_a dominates V. Since f = p_1 is projective (X projective over k), each p_1(C_a) is a closed subset of V, proper because C_a does not dominate V. Put V' := V \setminus \bigcup_a p_1(C_a). As V is integral (open in the integral X) and the union is finite and proper, V' is a nonempty open subscheme of X. Then C|_{V'} = 0 as a cycle, so Z|_{V'} = \widehat{Z}|_{V'} in Z^i(f^{-1}V'). Finally
   \widehat{Z}|_{V'} = \textstyle\sum_l n_l\, q_{l,V'*}[\mathrm{div}_{Q_{l,V'}}(f_l)],
where Q_{l,V'} := Q_l \times_X V' is open in the integral scheme Q_l, hence integral, q_{l,V'}: Q_{l,V'} \to f^{-1}V' is proper, and \mathrm{div}_{Q_{l,V'}}(f_l) = \mathrm{div}_{Q_l}(f_l)|_{V'} (codimension-1 subvarieties of the open Q_{l,V'} are exactly the codimension-1 subvarieties of Q_l contained in it, with identical local rings, hence identical coefficients), together with compatibility of proper pushforward with open restriction (flat base change for the cartesian square with the open immersion). Thus Z|_{V'} is rationally equivalent to zero in Z^i(f^{-1}V'), i.e. [Z|_{V'}] = 0 in CH^i(f^{-1}V'), so [Z] = 0 in the filtered colimit. This proves injectivity of \Phi_i, hence \Phi_i is an isomorphism.

(Remark. Generic flatness is the standard reason the same argument is phrased as 'shrink V so that the closures become flat over V'; in the present form flatness of the closures is not needed, because j_{V,\eta} itself is flat and the cycle-level rule (0.1) is all that is used. Nothing in the argument refers to projections of components of homotopy cycles beyond the dominance/non-dominance dichotomy, which is all (0.1) requires.)

=== 2. Descent of the vanishing to a nonempty open ===

Apply Step 1 with i = d. The class \alpha \in CH^d(X \times_k X) = CH^d(f^{-1}X) defines an element [\alpha] of colim_V CH^d(f^{-1}V), and \Phi_d([\alpha]) is the image of \alpha under the flat pullback j_\eta^*: CH^d(X \times_k X) \to CH^d(W_\eta) = CH^d(X_{k(X)}). By hypothesis this is 0. Since \Phi_d is an isomorphism, [\alpha] = 0 in the colimit; by the description of a filtered colimit (an element represented over V is zero iff it becomes zero over some V' \subset V), there exists a nonempty open V \subset X such that
   j_V^* \alpha = 0 \quad\text{in}\quad CH^d(V \times_k X) = CH_d(V \times_k X),
where j_V: V \times_k X \hookrightarrow X \times_k X is the open immersion.

=== 3. Localization: the class comes from a closed subset of the first factor ===

Set Y := X \setminus V, a closed subscheme of X, and let i: Y \times_k X \hookrightarrow X \times_k X be the closed immersion which is the complement of j_V. The localization exact sequence for Chow groups of the locally closed decomposition (X \times X) = (V \times X) \sqcup (Y \times X) (Fulton, Ch. 1, Thm 1.8) gives, in dimension d,
   CH_d(Y \times_k X) \xrightarrow{i_*} CH_d(X \times_k X) \xrightarrow{j_V^*} CH_d(V \times_k X) \to 0.
Since j_V^* \alpha = 0, exactness at the middle term yields \beta \in CH_d(Y \times_k X) with i_* \beta = \alpha. Choose a cycle representative B = \sum_e m_e [B_e] of \beta with B_e integral d-dimensional closed subschemes of Y \times_k X. The pushforward by a closed immersion sends [B_e] to [\kappa(B_e):\kappa(B_e)] \cdot [B_e] = [B_e], where B_e is now viewed as an integral closed subscheme of X \times_k X (the underlying reduced subscheme is unchanged, the field-extension degree is 1, and the support of B_e is contained in |Y \times_k X|). Hence i_* B = \sum_e m_e [B_e] is a d-dimensional cycle on X \times_k X representing \alpha and supported on Y \times_k X.

=== 4. Y is a proper closed subset ===

V is a nonempty open subscheme of the integral (hence irreducible) scheme X, so V is dense in X. Therefore every irreducible component of Y = X \setminus V has dimension \le d - 1 < d = dim X, so Y \neq X; i.e. Y is a proper closed subset of X. (Integrality is used exactly here, and also to ensure k(X) is a field, so that W_\eta is the generic fibre.)

Combining Steps 2-4: \alpha admits a d-dimensional cycle representative supported on Y \times_k X with Y \subsetneq X closed. This is the desired conclusion.

=== 5. The case d = 0 ===

If d = 0, then X is smooth, projective and integral of dimension 0 over k, hence X = Spec K with K/k finite separable; in particular k(X) = K and X_{k(X)} = Spec(K \otimes_k K) = X \times_k X as schemes, and the morphism Spec k(X) \to X is the identity of Spec K. The flat pullback CH^0(X \times_k X) \to CH^0(X_{k(X)}) is therefore the identity, so the hypothesis gives \alpha = 0. Taking Y := \emptyset (a proper closed subset of the nonempty X), the zero cycle is a 0-dimensional cycle representative of \alpha supported on Y \times_k X = \emptyset. The statement holds in this case as well.

This completes the proof in all cases.

(For orientation: as noted in the guidance, the transpose of this lemma, obtained by swapping the two factors of X \times_k X, gives support on X \times_k Y; together with the analogous statement for the transpose class this yields the two-sided support statement, and by the localization sequence for (X \setminus Y) \times (X \setminus Y) \subset X \times X the latter is equivalent to the vanishing of the image of \alpha in CH^d((X \setminus Y) \times_k (X \setminus Y)). None of these further steps is used above.)

statement: Let $\mathcal W$ be an integral scheme of finite type over a field $k$, let $f:\mathcal W\to\mathbb P^1_k$ be a dominant morphism, let $K=k(u)$ be the function field of $\mathbb P^1_k$, and let $W=\mathcal W\times_{\mathbb P^1_k}\operatorname{Spec}K$ be the scheme-theoretic generic fibre. For an integral closed subscheme $T\subset\mathcal W$ whose image under $f$ is dense, let $T^{\eta}$ denote the fundamental cycle of $T\times_{\mathbb P^1_k}\operatorname{Spec}K$. Then for every $g\in k(\mathcal W)^{\times}$, the cycle $\sum_x\operatorname{ord}_x(g)\,[\bar x^{\,\eta}]$, summed over the codimension-one points $x$ of $\mathcal W$ whose image under $f$ is the generic point of $\mathbb P^1_k$, where $\bar x$ is the closure of $x$ in $\mathcal W$, equals $\operatorname{div}_W(g)$ in $Z_{\dim\mathcal W-2}(W)$.
proof:
PROOF. Write $\eta\in\mathbb P^1_k$ for the generic point, so $\kappa(\eta)=K=k(u)$, and for an integral scheme $X$ write $X^{(1)}$ for its set of codimension-one points. Dominance of $f$ forces $\dim\mathcal W\ge 1$ (the image of a $0$-dimensional space is a point, never dense in $\mathbb P^1$). The proof is intrinsic and uses no external result; in particular it does not appeal to `generic_fibre_restriction_on_chow_groups`, which says nothing about divisors of rational functions.

=====================================================================
STEP 0. The order function on an arbitrary integral Noetherian scheme.

Let $X$ be integral and locally Noetherian with function field $k(X)$, let $x\in X^{(1)}$, put $R=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ (a one-dimensional Noetherian local domain with fraction field $k(X)$), and let $g\in k(X)^{\times}$. We use the standard definition of $\operatorname{ord}_x(g)$ valid without any normality hypothesis: write $g=a/b$ with $0\ne a,b\in R$, and set
   $\operatorname{ord}_x(g):=\ell_R(R/dgR)-\ell_R(R/dR)$ for any $0\ne d\in R$ with $dg\in R$
(where $\ell_R$ is length). Such a $d$ exists: take $d=b$. We check the formal properties we need.

(0.1) Finiteness of the lengths. $R$ is a one-dimensional Noetherian local domain and $d\ne0$, so every prime of $R$ containing $d$ is different from $(0)$, hence has height $1$ by Krull's principal ideal theorem, hence is the maximal ideal: $R/dR$ is a zero-dimensional Noetherian local ring, i.e. Artinian, of finite length. The same applies to $R/dgR$ since $dg\ne0$ in the domain $R$.

(0.2) Independence of $d$. Let $d,d'\in R\setminus\{0\}$ with $dg,d'g\in R$, and put $c:=d'$, $e:=dd'=dc$. Then $eg\in R$. Since $dcR\subset dR\subset R$ we have an exact sequence $0\to dR/dcR\to R/dcR\to R/dR\to0$, and multiplication by $d$ gives $R/cR\xrightarrow{\ \cdot d\ }dR/dcR$ an isomorphism (injective because $R$ is a domain). Hence $\ell(R/dcR)=\ell(R/dR)+\ell(R/cR)$. Applying the same argument to the element $a:=dg\in R$ gives $0\to aR/acR\to R/acR\to R/aR\to0$ with $aR/acR\cong R/cR$, so $\ell(R/egR)=\ell(R/dgR)+\ell(R/cR)$. Subtracting, $\ell(R/egR)-\ell(R/eR)=\ell(R/dgR)-\ell(R/dR)$, as required.

(0.3) Functoriality. If $\varphi:(R,K)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }(R',K')$ is an isomorphism of one-dimensional Noetherian local domains with fraction fields, and $g'=\varphi(g)$, then $\varphi$ carries admissible denominators to admissible denominators and induces $R/dR\cong R'/\varphi(d)R'$, $R/dgR\cong R'/\varphi(d)g'R'$; hence $\operatorname{ord}$ computed in $(R,K,g)$ equals $\operatorname{ord}$ computed in $(R',K',g')$. Thus $\operatorname{ord}$ depends only on the pair consisting of the local ring together with the element of its fraction field.

(0.4) Agreement with the classical definitions. If $R$ is a discrete valuation ring with uniformiser $\pi$ and $g=u\pi^{n}$, then taking $d=1$ for $n\ge0$ (resp. $d=\pi^{-n}$ for $n<0$) gives $\operatorname{ord}_x(g)=n-0=n$ (resp. $0-(-n)=n$), the valuation. In general, if $g\in R$ then $d=1$ gives $\operatorname{ord}_x(g)=\ell_R(R/gR)$, and if $g^{-1}\in R$ then $d=g^{-1}$ gives $\operatorname{ord}_x(g)=-\ell_R(R/g^{-1}R)$; so this is the usual principal-divisor multiplicity.

(0.5) Finiteness of the support. Write $g=a/b$ on a non-empty affine open $V=\operatorname{Spec}A\subset X$ with $0\ne a,b\in A$. If $\mathfrak p\in V^{(1)}$ satisfies $a,b\notin\mathfrak p$, then $g\in A_{\mathfrak p}^{\times}=\mathcal O_{X,x}^{\times}$, and then $d=1$ gives $\operatorname{ord}_x(g)=0$. By Krull's principal ideal theorem the height-one primes containing $a$ (resp. $b$) are exactly the finitely many minimal primes of $(a)$ (resp. $(b)$). The complement $X\setminus V$ is closed Noetherian, hence has finitely many irreducible components, so contains only finitely many points of $X^{(1)}$. Thus $\{x\in X^{(1)}:\operatorname{ord}_x(g)\ne0\}$ is finite and
   $\operatorname{div}_X(g):=\sum_{x\in X^{(1)}}\operatorname{ord}_x(g)\,[\overline{\{x\}}]$ is a well-defined element of $Z_{\dim X-1}(X)$.

We also use the standard fact that an integral scheme of finite type over a field is catenary and equidimensional, so for every irreducible closed $Z\subset X$ one has $\operatorname{codim}(Z,X)=\dim X-\dim Z$; in particular $x\in X^{(1)}$ iff $\dim\overline{\{x\}}=\dim X-1$.

=====================================================================
STEP 1. The generic fibre $W$.

(1.1) Underlying space. For any morphism $f:X\to Y$ and any $y\in Y$, the fibre $X\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)$ has underlying space homeomorphic to $f^{-1}(\{y\})$ with the subspace topology: on affines $Y=\operatorname{Spec}R$, $X=\operatorname{Spec}B$, $y\leftrightarrow\mathfrak p$, the fibre is $\operatorname{Spec}(S^{-1}(B/\mathfrak pB))$ with $S=R\setminus\mathfrak p$, whose primes are exactly the $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}B$ with $\mathfrak q\supset\mathfrak pB$ and $\mathfrak q\cap S=\emptyset$, i.e. $\mathfrak q\cap R=\mathfrak p$, and the closed sets match the subspace topology. Applying this to $\mathcal W\to\mathbb P^1_k$ and $y=\eta$, we identify
   $|W|=\{w\in|\mathcal W|:f(w)=\eta\}$ with the subspace topology, and for $w\in W$, $\overline{\{w\}}^{\,W}=\overline{\{w\}}^{\,\mathcal W}\cap W$.

(1.2) Affine description. Since $f$ is dominant, $f^{-1}(\mathbb A^1_u)$ and $f^{-1}(\mathbb A^1_{1/u})$ are non-empty open subsets covering $\mathcal W$; their affine opens form a basis of $\mathcal W$. For such an affine $V=\operatorname{Spec}A\subset f^{-1}(\mathbb A^1_u)$, the map $k[u]\to A$ is injective (its kernel is a prime; if non-zero it is generated by an irreducible non-constant $h(u)$, and then $V\subset f^{-1}(V(h))$, a proper closed subset, contradicting that the non-empty open $V$ of the irreducible space $\mathcal W$ is dense). With $S=k[u]\setminus\{0\}$ we get
   $V\cap W=V\times_{\mathbb P^1_k}\operatorname{Spec}K=\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_{k[u]}S^{-1}k[u])=\operatorname{Spec}S^{-1}A$,
and $S^{-1}A$ is a finitely generated $K$-algebra (the $k$-algebra generators of $A$ generate it over $K$, since $1/s\in K$ for $s\in S$). Hence $W$ is of finite type over $K$. If $w\in V\cap W$ corresponds to $\mathfrak q\subset A$, then $f(w)=\eta$ means $\mathfrak q\cap k[u]=(0)$, i.e. $\mathfrak q\cap S=\emptyset$, so the elements of $S$ are already units of $A_{\mathfrak q}$, and localisation is transitive:
   $\mathcal O_{W,w}=(S^{-1}A)_{S^{-1}\mathfrak q}\cong S^{-1}(A_{\mathfrak q})=A_{\mathfrak q}=\mathcal O_{\mathcal W,w}$   (canonical).

(1.3) $W$ is integral, and $k(W)=k(\mathcal W)$. Let $\xi$ be the generic point of $\mathcal W$. Since $f$ is dominant, $\overline{\{f(\xi)\}}\supset f(\overline{\{\xi\}})=f(\mathcal W)$ is dense, so $f(\xi)=\eta$ and $\xi\in W$; in particular $W\ne\emptyset$. Every non-empty open of $W$ is $U\cap W$ with $U\subset\mathcal W$ open and meeting $W$, hence $U\ne\emptyset$, hence $\xi\in U$; so $\{\xi\}$ is dense in $W$ and $W$ is irreducible. By (1.2) every local ring of $W$ is a local ring of the integral scheme $\mathcal W$, hence a domain, so $W$ is reduced. Thus $W$ is integral, with generic point $\xi$, and
   $k(W)=\mathcal O_{W,\xi}\cong\mathcal O_{\mathcal W,\xi}=k(\mathcal W)$.
This canonical identification is what allows us to regard $g\in k(\mathcal W)^{\times}$ as an element of $k(W)^{\times}$; equivalently, on affines, $\operatorname{Frac}(S^{-1}A)=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ because $A\subset S^{-1}A\subset\operatorname{Frac}A$ and $S^{-1}A$ is a domain.

(1.4) Dimension. By Noether normalization, for an integral scheme of finite type over a field, dimension equals the transcendence degree of the function field. Hence
   $\dim W=\operatorname{trdeg}_K k(W)=\operatorname{trdeg}_K k(\mathcal W)=\operatorname{trdeg}_k k(\mathcal W)-\operatorname{trdeg}_k K=\dim\mathcal W-1$,
using $\operatorname{trdeg}_k K=1$.

(1.5) The same argument applies verbatim to any integral closed subscheme $T\subset\mathcal W$ with $f(T)$ dense (then $T\to\mathbb P^1_k$ is dominant, and $T$ is integral of finite type over $k$): $T^\eta:=T\times_{\mathbb P^1_k}\operatorname{Spec}K$ is integral of dimension $\dim T-1$, with function field $k(T)$, and it is a closed subscheme of $W$ (base change of the closed immersion $T\hookrightarrow\mathcal W$). Its fundamental cycle is therefore, by definition, the reduced closed subscheme $|T^\eta|_{\mathrm{red}}$ with coefficient $1$; since $T^\eta$ is integral it is already reduced, and its generic point is the generic point of $T$. Thus the notation $[T^\eta]$ in the statement is well defined.

=====================================================================
STEP 2. Codimension-one points of $W$ are exactly the horizontal codimension-one points of $\mathcal W$.

Let $w\in W$ and let $Z_w:=\overline{\{w\}}^{\,\mathcal W}$, integral. Since $f(w)=\eta$, $\overline{f(Z_w)}\supset\overline{\{\eta\}}=\mathbb P^1_k$, so $Z_w\to\mathbb P^1_k$ is dominant and (1.5) applies to $T=Z_w$. By (1.1),
   $\overline{\{w\}}^{\,W}=Z_w\cap W=|Z_w^\eta|$,
so by (1.5) and (1.4),
   $\dim\overline{\{w\}}^{\,W}=\dim Z_w^\eta=\dim Z_w-1$.
Therefore, using the codimension formula of Step 0 for the varieties $W$ over $K$ and $\mathcal W$ over $k$,
   $w\in W^{(1)}\iff\dim\overline{\{w\}}^{\,W}=\dim W-1\iff\dim Z_w-1=\dim\mathcal W-2\iff\dim Z_w=\dim\mathcal W-1\iff w\in\mathcal W^{(1)}$.
Thus the inclusion $W\hookrightarrow\mathcal W$ identifies $W^{(1)}$ bijectively with $\{x\in\mathcal W^{(1)}:f(x)=\eta\}$, the bijection being the identity on underlying points.

Concretely, on an affine $V=\operatorname{Spec}A$ as in (1.2), primes of $S^{-1}A$ are the $S^{-1}\mathfrak p$ with $\mathfrak p\cap S=\emptyset$, and since every chain ending at $\mathfrak p$ consists of primes contained in $\mathfrak p$ and hence disjoint from $S$, one has $\operatorname{ht}(S^{-1}\mathfrak p)=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)$; and $\mathfrak p\cap S=\emptyset\iff\mathfrak p\cap k[u]=(0)\iff$ the point maps to $\eta$. This is the same bijection.

Moreover, for $x\in\mathcal W^{(1)}$ with $f(x)=\eta$, the closure of the corresponding $y\in W^{(1)}$ is, on $V=\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $x\leftrightarrow\mathfrak p$,
   $\overline{\{y\}}^{\,W}=V(S^{-1}\mathfrak p)_{\mathrm{red}}=\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(S^{-1}(A/\mathfrak p)\bigr)_{\mathrm{red}}=\operatorname{Spec}S^{-1}(A/\mathfrak p)$
(a domain, so reduced), and this is precisely the scheme $\bar x\times_{\mathbb P^1_k}\operatorname{Spec}K=\operatorname{Spec}\bigl((A/\mathfrak p)\otimes_{k[u]}K\bigr)=\operatorname{Spec}S^{-1}(A/\mathfrak p)$. Hence, as cycles on $W$,
   $[\bar x^{\,\eta}]=[\overline{\{y\}}^{\,W}]$, with coefficient $1$ on both sides,
and by (1.5) each has dimension $\dim\bar x-1=(\dim\mathcal W-1)-1=\dim\mathcal W-2=\dim W-1$.

=====================================================================
STEP 3. Equality of the coefficients.

Let $x\in\mathcal W^{(1)}$ with $f(x)=\eta$, and let $y\in W^{(1)}$ be the corresponding point. On $V=\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $x\leftrightarrow\mathfrak p$ we have, exactly as in (1.2) (using $S\cap\mathfrak p=\emptyset$),
   $\mathcal O_{\mathcal W,x}=A_{\mathfrak p}\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }(S^{-1}A)_{S^{-1}\mathfrak p}=\mathcal O_{W,y}$,
the map being $a/t\mapsto(a/1)/(t/1)$. Under the identifications $\operatorname{Frac}A_{\mathfrak p}=k(\mathcal W)$ and $\operatorname{Frac}(S^{-1}A)_{S^{-1}\mathfrak p}=k(W)$ of Step 1.3 this isomorphism is the identity on $\operatorname{Frac}A$; in particular it carries $g\in k(\mathcal W)^{\times}$ to $g\in k(W)^{\times}$. By the functoriality (0.3) of $\operatorname{ord}$, which shows that $\operatorname{ord}$ is computed from the local ring and the element of its fraction field alone,
   $\operatorname{ord}^{\mathcal W}_x(g)=\operatorname{ord}^{W}_y(g)$.

Now assemble, using (0.5) for finiteness, the definition of $\operatorname{div}$, the bijection of Step 2 and the equality of coefficients just proved:
   $\operatorname{div}_W(g)=\sum_{y\in W^{(1)}}\operatorname{ord}^{W}_y(g)\,[\overline{\{y\}}^{\,W}] =\sum_{\substack{x\in\mathcal W^{(1)}\\ f(x)=\eta}}\operatorname{ord}^{\mathcal W}_x(g)\,[\bar x^{\,\eta}]$,
term by term. Both sides are cycles of pure dimension $\dim W-1=\dim\mathcal W-2$ on $W$, by Step 2, so the equality takes place in $Z_{\dim\mathcal W-2}(W)$, as claimed.

=====================================================================
STEP 4. Edge cases.

(i) $\dim\mathcal W=1$. Then $\dim W=0$ by (1.4); an integral $0$-dimensional $K$-scheme of finite type has no codimension-one points (its generic point has codimension $0$), so $W^{(1)}=\emptyset$, and by the bijection of Step 2 no codimension-one point of $\mathcal W$ maps to $\eta$ (equivalently: a closed point of a curve of finite type over $k$ maps to a closed point of $\mathbb P^1_k$, never to $\eta$). Both sides of the asserted equality are then the empty sum, i.e. the zero cycle in $Z_{-1}(W)=0$.
(ii) $g\in k^{\times}$. Then $g$ is a unit in every local ring, so $d=1$ gives $\operatorname{ord}=0$ at every codimension-one point on both sides, and both cycles are $0$.
(iii) If $x\in\mathcal W^{(1)}$ maps to a closed point of $\mathbb P^1_k$, then $x\notin W$; such $x$ is excluded from the sum on the left and, being not a point of $W$, does not occur on the right either. This is exactly why only horizontal codimension-one points appear.

This completes the proof. \qed

statement: Let k be a field, let L/k be a field extension, and let t be an indeterminate over k. Write S = k[t] \ {0}, viewed as a multiplicative subset of L[t]. Then the canonical homomorphism S^{-1}L[t] → L ⊗_k k(t) sending a/s (a ∈ L[t], s ∈ S) to a ⊗ (1/s) is an isomorphism. Consequently L ⊗_k k(t) is an integral domain whose fraction field is L(t) := Frac(L[t]), and the canonical homomorphisms L → L ⊗_k k(t) and k(t) → L ⊗_k k(t) are injective, so that L(t) contains both L and k(t).
proof:
We write S = k[t] \ {0}. Note first that S is a multiplicative subset of L[t]: it contains 1, it is closed under multiplication (k[t] is a ring, and a product of nonzero polynomials over the field k is nonzero), and 0 \notin S. Also k(t) = S^{-1}k[t] by definition of the rational function field.

Notation. For a ring homomorphism we write A^\times for the unit group. The k-algebra A := L \otimes_k k(t) has commuting k-algebra maps i_L : L \to A, a \mapsto a \otimes 1, and i_K : k(t) \to A, x \mapsto 1 \otimes x. Since they commute, the universal property of the polynomial ring gives a unique k-algebra homomorphism
  \beta : L[t] \longrightarrow A, \qquad \beta\Big(\textstyle\sum_i a_i t^i\Big) = \sum_i (a_i \otimes 1)(1 \otimes t)^i = \sum_i a_i \otimes t^i .
For s = \sum_i c_i t^i \in k[t] (c_i \in k) we have, using balancing of the tensor product over k (c_i \otimes t^i = (c_i\cdot 1)\otimes t^i = 1 \otimes (c_i t^i)),
  \beta(s) = \sum_i c_i \otimes t^i = 1 \otimes \Big(\sum_i c_i t^i\Big) = 1 \otimes s .
In the statement of the lemma, an expression a \otimes (1/s) with a \in L[t] is shorthand for \beta(a)\cdot(1\otimes(1/s)); when a \in L it is literally the pure tensor.

STEP 1: Construction of \psi : S^{-1}L[t] \to L \otimes_k k(t).
For s \in S \subset k[t] we have \beta(s) = 1\otimes s, which is a unit of A with inverse 1\otimes(1/s), since (1\otimes s)(1\otimes(1/s)) = 1\otimes(s\cdot 1/s) = 1\otimes 1 = 1_A. Thus \beta(S) \subset A^\times. By the universal property of localization there is a unique ring homomorphism
  \psi : S^{-1}L[t] \longrightarrow A, \qquad \psi(a/s) = \beta(a)\,(1\otimes(1/s)) \ \ (\text{denoted } a\otimes(1/s)).
Explicitly, for a = \sum_i a_i t^i one gets \psi(a/s) = \sum_i a_i \otimes (t^i/s), because (a_i\otimes t^i)(1\otimes(1/s)) = a_i\otimes(t^i/s).

STEP 2: Construction of \theta : L \otimes_k k(t) \to S^{-1}L[t].
Define B : L \times k(t) \to S^{-1}L[t] as follows: for a \in L and x \in k(t), choose a representation x = f/g with f \in k[t], g \in S, and put B(a,x) := (a f)/g, where af is the product taken in L[t].

Well-definedness in the second variable: if f/g = f'/g' in k(t) = Frac(k[t]), then fg' = f'g in k[t], hence also in L[t]. Therefore (af)g' = (af')g in L[t], which is exactly the equality (af)/g = (af')/g' in S^{-1}L[t].

k-bilinearity:
(i) B(a+a', f/g) = ((a+a')f)/g = (af + a'f)/g = (af)/g + (a'f)/g = B(a,f/g) + B(a',f/g).
(ii) With x = f/g and y = f'/g' we have x+y = (fg'+f'g)/(gg'), so
     B(a, x+y) = (a(fg'+f'g))/(gg') = (afg')/(gg') + (af'g)/(gg') = (af)/g + (af')/g' = B(a,x)+B(a,y),
     where (afg')/(gg') = (af)/g holds because (afg')\cdot g = (af)\cdot(gg') in L[t].
(iii) For \lambda \in k: \lambda\cdot(f/g) = (\lambda f)/g in k(t), and B(\lambda a, f/g) = ((\lambda a)f)/g = (a(\lambda f))/g = B(a, f/g)\text{ scaled} = B(a, \lambda\cdot f/g).
By the universal property of the tensor product there is a unique additive homomorphism
  \theta : L\otimes_k k(t) \longrightarrow S^{-1}L[t], \qquad \theta(a\otimes x) = B(a,x),
so \theta(a\otimes(f/g)) = (af)/g.

STEP 3: \psi and \theta are mutually inverse.
Both maps are additive, so it suffices to check on generating sets.

(a) For a/s \in S^{-1}L[t], writing a = \sum_i a_i t^i:
  \theta(\psi(a/s)) = \theta\Big(\sum_i a_i\otimes(t^i/s)\Big) = \sum_i (a_i t^i)/s = a/s .

(b) For a pure tensor a\otimes(f/g) \in L\otimes_k k(t) (a\in L, f\in k[t], g\in S):
  \psi(\theta(a\otimes(f/g))) = \psi\big((af)/g\big) = \beta(af)\,(1\otimes(1/g)) = \beta(a)\beta(f)\,(1\otimes(1/g)),
using that \beta is a ring homomorphism. Since f \in k[t], Step 1's computation gives \beta(f) = 1\otimes f, hence
  \psi(\theta(a\otimes(f/g))) = \beta(a)\,(1\otimes f)(1\otimes(1/g)) = \beta(a)\,(1\otimes(f/g)) = (a\otimes 1)(1\otimes(f/g)) = a\otimes(f/g),
where the last equality is the definition of multiplication in the tensor product of k-algebras. Since pure tensors additively generate L\otimes_k k(t), \psi\circ\theta = \mathrm{id}.

Thus \psi is a bijection with inverse \theta; since \psi is a ring homomorphism, \theta is a ring homomorphism as well, and \psi is an isomorphism of rings (equivalently of k-algebras).

STEP 4: L\otimes_k k(t) is an integral domain.
It suffices to prove S^{-1}L[t] is a domain. L[t] is a domain: for nonzero p,q \in L[t], deg(pq) = deg p + deg q (the leading coefficient is the product of leading coefficients, nonzero in the field L), so pq \neq 0. Now let (a/s),(b/r) \in S^{-1}L[t] with (a/s)(b/r) = 0. Then (ab)/(sr) = 0, so by the definition of equality in a localization there is h \in S with h\cdot ab = 0 in L[t]. As h \neq 0 and L[t] is a domain, ab = 0, hence a = 0 or b = 0, i.e. a/s = 0 or b/r = 0. So S^{-1}L[t] is an integral domain.

STEP 5: The canonical maps L \to L\otimes_k k(t) and k(t) \to L\otimes_k k(t) are injective.
Via the isomorphism \psi these maps become:
  \iota_L : L \to S^{-1}L[t], \ \lambda \mapsto \lambda/1, \qquad \iota_K : k(t) \to S^{-1}L[t], \ f/g \mapsto f/g .
Both are well-defined ring homomorphisms (for \iota_K: if f/g = f'/g' in k(t) then fg'=f'g in k[t] \subset L[t], hence f/g = f'/g' in S^{-1}L[t]).
Injectivity of \iota_L: \lambda/1 = 0 in S^{-1}L[t] iff there exists s \in S with s\cdot\lambda = 0 in L[t]; since s \neq 0 and L[t] is a domain, \lambda = 0.
Injectivity of \iota_K: f/g = 0 in S^{-1}L[t] iff there exists s\in S with s f = 0 in L[t]; since s\neq 0 and L[t] is a domain, f = 0 in k[t], i.e. f/g = 0 in k(t).

STEP 6: The fraction field of S^{-1}L[t] is L(t) := Frac(L[t]).
Let F := Frac(L[t]). The inclusion \iota : L[t] \hookrightarrow F sends S into F^\times, so it induces a ring homomorphism
  \varphi : S^{-1}L[t] \longrightarrow F, \qquad \varphi(a/s) = \iota(a)/\iota(s),
which is injective: a/s = 0 in F iff \iota(a) = 0 in L[t] (as \iota(s)\neq 0 and F is a field) iff a = 0 iff a/s = 0 in S^{-1}L[t].
By the universal property of the fraction field, \varphi extends to a field homomorphism
  \Phi : \mathrm{Frac}(S^{-1}L[t]) \longrightarrow F, \qquad \Phi(r/r') = \varphi(r)/\varphi(r'),
well defined because \varphi(r') \neq 0 for r' \neq 0. \Phi is injective (a homomorphism of fields with \Phi(1)=1).
For surjectivity, let E := \mathrm{im}(\Phi); E is a subfield of F. We claim E = F. First, E contains \varphi(S^{-1}L[t]); in particular it contains \varphi(\lambda/1) = \lambda/1 for all \lambda \in L, and it contains \varphi(f/g) = f/g for all f \in k[t], g \in S, so it contains the image of k(t) and in particular t/1. The subring of F generated by \{\lambda/1 : \lambda\in L\} \cup \{t^n/1 : n\ge 0\} contains every \sum_i \lambda_i t^i /1 with \lambda_i \in L, i.e. it contains \iota(L[t]). Hence E, being a field containing that subring, contains the fraction field of \iota(L[t]), which is all of F. Thus E = F and \Phi is an isomorphism.

STEP 7: L(t) contains both L and k(t), compatibly.
The isomorphism \Phi identifies \mathrm{Frac}(L\otimes_k k(t)) with L(t). Under this identification the image of L \subset L\otimes_k k(t) (Step 5) is \{\lambda/1 : \lambda \in L\} \cong L, and the image of k(t) is \{f/g : f\in k[t], g\in S\} \cong k(t); both inclusions were proved injective in Step 5, and directly: \lambda/1 = 0 in L(t) iff \lambda = 0 in L[t], and f/g = 0 in L(t) iff f = 0 in L[t] iff f = 0 in k[t]. Moreover the subfield of L(t) generated by these two copies of L and k(t) is all of L(t): the subring they generate contains every polynomial \sum_i \lambda_i t^i (as \sum_i \lambda_i\cdot t^i with t \in k(t)), hence contains L[t], hence its fraction field contains Frac(L[t]) = L(t). This is the same conclusion reached at the end of Step 6.

All claims of the lemma are established: S^{-1}L[t] \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } L\otimes_k k(t), a/s \mapsto a\otimes(1/s), is an isomorphism; L\otimes_k k(t) is an integral domain with fraction field L(t) = Frac(L[t]); and the canonical maps L \to L\otimes_k k(t) and k(t) \to L\otimes_k k(t) are injective, so that L(t) contains both L and k(t).

statement: Let k be a field, let R be a discrete valuation ring which is a k-algebra, with fraction field K and residue field E, and let Y/k be smooth projective. Write \mathcal{Y} = Y \times_k \operatorname{Spec} R, with generic fibre Y_K = Y \times_k \operatorname{Spec} K and special fibre Y_E = Y \times_k \operatorname{Spec} E. For n \ge 0 let bc_K: CH^n(Y) \to CH^n(Y_K) and bc_E: CH^n(Y) \to CH^n(Y_E) be the flat pullbacks, and let sp: CH^n(Y_K) \to CH^n(Y_E) be the specialization homomorphism that sends an integral closed subscheme W \subset Y_K to i^![\overline{W}], where \overline{W} is the closure of W in \mathcal{Y} and i: Y_E \to \mathcal{Y} is the special fibre. Then sp \circ bc_K = bc_E.
proof:
Proof. Let pi be a uniformizer of R. Since R is a nonzero k-algebra, the structure map k -> R is injective. If a is in k^times, its image in R is a unit, so its image in E=R/(pi) is nonzero. Thus k -> E is injective; similarly k -> K. Hence K and E are flat k-algebras, and bc_K, bc_E are flat pullbacks.

If Y is empty, all Chow groups are zero. Assume Y nonempty. Smooth schemes over a field are regular, and regular Noetherian local rings are domains. Therefore the irreducible components of Y are open and closed. Since Y is projective, it has finitely many components, so Y is a disjoint union of integral open and closed subschemes Y_a. Chow groups decompose as direct sums over this disjoint union, and the maps bc_K, bc_E, and sp respect this decomposition because base change and taking closures preserve open and closed components. Thus it suffices to prove the statement when Y is integral.

Assume now that Y is integral. Both sides of the desired equality are group homomorphisms: bc_K and bc_E are flat pullbacks, and sp is a homomorphism by the provided lemma dvr_specialization_map. Hence it is enough to prove the equality on the class [W] of an integral closed subscheme W subset Y of codimension n.

We first record a basic equidimensionality fact. Let V be an integral scheme of finite type over k and let F/k be any field extension. Then every irreducible component of V_F has dimension dim V. Indeed, reduce to V=Spec A affine. Let d=dim A and choose a Noether normalization B=k[t_1,...,t_d] -> A which is finite and injective. Since A is a domain, A is torsion-free over B. A finite torsion-free module over a Noetherian domain embeds in a finite free module (choose generators in the fraction field and clear denominators), so there is an injection of B-modules A -> B^r. Tensoring with F over k, which is flat, gives an injection of B_F-modules A_F -> B_F^r. Thus A_F is torsion-free over the domain B_F. Consequently no nonzero element of B_F is contained in a minimal prime of A_F, so every minimal prime p of A_F contracts to (0) in B_F. Since A_F is finite over B_F, dim A_F/p = dim B_F = d. For general V, choose a dense affine open U subset V; every irreducible component of V_F meets U_F in a dense open subset, hence has the same dimension as that component of U_F, which is d by the affine case.

Set W_R = W times_k Spec R, W_K = W times_k Spec K, and W_E = W times_k Spec E. The scheme W_R is a closed subscheme of Ycal with generic fibre W_K and special fibre W_E. We claim that W_R is flat over R. Locally on W, write W=Spec A with A a finitely generated k-algebra. As a k-vector space A is free, and since R is a k-algebra, A tensor_k R is a free R-module. Hence W_R is flat over R.

Because W_R is flat over the DVR R, multiplication by pi is injective on O_{W_R}. Therefore the localization map O_{W_R} -> O_{W_R} tensor_R K is injective, so the scheme-theoretic closure of W_K in W_R, and hence in Ycal, is all of W_R. Also, if p is an associated point of W_R, then p=Ann(x) for some nonzero local section x; injectivity of multiplication by pi gives pi x nonzero, so pi is not in p and p intersect R=(0). Thus every associated point of W_R lies in the generic fibre.

By the equidimensionality fact applied to W and F=K, every irreducible component of W_K has dimension dim W. Since every component of W_R meets the generic fibre and W_R is flat over R, every component of W_R has dimension dim W+1. Thus W_R is equidimensional of codimension n in Ycal.

By definition of flat pullback of a fundamental cycle, bc_K([W]) is represented on Y_K by the sum over the generic points xi of the irreducible components of W_K of length_{O_{W_K,xi}}(O_{W_K,xi}) [xi]. For such a point xi, xi is an associated point of W_R and pi is invertible in O_{W_R,xi}; hence O_{W_K,xi}=O_{W_R,xi}. Taking closures in Ycal, the corresponding cycle is the sum over the generic points xi of the irreducible components of W_R of length_{O_{W_R,xi}}(O_{W_R,xi}) [closure xi]; denote this cycle by [W_R].

Now apply sp. By the definition of sp on integral cycles and by linearity (dvr_specialization_map), sp(bc_K([W])) is the refined Gysin pullback of this cycle along i:Y_E -> Ycal. Thus sp(bc_K([W])) = i^![W_R].

The closed immersion i:Y_E -> Ycal is the effective Cartier divisor defined by pi. Since pi is a non-zero-divisor on O_{W_R}, no irreducible component of W_R is contained in Y_E; equivalently, the cycle W_R meets Y_E properly. For a cycle Z meeting an effective Cartier divisor D=V(pi) properly, the refined Gysin pullback along D is the Cartier divisor cycle div_Z(D). In local terms, if Z=Spec A and pi is a non-zero-divisor on A, then i^![Z] = sum over eta in V(pi)^{(0)} of length_{A_eta}(A_eta/pi A_eta) [eta], where eta runs over the codimension-one points of Z lying in D. This is the codimension-one Cartier-divisor computation of refined Gysin (equivalently, the derived tensor product A tensor^L_R R/(pi) has only H_0=A/(pi)). Applying this to Z=W_R gives sp(bc_K([W])) = sum over eta of length_{O_{W_R,eta}}(O_{W_R,eta}/pi) [eta], where eta runs over the generic points of the irreducible components of W_E.

But W_E is exactly the closed subscheme of W_R defined by pi, so O_{W_R,eta}/pi = O_{W_E,eta}. Therefore sp(bc_K([W])) = sum over eta of length_{O_{W_E,eta}}(O_{W_E,eta}) [eta].

On the other hand, by the same definition of flat pullback along the field extension E/k, bc_E([W]) is represented on Y_E by the sum over the generic points eta of the irreducible components of W_E of length_{O_{W_E,eta}}(O_{W_E,eta}) [eta]. Hence sp(bc_K([W]))=bc_E([W]) as cycles, and therefore as Chow classes.

Since both sides are homomorphisms and the equality holds on generators [W], we conclude sp composed with bc_K equals bc_E on CH^n(Y). This completes the proof.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let p_1, p_2: X\times_k X \to X be the two projections, let L/k be a field extension, and let \alpha \in CH^d(X\times_k X) have zero image in CH^d(X_L\times_L X_L). Then for every integer i with 0 \le i \le d, every \beta \in CH^i(X) and every \gamma \in CH^{d-i}(X), the intersection number \deg(p_1^*\beta \cdot p_2^*\gamma \cdot \alpha) is zero, where \deg: CH_0(X\times_k X) \to \mathbb{Z} is the degree of a zero-cycle.
proof:
Setup. Put W := X \times_k X, with projections p_1, p_2 : W \to X. Since X/k is smooth projective of pure dimension d, W/k is smooth projective of pure dimension 2d; in particular W is integral, regular, and proper over k, so its Chow groups carry the graded-commutative intersection product (the Fulton--MacPherson/DLZ product on a smooth variety) with CH^{2d}(W) = CH_0(W). The structure morphism X \to \operatorname{Spec} k is smooth of relative dimension d, hence flat; p_1 (resp. p_2) is the base change of it by p_2 : W \to X (resp. p_1), hence p_1 and p_2 are flat of relative dimension d. Flat pullback preserves codimension (Fulton, Intersection Theory, Ch. 1.7), so it gives homomorphisms p_1^* : CH^i(X) \to CH^i(W) and p_2^* : CH^{d-i}(X) \to CH^{d-i}(W). Fix i with 0 \le i \le d, \beta \in CH^i(X), \gamma \in CH^{d-i}(X), and set
\[ \xi \;:=\; p_1^*\beta \,\cdot\, p_2^*\gamma \,\cdot\, \alpha \;\in\; CH^{i+(d-i)+d}(W) = CH^{2d}(W) = CH_0(W), \]
the product being taken in the Chow ring of W. The number whose vanishing we must prove is exactly \deg(\xi) under the degree homomorphism \deg : CH_0(W) \to \mathbb Z, so it suffices to show \xi has degree 0.

Step 1 (the degree homomorphism). We use the standard degree map on zero-cycles of a scheme of finite type over a field (Fulton, Ch. 1.1 and Ex. 1.4.3). Concretely, for a zero-cycle z = \sum_j m_j [w_j] on W, with the m_j \in \mathbb Z and the w_j closed points of W (their residue fields \kappa(w_j) are finite over k since W is of finite type over k, by Zariski's lemma), one defines
\[ \deg(z) \;:=\; \sum_j m_j\,[\kappa(w_j):k]. \]
(The coefficients m_j are the coefficients of the cycle; a length interpretation, if desired, is \operatorname{length}_{\mathcal O_{Z,w_j}}\mathcal O_{Z,w_j} for the zero-dimensional closed subscheme Z whose fundamental cycle is being measured, not the length of the ambient local ring \mathcal O_{W,w_j}.) This assignment is \mathbb Z-linear on Z_0(W) and vanishes on rationally equivalent zero-cycles: by the usual reduction on divisors it is enough to check that \deg(\operatorname{div}(r)) = 0 for every integral closed subscheme T \subset W of dimension 1 and every r \in k(T)^\times. Since W is proper over k, so is T; taking the normalization \nu : \widetilde T \to T, a finite birational morphism of proper curves over k, one has \deg(\operatorname{div}(r)) = \sum_{x \in \widetilde T^{(0)}} \operatorname{ord}_x(\nu^* r)\,[\kappa(x):k] = 0 by the product formula on the proper curve \widetilde T. Hence deg descends to a well-defined group homomorphism \deg : CH_0(W) \to \mathbb Z. We only use this standard fact; it is not re-derived from any finiteness assertion about function fields of curves (which have transcendence degree 1 over k).

Step 2 (torsion-freeness of the kernel). By hypothesis \alpha \in CH^d(X \times_k X) maps to 0 in CH^d(X_L \times_L X_L), and X/k is smooth projective of dimension d with L/k a field extension. Applying the proved lemma kernel_classes_are_torsion (Spark) to X/k, L/k and \alpha, there exists an integer n \ge 1 such that
\[ n \cdot \alpha = 0 \quad\text{in } CH^d(W). \]

Step 3 (multiplying by the fixed external class). The intersection product on CH^*(W) is \mathbb Z-bilinear, so for u := p_1^*\beta \cdot p_2^*\gamma \in CH^d(W) we have n \cdot (u \cdot \alpha) = u \cdot (n \cdot \alpha). Indeed, writing the product as the image of the bilinear map CH^d(W) \times CH^d(W) \to CH^{2d}(W), bilinearity gives u\cdot(n\alpha) = u\cdot(\alpha+\cdots+\alpha) = u\cdot\alpha+\cdots+u\cdot\alpha = n\cdot(u\cdot\alpha). Moreover u \cdot 0 = 0: by distributivity u\cdot 0 = u\cdot(0+0) = u\cdot 0 + u\cdot 0, and cancelling in the abelian group CH^{2d}(W) yields u\cdot 0 = 0. Therefore
\[ n \cdot \xi \;=\; n\cdot(u\cdot\alpha) \;=\; u\cdot(n\cdot\alpha) \;=\; u \cdot 0 \;=\; 0 \quad\text{in } CH_0(W). \]
