Step 4 (conclusion). The homomorphism deg is \mathbb Z-linear, so 0 = \deg(n\cdot\xi) = n\cdot\deg(\xi) in \mathbb Z. Since n \ge 1 and \mathbb Z is torsion-free, \deg(\xi) = 0. Unwinding the definition of \xi, this is precisely
\[ \deg\bigl(p_1^*\beta \cdot p_2^*\gamma \cdot \alpha\bigr) = 0 \in \mathbb Z, \]
which is the required statement.

Boundary cases. No separate treatment is needed: if i = 0 then \beta \in CH^0(X) = \mathbb Z\cdot[X] and p_1^*\beta is a multiple of the unit [W], so the same computation applies; if i = d then \gamma \in CH^0(X) and p_2^*\gamma is a multiple of [W]; and if d = 0 then i = 0, W = \operatorname{Spec}(K) for a field K finite over k when X is a point-like variety of dimension 0, CH^0(W) = CH_0(W), and Steps 2--4 read literally the same way (flatness of p_1, p_2 of relative dimension 0 is immediate). In every case the argument above gives the vanishing of the degree.

Thus for all 0 \le i \le d, all \beta \in CH^i(X) and all \gamma \in CH^{d-i}(X), the intersection number \deg(p_1^*\beta \cdot p_2^*\gamma \cdot \alpha) is zero. The only external input beyond the standard properties of the Chow ring and the degree map on a scheme of finite type over a field is the proved lemma kernel_classes_are_torsion.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let L/k be a field extension, let \Delta \subset X\times_k X be the diagonal, and let \alpha \in CH^d(X\times_k X) have zero image in CH^d(X_L\times_L X_L). If there exist an integer N \ge 1 and a d-dimensional cycle representative Z of \alpha^{\circ N} such that \dim(\mathrm{Supp}(Z)\setminus \Delta) \le d-1, then \alpha^{\circ M} = 0 for some M \ge 1, where powers are taken for composition of correspondences.
proof:
Write R := CH^d(X \times_k X), and equip R with the product of correspondences
  \gamma \circ \delta := p_{13*}(p_{12}^*\gamma \cdot p_{23}^*\delta),
p_{12},p_{23},p_{13}: X^3 \to X\times_k X the three projections. This product is associative and bilinear (it is the ring structure of correspondences on X; associativity is part of the ring structure invoked in Spark/lemma_46, which asserts that base change is a *ring* homomorphism for this product). Consequently all powers \gamma^{\circ m} (m \ge 1) are well defined, independently of bracketing, and (\gamma^{\circ m})^{\circ r} = \gamma^{\circ mr} for all m,r \ge 1.

Let bc: CH^d(X\times_k X) \to CH^d(X_L\times_L X_L) be the flat base-change homomorphism (flat pullback along X_L\times_L X_L \to X\times_k X, which is the base change of Spec L \to Spec k; note X_L\times_L X_L \cong (X\times_k X)\times_k Spec L since fibre products commute with base change). By Spark/lemma_46, bc is a ring homomorphism for the product \circ; in particular
  bc(\gamma\circ\delta) = bc(\gamma)\circ bc(\delta)  for all \gamma,\delta\in R.   (1)

Set K := ker(bc) and put \beta := \alpha^{\circ N} \in R.

Step 1: \beta \in K. Since bc is a ring homomorphism, (1) gives by induction on m that bc(\gamma^{\circ m}) = bc(\gamma)^{\circ m} for every m \ge 1. Applying this to \gamma = \alpha and m = N, and using the hypothesis bc(\alpha) = 0,
  bc(\beta) = bc(\alpha^{\circ N}) = bc(\alpha)^{\circ N} = 0^{\circ N} = 0,
where the last equality uses that 0 is an absorbing element for \circ (bilinearity of the product). Hence \beta \in K.

Step 2: the invariant e(\beta) is defined and satisfies e(\beta) \le d-1. For \gamma \in R let e(\gamma) denote the minimum, over all d-dimensional cycle representatives W of \gamma on X\times_k X, of \dim(\mathrm{Supp}(W)\setminus\Delta), with the convention \dim\emptyset = -1. This minimum exists: the collection of d-dimensional cycle representatives of a fixed class is non-empty, and each value \dim(\mathrm{Supp}(W)\setminus\Delta) lies in the finite set \{-1,0,\dots,d\} (as \mathrm{Supp}(W) is a closed subset of the d-dimensional variety X\times_k X of dimension at most d, so its locally closed subset \mathrm{Supp}(W)\setminus\Delta has dimension \le d, and is empty or of some dimension in \{0,\dots,d\}). By hypothesis there exists a d-dimensional cycle representative Z of \alpha^{\circ N} = \beta with \dim(\mathrm{Supp}(Z)\setminus\Delta) \le d-1. Since e(\beta) is the minimum over all such representatives,
  e(\beta) \le \dim(\mathrm{Supp}(Z)\setminus\Delta) \le d-1.
(In particular, if \mathrm{Supp}(Z) \subseteq \Delta then e(\beta) = -1 \le d-1, so the degenerate case d = 0 is also covered.)

Step 3: apply Spark/lemma_53 to \beta. The lemma applies verbatim: X/k is smooth projective of dimension d, L/k is a field extension, \Delta \subset X\times_k X is the diagonal, K = \ker(CH^d(X\times_k X)\to CH^d(X_L\times_L X_L)); and we have shown \beta \in K with e(\beta) \le d-1. Its conclusion is
  \beta^{\circ (d+1)} = 0 \quad\text{in } CH^d(X\times_k X),
where the power is composition of correspondences.

Step 4: conclude nilpotence of \alpha. By associativity of \circ,
  \alpha^{\circ N(d+1)} = (\alpha^{\circ N})^{\circ (d+1)} = \beta^{\circ (d+1)} = 0.
Since N \ge 1 and d+1 \ge 1, the integer M := N(d+1) satisfies M \ge 1. Thus \alpha^{\circ M} = 0 for some M \ge 1, which is exactly the required conclusion.

(No edge case is missed: when d = 0 the hypothesis forces e(\beta) = -1 \le -1 = d-1, Step 3 yields \beta = \beta^{\circ 1} = 0 and one may take M = N = N(d+1); when d \ge 1 the argument above applies unchanged.)
